CHAPTER-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
ANNUAL PLAN 2022-23 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee is pleased to note the trend of increasing allocation to the Ministry, 
which underscores the importance being given to expanding and improving the National 
Highways network across the country. The Committee, however, notes that the Ministry has 
not been able to attract private investment at a similar pace. This is partly the reason for the 
high IEBR component in the last few years which is mainly why the huge debt burden is 
currently being faced by NHAI. The Committee appreciates that the IEBR co mponent has 
been kept to a nominal Rs. 0.01 crore for FY 2022 -23, with the Budgetary support made to 
the Ministry covering for the shortfall in the IEBR component. The Committee, however, feels 
that neither high budgetary support alone, nor high IEBR compo nent will be able to suffice 
the investment requirements for the rapid pace of NH development across the country in the 
long run. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry may work upon 
resolving the apprehensions of the private secto r which are limiting their participation in the 
road infrastructure sector in the last few years, by working in close coordination with the 
concessionaires and financial institutions. 
(Para 24) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 The position with regard to high IEBR component in the last few years and the 
budgetary support made for the shortfall in the IEBR in the current FY has been noted. The 
Committee’s recommendation is to resolve the apprehensions of the private sector which are 
limiting their participation in the road infrastructure sector in the last few years, by working 
in close coordination with the concessionaires and financial institutions. 
1.2 The Ministry has come out with several innovative funding mechanisms to increase 
private investments after 20 14. During 2007 -14, private investments were confined to only 
BOT projects. Now, apart from BOT, HAM projects, we are also getting private investments 
through monetization of National Highways under TOT, InvIT (Infrastructure Investment 
Trust) and through SPVs (Special Purpose Vehicles). The private investments during 2007-14 
were about Rs. 1,08,481 crores, which came only from BOT projects. The private 
investments has increased to Rs. 1,69,214 crores during 2014 -21 from BOT, HAM, TOT and 
SPV. 
1.3 Further a dditional steps have been taken to resolve apprehensions of the private 
sector, including but not limited to: 
   Resolving Stuck projects  – NHAI has implemented a Stuck Projects policy 
and is trying to resolve pending disputes through one -time settlement process. Through 
this process, NHAI hopes to recycle money in the infrastructure space and promote 
investment in new projects. NHAI has also introduced a Termination Projects guideline 

3 
 
to standardize the implementation of complex MCA (Model Concession Agreem ent) 
clauses. 
   Encouraging new industry categories – NHAI is encouraging new investor 
classes, like institutional investors, specialized O&M (Operation & Maintenance) 
contractors, specialized tolling agencies etc. in the roads sector to diversify the investor 
base and encourage traditional investors to focus on their core competencies. 
   Amendment in Model Concession Agreements  – NHAI has introduced 
various amendments in the MCAs for BOT (Toll), and Hybrid Annuity to encourage 
private participation and  these amendments have received positive feedback from the 
market. Innovations such as Dispute Resolution Board, sharing of traffic risk etc. have 
been appreciated. Further, NHAI is now committing 90% of Construction Zone in BOT 
Toll projects at Appointed Date. This, when added with the removal of the requirement 
of Capacity Augmentation by the Concessionaire, removes a lot of chances of disputes 
in the Contracts. 
 
 
Vacancies in NHAI 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee is highly distressed to note that despite the recommendations to the 
Ministry year after year, NHAI, with a budgetary allocation of Rs. 134,015 crores, is still 
operating with only 61.2 percent of its sanctioned strength. The Committee fails to 
understand how NHAI will be able to do justice to its mandate with more than a third of its 
sanctioned strength being vacant. The Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry 
should take immediate measures to fill the vacancies in NHAI in shortest possible time. 
(Para 35) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 With regard to the observation of the Committee, it is stated that continuous efforts 
for filling up the vacant posts have been made and after analysing the hindrances in filling up 
of the vacancies, various re medial measures have been undertaken from time to time. The 
following are the few important measures undertaken to fill up the vacant posts and meet the 
manpower requirements arisen from time to time: -  
 During the last two years, recruitment of 499 posts on promotion / Direct Recruitment 
(DR) / Deputation has been undertaken. 
 To overcome shortage of technical manpower and to meet the temporary requirement 
of manpower due to increased workload on account of Bharatmala projects, 449 
Technical personnel in th e category of Site Engineers / Young Professionals have 
been engaged on contract basis. Further action for recruitment of 200 Young 
Professional (Technical) based on GATE Scores is also underway. 
 To keep NHAI as a lean and thin organisation, technical manp ower was being 
engaged on deputation from other organisations and simultaneously, regular intake of 
officers is being undertaken in a phased manner at Deputy Manager level through 
GATE/Engineering Services Examination. 

4 
 
 80 posts of Deputy Manager (Technical ) based on GATE, 2020/2021 scores on DR 
mode completed. 
 69 Deputy Manager (Tech.) in 2022 based on ESE -2020 marks have been selected, 
out of which 31 have already joined. 
 The remaining unfilled vacancies would be filled -up next year based on GATE 
Score/ESE, 2021 marks. 
 Recruitment action for filling up of 193 posts is already underway. 
 In Finance Cadre, recruitment action for filling up 62 posts is underway. However, 
due to stay by the Hon’ble High Court of Odisha, the recruitment for most of these 
posts is held up. 
 The Recruitment Rules (RRs) of Technical and Finance Cadre have been revised and 
fresh recruitment based on the revised RRs has been undertaken. 
 135 vacancies will be filled in 2022 -2023, 2023 -2024 under promotion quota in 
Finance and Technical Cadre. 
 17 posts of Deputy Manager (Fin.) and 02 posts of Jr. Hindi Translator have been 
taken-up for recruitment through National Testing Agency on DR basis. Further, 13 
posts of Asst. Manager (Legal) are proposed to be filled on DR through 
NTA/NLU/BESIL. 
 RRs of Technical Cadre has been revised by the Ministry recently to attract more 
officers of State PWDs having core experience in road sector.

4.2 The Ministry is giving full attention to M&R of NHs and for that the use of Network

4.3 The Ministry is taking up maintenance of completed works of National Highways

maintenance. Long term contract maintenance also includes stretches bid out on Toll, Operate

4.4 It is pertinent to mention in this context that most of the developed countri es have a 
network of developed Highways and Expressways and have almost reached saturation stage; 
they are presently focusing on maintenance of these developed assets; hence expenditure is 
incurred primarily on maintenance of Highways. In India, the Govern ment is presently laying 
emphasis on development of National Highways including Expressways besides maintenance

Further Recommendation/Observation 
4.14 The Committee notes that effectively about Rs. 5,000 crores are being spent 
annually on Maintenance & Repair of National Highways from the budget head of the 
Ministry on account of one portion of M&R being paid out of the  Capital head and 
additional expenditure by NHAI on M&R. It may be noted that Rs. 5,000 crores is still 
effectively just about 2.5 percent of the overall BE 2022 -23 allocation of Rs. 199,107.71 
crores, which is a far cry from the way forward suggested by NITI Aayog to begin with 
earmarking 10 percent of its annual budget for road and highways for maintenance to 
move towards the developed country norm of earmarking 40 per cent to 50 per cent of 
the budget for roads and highways for maintenance. The Committee  understands that 
the requirements of the Indian road sector are different from that of the developed 
countries but this does not mean that maintenance of the NH network of the country 
can be accorded a lower priority than the expansion of the NH network. High quality 
maintenance and repair of the existing network - including frequent monitoring of the 
road quality as well as carrying out preemptive repair works, where needed - will give 
a direct boost to the efforts of the Ministry to minimize the number o f road accidents 
happening on the NH network across the country. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry may spend higher amounts on regular maintenance 
checks of the NH network across the country. 
4.15 The Committee takes note of the variou s measures taken by the Ministry to 
minimize the number of road accidents on National Highways in the country. Given 
the extremely high number of road accidents happening in the country, a large 
percentage of which takes place on National Highways, there i s a pressing need for 
taking remedial measures on a war footing. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry may evolve a robust mechanism to ensure that ample safety provisions are in 
place on the NH network across the country and that periodic checks are made 
without fail, to ensure continued compliance of the required safety provisions 
throughout the NH network. Further, the Committee recommends that once it has 
been ascertained that sufficient progress has been made in the rectification of black 
spots th at have been identified at present, the Ministry / NHAI may review the 
definition of black spots on National Highways to include accident -prone stretches 
where, say, more than 5 fatalities have taken place during the last three years, as 
compared to the pr esent definition of black spots wherein only stretches where more 
than 10 fatalities have taken place during the last three years are considered to be 
black spots. This would allow the Ministry / NHAI to work on the rectification of more 
accident-prone stretches across the country.

5.5 The legislature introduced under Section 29A to the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 
1996 (“the Act”) vide the Amendment Act 3 of 2016. The aforesaid amendment came into 
force with effect from 23.10.2015. Section 29A of the Act further amended in the year 
2019. The net effect of th e above referred two amendments is that in the matter of 
arbitrations, other than International Commercial Arbitration, a time limit for conclusion of 
arbitration proceedings was introduced. Section 29A of the Act, as it stands today, provides 
that an arbi tral tribunal has to publish the award within a period of twelve months  from 
the date of completion of pleadings under Section 29A.

provided under Section 29A(3) that parties by their consent, can extend the period of 
making the award for a furt her period not exceeding six months. If the award is not made 
within the period of one and half years, the mandate of the tribunal shall terminate. 
However, power has been vested in the “Court” to extend the period.

BHARATMALA PARIYOJANA PHASE-I 
Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee is deeply concerned to note that though the original timeline for 
Bharatmala Phase-I targeted its completion by 2021 -22, only 20,632 km (59.28% of total) 
has been awarded while only 7,375 km (21.19% of total ) has been constructed by December, 
2022 out of the overall target of 34,800 km. This has led to the targeted timeline for 
completion now being estimated at FY27 while the estimated cost of BMP Phase -I has almost 
doubled from Rs. 5.35 lakh crores to Rs. 10.63 lakh crores. Considering that the Ministry has 
managed to construct only about 21.19% of the Phase -I length during more than four years 
since the inception of the scheme, the Committee is of the view that the targeted completion 
estimate of FY27 will p rove to be a great challenge to the Ministry. Given the direct 
correlation between delays on project cost and the positive ripple effects that the timely 
completion of BMP Phase -I will have on several inter -linked economic sectors, it is 
necessary that the Ministry undertakes all-out measures to ensure that the revised target for 
completion of BMP Phase -I is met and the bottlenecks being faced by the Ministry in the 
execution of Phase-I so far may be proactively ironed out. 

50 
 
(Para 65) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1 The Phase I of Bharatmala Pariyojana was approved by the CCEA in October 2017 
for development of 34,800 km of National Highway Corridors. Immediately after the 
approval, consultants were appointed to prepare detailed project report (DPRs) for ~20,000 
km in 2017 and 2018. Preparation of a high quality Detailed Project Report requires 12 – 18 
months and completing land acquisition and obtaining all statutory clearances takes another 
12 – 15 months. Accordingly, it could be seen that the implementation of P hase I has been 
proceeding at a rapid pace with 22,352 km awarded (out of 34,800 km) as of April 2022. 
Further, 521 km have been approved by the Competent Authority and are being awarded. In 
addition, preparation of Detailed Project Report is at an advance d stage for all the remaining 
length to be awarded in Phase I of Bharatmala Pariyojana wherein the Land acquisition and 
other pre -construction activity have been taken up and It has been targeted to award the 
balance length in the next two financial years, viz. by FY 2023-24.  
 
6.2 As far as implementation is concerned, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways and 
its implementing agencies constructed ~24,000 km of National Highways (including 
Bharatmala Pariyojana) in FY 2020 -21 & FY 2021-22 at an average pace of ~12,000 km per 
year (33 km per day), which is unprecedented in the history of the country and is significantly 
higher than the annual highway construction in other countries. Further, the program has 
witnessed construction of works of ~9,115 km, with a majority of these works completed are 
4 Lane + National Highway corridors. It is to be noted that the flagship Delhi – Mumbai 
corridor conceptualized in 2018 is targeted to be completed and opened for traffic from June, 
2022 onwards in various stretches. In comparison, some of the world’s largest road 
infrastructure projects like 1,167 Km long Trans-Java road in Indonesia, commenced in 1995, 
took more than 2 decades to get completed in 2019. Similarly, the 217 km long Shin Tom ei 
Expressway in Japan, commissioned in the early 2000s took almost a decade for completion.  
6.3 Further, multiple agencies/steps are required to complete the project and Ministry and 
its implementing agency took multiple steps to expedite award and construction:    
 
a. Revision in scope of DPR consultants to enable deployment of retired revenue 
department officials to support the State Governments in expediting land 
acquisition 
b. Frequent reviews with the State Governments to resolve issues with land 
acquisition and other clearances 
c. Compensation to State Governments for setting up Special Land Acq uisition 
Units with dedicated staff for acquiring land for National Highway projects 
d. Launch of Bhoomi -Rashi portal to digitize the Land Acquisition notification 
process and avoid parking of public funds with the Competent Authority for

approval and publication of Land Acquisition notifications. Further, issues 
pertaining to delays in CALA performance are comprehensively tracked in 

51 
 
review meetings at all levels including at the lev els of Secretary (MoRTH), 
Chairman (NHAI), DG (MoRTH) and Members (NHAI). 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
6.4 The Committee is glad to note that the Ministry of Road Transport and 
Highways and its implementing agencies have constructed about 24,000 km of National 
Highways (including Bharatmala Pariyojana) in FY 2020 -21 & FY 2021 -22 at an 
average pace of about 12,000 km per year (33 km per day), which is unprecedented in 
the history of the country and is significantly higher than the annual highway 
construction in other countries. The Committee takes note of the various steps taken   
by the implementing agency to expedite award and construction of road projects in the 
country. The Committee, however, still feels that having more reasonable targeted 
timeline of completion of road projects would help the Ministry in having more clarity 
in its long -term road infrastructure planning as well as capital allocation. The 
Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry may review the procedure it 
presently follows to estimate the projected completion date of its road projects and give

Maintain NH assets by adopting a maintenance management system (MMS). Earmark 
funds from the Central Road Fund (CRF) for maintenance activities. India should 
begin with earmarking 10 percent of its annual budget for road and highways for

12.  The Committee is surprised to note that the Ministry has sanctioned just 5 R& D 
schemes worth merely Rs. 2.04 crores during the last 3 financial years. For comparison,

differing economies owing to differences in requirements and present focus, the magnitude of 
difference in the importance being given to R&D and related activities points to the need for 
the Ministry to have a major rethink about its missing focus on R&D in the road sector. The 
Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry may strive to sanction more and more 
R&D schemes and work with best global institutions in this field in order to carve out niche 
solutions for the varied problems plaguing the Indian road sector at present. The Committee

16. The Committee observes that the lack of service roads alongside National Highways 
causes inconvenience to local residents and is, at times, the cause of road accidents. The land

should be given the benefits of service roads along National Highways. The Committee feels 
that service roads are an integral part of National Highways and therefore, recommends that 
the Ministry may make it mandatory to have service roads along NHs to the extent possible 
and provisions for the same may be included in the tender document for NH projects. 
(Para 117)  
Reply of the Ministry 
16.1 Service roads are generally provided at the locations wherever inter -mixing of local 
traffic with through traffic is very high resulting in conge stion. Accordingly, provision of 
service roads is made in national highway projects wherever found necessary.  
16.2 With reference to greenfield corridors developed, development of service roads would 
not stay in line with the concept of access -controlled corridors and would diminish the 
benefits of these flagship corridors. However, the Ministry takes up development of 
underpasses along the corridor to ensure un -encumbered movement of local residents with 
additional provisions made as per site requirements. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
16.3  The Committee observes that having service roads directly helps in reducing the 
number of accidents taking place on National Highways. The Ministry, therefore, 
should carry out thorough analysis of the positive i mpact of service roads in terms of 
road safety and thereafter come upon the decision of whether or not to have provisions 
for service roads in a given National Highways project. The Committee further 
recommends that cost should not be the deciding factor w hen considering the 
practicality of having service roads in a NH project and ensuring top-notch level of road 
safety should be the top priority of the Ministry / NHAI.

(ESC), Traction Control etc. in vehicles sold across the country. The Committee furthe r 
recommends that the Ministry may seek higher budgetary allocation under all these 
crucial heads in future so as to enable enhanced focus on the important activities 
carried out under these heads. This would significantly enhance the safety and pace of 
the transportation on the National Highway network across the country.  
(Para 3.14) 
 
 
ANNUAL PLAN 2022-23   
 The Committee notes that effectively about Rs. 5,000 crores are being 
spent annually on Maintenance & Repair of National Highways from the budget head 
of the Ministry on account of one portion of M&R being paid out of the Capital head 
and additional expenditure by NHAI on M&R. It may be noted that Rs. 5,000 crores is 
still effectively just about 2.5 percent of the overall BE 2022 -23 allocation of Rs . 
199,107.71 crores, which is a far cry from the way forward suggested by NITI Aayog to 
begin with earmarking 10 percent of its annual budget for road and highways for 
maintenance to move towards the developed country norm of earmarking 40 per cent to 
50 p er cent of the budget for roads and highways for maintenance. The Committee 
understands that the requirements of the Indian road sector are different from that of 
the developed countries but this does not mean that maintenance of the NH network of 
the coun try can be accorded a lower priority than the expansion of the NH network. 
High quality maintenance and repair of the existing network - including frequent 
monitoring of the road quality as well as carrying out preemptive repair works, where 
needed - will give a direct boost to the efforts of the Ministry to minimize the number of 
road accidents happening on the NH network across the country. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry may spend higher amounts on regular 
maintenance checks of the NH network across the country.  
(Para 4.14) 
 The Committee takes note of the various measures taken by the Ministry 
to minimize the number of road accidents on National Highways in the country. Given 
the extremely high number of road accidents happening i n the country, a large 
percentage of which takes place on National Highways, there is a pressing need for 
taking remedial measures on a war footing. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry may evolve a robust mechanism to ensure that ample safety provis ions are in 
place on the NH network across the country and that periodic checks are made without 
fail, to ensure continued compliance of the required safety provisions throughout the 
NH network. Further, the Committee recommends that once it has been ascer tained 
that sufficient progress has been made in the rectification of black spots that have been 
identified at present, the Ministry / NHAI may review the definition of black spots on 

67 
 
National Highways to include accident-prone stretches where, say, more than 5 fatalities 
have taken place during the last three years, as compared to the present definition of 
black spots wherein only stretches where more than 10 fatalities have taken place 
during the last three years are considered to be black spots. This wou ld allow the 
Ministry / NHAI to work on the rectification of more accident -prone stretches across 
the country.  
(Para 4.15) 
 
NATIONAL HIGHWAYS AUTHORITY OF INDIA 
Vacancies in NHAI 
The Committee is concerned to note that 114 posts out of the 317 ( i.e., 35.96 
percent) sanctioned strength of the Finance Cadre posts of NHAI are lying vacant at 
present. Given the fact that NHAI implements road projects worth thousands of crores, 
it is crucial to have close financial scrutiny of the ongoing projects of NHAI as well as its 
disputes with third parties. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that NHAI 
may take urgent steps to ensure that the vacancies existing in the Finance cadre are 
filled at the earliest.  
(Para 4A.6) 
 
PENDING ARBITRATION CASES 
The Committee notes that almost the same number of cases have been referred 
to CCIE-2 as compared to cases referred to CCIE -1 and CCIE -3 combined, while the 
number of cases resolved by CCIE -2 is much more than the combined number of cases 
resolved by CCIE -1 and C CIE-3. Speedy disposal of disputes between the parties 
(NHAI & the Concessionaire/ Contractor/ Consultant) directly enables speedier 
completion of road projects stuck due to disputes with the concessionaires. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the M inistry may look into difficulties, if any, 
being faced by certain CCIEs in timely resolution of cases and if needed, consider the 
constitution of more CCIEs to enable faster parallel processing of disputes. Further, the 
Committee desires to be apprised of  the number of cases wherein arbitration could not 
be completed within the time limit of 12 months, as stipulated by Section 29A of the 
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, and the number of cases wherein the "Court" 
has extended the period of mandate of the tribunal.  
(Para 5.8) 
 
 
 
BHARATMALA PARIYOJANA PHASE-I 

68 
 
 The Committee is glad to note that the Ministry of Road Transport and 
Highways and its implementing agencies have constructed about 24,000 km of National 
Highways (including Bharatmala Pariyojana) in FY 2020 -21 & FY 2021 -22 at an 
average pace of about 12,0 00 km per year (33 km per day), which is unprecedented in 
the history of the country and is significantly higher than the annual highway 
construction in other countries. The Committee takes note of the various steps taken   
by the implementing agency to ex pedite award and construction of road projects in the 
country. The Committee, however, still feels that having more reasonable targeted 
timeline of completion of road projects would help the Ministry in having more clarity 
in its long -term road infrastruct ure planning as well as capital allocation. The 
Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry may review the procedure it 
presently follows to estimate the projected completion date of its road projects and give 
some consideration to the various hurdles expected to take place in projects.  
(Para 6.4) 
The Committee feels that the Port Connectivity Projects envisaged under the 
Bharatmala Pariyojana will have significant positive impact on the growth of the 
shipping sector in the country. The Committee notes the submission of the Ministry that 
there has been no delay on part of the Ministry for implementation of the Port 
Connectivity Projects under Bharatmala Pariyojana. However, it is evident that the 
Port Connectivity Projects are drastically delayed, even  more so than the overall 
delayed progress of the Bharatmala Pariyojana Phase -I. While the Committee 
appreciates the increased pace of road construction per day in the country and the 
optimistic targeted timelines for ambitious projects, the Committee feel s that the 
Ministry should try to be more realistic while coming up with targeted timelines for 
completion of projects during the planning stage. The Committee, therefore, reiterates 
its ‘Further Recommendation/Observation’ made under para 6.4 of Chapter I II of this 
Report.  
(Para 7.6) 
 
MAINTENANCE AND REPAIR OF NATIONAL HIGHWAYS 
The Committee reiterates its ‘Further Recommendation/Observation’ made 
under para 4.14 of Chapter III of this Report. The Committee further reiterates its 
original recommendation that the Ministry may act upon the way forward suggested by 
NITI Aayog and allocate much higher budgetary allocation than presently done for 
Maintenance & Repair (M&R) of NHs across the country.  
(Para 10.6) 
The Committee reiterates its ‘Further Recommendat ion/Observation’ made 
under para 4.14 of Chapter III of this Report.  
(Para 11.6) 
 

69 
 
RESEARCH, TRAINING, STUDIES AND OTHER ROAD SAFETY SCHEMES  
The Committee is dismayed to note that research schemes amounting to only Rs. 
17.89 crores have been sanctioned by  the Ministry during the last 3 financial years. The 
Committee feels that given the multifaceted, diverse range of issues faced by the Indian 
road sector, a much higher focus needs to be laid on carrying out quality scientific 
research into coming up with possible solutions to the same. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry may undertake a holistic review of the research 
requirements of the Indian road sector and ensure that sufficient budgetary allocations 
are made to carry out the same in the upcoming financial years.  
(Para 12.3) 
The Committee is surprised to note that the issue of trespassing by stray cattle 
and other animals is still under examination by the Ministry. The issue of stray cattle is 
a long -standing one and the Ministry/ NHAI must ensure that suitable measures are 
undertaken to minimize such incidents, in close cooperation with local authorities. 
Issues of negligence on the part of local authorities may be taken up with the State 
Government concerned. Further, the Committe e desires to know whether incidents of 
trespassing by stray animals have also been witnessed on access -controlled highways in 
the country, despite having barriers on either side of the carriage-way.  
(Para 13.2) 
The Committee desires to be apprised of the response furnished by the Ministry 
of Education to the request made by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways for 
inclusion of lessons to spread awareness about good driving habits, traffic laws, Good 
Samaritan Law, etc. at the school level itself.  T he Committee also notes that the reply 
furnished by the Ministry does not make any mention of the estimated date of 
finalization of the Scheme for Cashless Treatment of Road Accident Victims and desires 
to be apprised of the same.  
(Para 14.5) 
 
SCHEME ON WOMEN SAFETY  
The Committee notes the various steps being taken by the Ministry to bolster 
road safety on the NH network in India by means of provision of proper signboards, 
street lights, road safety audit etc. The Committee however desires to be apprised  of the 
mechanism in place to ensure that such safety provisions are well -maintained and that 
their implementation is checked from time to time, not just at the construction stage of 
projects. The Committee further recommends that suitable steps may be tak en to 
enable citizens to report the lack of safety provisions on certain stretches of National 
Highways, through both online and offline mediums.  
(Para 15.7) 
 

70 
 
 
MISCELLANEOUS 
Provisions for service roads 
 The Committee observes that having service roads directly helps in reducing the 
number of accidents taking place on National Highways. The Ministry, therefore, 
should carry out thorough analysis of the positive impact of service roads in terms of 
road safety and thereafter come upon the decision of wheth er or not to have provisions 
for service roads in a given National Highways project. The Committee further 
recommends that cost should not be the deciding factor when considering the 
practicality of having service roads in a NH project and ensuring top-notch level of road 
safety should be the top priority of the Ministry / NHAI.  
(Para 16.3) 
Five Year Vision Plan for Infrastructure Sector 
The Committee notes that the reply furnished by the Ministry does not make any 
mention about the steps taken by the Ministry to strengthen public transport and 
shared mobility through regulatory reforms, and to strengthen connectivity to top 
hundred tourist destinations. Given the rapidly increasing number of vehicles in the 
country as well as to tackle the issue of air  pollution, promoting public transportation is 
the need of the hour. On the other hand, strong road connectivity to top tourist 
destinations in the country has a direct positive effect on the footfall attracted at these 
destinations, thereby increasing eco nomic opportunities. The Committee, therefore, 
desires to be apprised of the action taken by the Ministry to strengthen public transport 
and to improve NH connectivity to top tourist destinations.  
(Para 17.11) 
Driving Training Centres 
The Committee is gla d to note that 213 proposals have been received from 
different States under the one -time assistance scheme for setting up of model Driving 
Training Centres (DTCs) in the country. The Committee, however, notes that the 
Ministry has not furnished information regarding the number of districts in the country 
wherein Driving Training Centres are functional at present and desires to be apprised 
of the same, alongwith plans, if any, to encourage setting up of DTCs in the districts 
wherein DTCs do not exist at present.  
(Para 18.3)

Tourism and Culture deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Tourism on the 
recommendations/observations as contained in its Three Hundred and Eighteenth Report on 
Demands for Grants 2022 -23 of the Ministry of Tourism which was presented to b oth the

respect of all the recommendations/observations contained in the Report. The replies ha ve been

CHAPTER-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
 
II) ANALYSIS OF BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS FOR 2022-23 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. From a perusal of Table No. 2, the Committee is constrained to note that there is a 
substantial underutilization of the budgeted funds during the FY 2021 -22. Against the RE 2021 -
22 allocation of Rs. 969.80 crore, only 47.70% amounting to Rs. 462.55 crore could be spent till 
the 31st January, 2022. It means that the remaining expenditure would have to be squeezed in 
the last two months of FY 2021 -22. Since as per norms stipulated by the Ministry of Finance, 
there is a ceiling o f 25% on expenditure in the last quarter, occurrence of huge savings is a 
certainty. It may be pertinent to mention here that a zero based budgeting exercise which 
requires that budget request be evaluated thoroughly, starting from zero base, is in practic e and 
the financial outlays are earmarked based on factors like past trend of expenditure, stages of 
formulation/implementation of various projects, the pre -projects approvals etc. Therefore, 
savings of Rs. 1056.97 crore vis -à-vis the BE 2021 -22 allocation  not only betrays fiscal 
indiscipline by way of underutilization of the earmarked funds which will have an adverse 
bearing on infrastructure development oriented activities of the Ministry, but is also indicative of 
shortcomings in budgetary planning and m onitoring of the budgeted funds. The Committee 
observes that a resource constrained country like India cannot afford to keep a vast chunk of its 
resources locked up and surrendered towards the end of the financial year. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends  that realistic projection of fund requirements should be given utmost 
priority at the highest level of the Ministry so that the Budget Estimates are formulated with 
application of proper financial yardsticks and large variations between the Budget Estimat es, 
Revised Estimates and Actual Expenditure needs to be avoided. The Ministry must also pay 
attention to streamlining its monitoring mechanism and ensure optimal and more efficient 
deployment and utilization of its financial resources for smooth execution  of its programmes 
within the approved cost and designated timeline. 
(Para 20) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 The observations/recommendations of the Hon‟ble Committee have been taken note of.  
It is submitted that during the financial year 2021 -2022, against the RE allocation of Rs. 969.80 
crores, the Ministry could incur expenditure to the tune of Rs. 803.90 crores, which comes to 

3 
 
 
82.89%. There are a several reasons which led to less expenditure by the Ministry during the first 
two quarters of the financial ye ar. The pandemic situation was still prevailing in the country and 
the implementation of various Schemes of the Ministry was severely affected.  Further, the 
Swadesh Darshan Scheme was under review by the Government and no new projects we re 
sanctioned during the year. The Global Media Publicity was not carried out due to the pandemic 
situation and ban on operation of international commercial flights resulting in  lack of 
international tourism. 
1.2 Major two schemes of the Ministry of Tourism viz. Swadesh Darshan and PRASHAD are 
being implemented by the State/UT Governments and further release of the fund depends based 
on timely utilisation of fund earlier provided.  
1.3 Pursuant to the recommendations of the Committee, suitable instructions were g iven to 
the Program Divisions of the Ministry to apply due diligence while projecting budgetary 
requirements. The Ministry is closely monitoring the expenditure status periodically at the 
highest level.

2. The Committee in its 288 th Report had recommended that to provide relief to the tourism 
and hospitality sector so as to enhance export competitiveness of Indian tourism, the payments 
received by all the tourism and hospitality entities in convertible foreign exchange be considered 
as "deemed export" and exempted from GST and the concept of zero rating be applied to tourism 
foreign exchange earnings. In this connection, the Ministry in its action Taken Notes had stated 
that "…this is a policy decision to be taken by GST Council, a re ference from Ministry of 
Tourism is being made to GST Council in this regard…" The Committee reiterates its 

11 
 
 
recommendation that tourism services provided to foreign tourists in India on receipt of foreign 
exchange should be treated as "deemed export" and s uch transactions should be zero -rated for 
GST without stopping the flow of input credits. 
(Para 69) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 The Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance has examined the matter. The 
comments are submitted as under:   
2.2 Export of Services is defined at section 2(6) of the IGST Act, 2017 as " the supply of any 
service when the supplier of service is located in India; the recipient of service is located outside 
India; the place of supply of service is outside India; the payment for such se rvice has been 
received by supplier of service in convertible foreign exchange...... and the supplier of service 
and the recipient of service are not merely establishments of a distinct person....".  Thus, there 
are few conditions for service to qualify as export. In the issue under consideration, place of 
supply of tour operator service is the place where the service is performed. The place of supply 
of hotel accommodation service is the location of the premise. Accordingly, such services do not 
qualify as export as place of supply is not outside India. 
2.3 Tour operator services supplied to a foreign touri st are also not zero rated as “ zero rated 
supply” means any of the following supplies of goods o r services or both, namely: -(a) export of 
goods or services or both; or (b) supply of goods or services or both to a special Economic Zone 
developer or a special Economic Zone developer or a special Economic Zone unit"  (Section 16 
of IGST Act, 2017 refers). 
2.4 Only supply of goods manufactured in India to certain specific recipients are classified 
as deemed exports under section 147 of the CGST Act , 2017 . “Deemed exports ” means such 
supplies of goods as may be notified under Section 147. ( Section 2(39) of the CGST Act, 2017 
refers). 
2.5 The GST Council in its 47 th meeting held on 28 th and 29th June, 2022 has recommended 
relief to the tour operators by recommending the foreign component of a tour provided to foreign 
tourist (where such tour involved both dom estic and foreign component) would not attract GST. 
The recommendation would be prospective and come into effect from the 18th July, 2022.

III) CONTRIBUTION OF TOURISM TO GDP 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee notes that as per the World Travel and Tourism Council (WTTC), prior to 
the COVID -19 pandemic, Travel and Tourism accounted for 10.4% of global GDP. In many 
parts of the world, tourism is a major engine of growth. The Committee in its 275 th Report 
presented to the Parliament on the 3 rd March, 2020 had noted that the contribution of tourism to 
national GDP was over 10% for most countries where tourism happens to be the main driver of 
national economy. However, in India which has unique endowments of biodiversity, forests, 
rivers, its rich culture and heritage and many World Heritage sites, the tourism sector has not 

22 
 
 
proved to be the proverbial engine of growth for our economy. This is evident from the fact that 
India's total share in global international arrivals remains a modest 1.57% against the target of 
3 per cent s et by the NITI Aayog to be achieved by 2022. Similarly, the contribution (direct and 
indirect) of tourism in the GDP and the total jobs in the country are estimated to be 5.16 per cent 
and 15.34 per cent respectively during 2019 -20. The Committee is of the  firm view that if India 
has to move towards becoming a USD 5 trillion economy and a global economic powerhouse, as 
envisioned by our Hon'ble PM Shri Narendra Modi, then the contribution of tourism to India's 
GDP has to be raised from the current 5.16% to 10% in the next five years. The Committee, 
while welcoming the various measures taken by the Ministry to double the contribution of 
tourism to India's GDP, feels that the vast untapped potential of India as a tourism destination 
cannot be realized unless t ourism is included in the Concurrent List of the Constitution of India. 
Taking note of the fact that Travel and Tourism does not figure in the Centre, State or 
Concurrent Lists and since in a federal polity like ours, the responsibility for policy making a nd 
implementation of tourism projects are fra gmented across different levels -Central and State 
Governments and coordination between them is often lacking due to absence of clearly defined 
mandate, the Committee in its 288 th Report had recommended inclusion  of tourism in the 
Concurrent List. Since tourism is yet to be included in the Concurrent List, the Committee 
reiterates its recommendation for inclusion of tourism in the Concurrent List of the Constitution 
of India. The Committee is convinced that this w ill go a long way in channelizing the 
development of tourism and positioning and maintaining tourism development as a national 
priority. 
(Para 30) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 Travel & Tourism Sector has backward and forward linkages with other sectors of the  
economy, like transport, construction, handicrafts, manufacturing, horticulture, agriculture and 
involves multiple issues falling under the purview of both Centre and State Governments. 
Ministry of Tourism being the nodal Ministry for the development of t ourism sector in the 
country has set up several mechanisms for holding consultations with the State Governments, 
Central Ministries and private stakeholders on different subjects to create convergence and 
synergy across multiple agencies and programme for the development & growth of tourism 
sector in the country. These steps have been able to create robust mechanism for facilitating the 
implementation of the tourism policies and programmes, resulting in the growth of the tourism 
sector over the years. The F oreign Tourist Arrivals (FTAs) increased from 5.78 Million in 2010 
to 10.93 Million in 2019. Similarly, Foreign Exchange Earnings (FEEs) from Tourism increased 

23 
 
 
from Rs. 66,172 crore in 2010 to Rs.2,11,661 crore in 2019. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
2.2 The reply of the Ministry does not address the issue. The Committee has time and 
again raised the matter of inclusion of Tourism in Concurrent List in its previous 
recommendations (refer to Para 4.2 of the 298 th Report and Para 72 of the 288 th Report of 
the Committee). The Committee is of the view that inclusion of Tourism in the Concurrent 
List will help in simplifying the issues of the pandemic -hit Indian Tourism Sector since 
tourism is a multi -sectoral activit y and inclusion of tourism in the Concurr ent List will 
play an important role in facilitating the issues involved with multiple Ministries/ 
Organisations at Central level as well as with the States/Union Territories to create 
convergence and synergy of actions across multiple agencies and program mes. The 
Ministry should inform the Committee whether any action has been taken by the Ministry 
on this longstanding recommendation of the Committee. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee observes that Emirate of Dubai does not have the abundant wealth of 
natural oil reserves and nor does it have a pre -existing plethora of natural, historical and 
internationally significant tourist sites. Despite that, it has emerged as a multi -billion dollar 
economy and amongst the world's most visited tourist de stinations, all based on the 
Government's tourism centric approach towards national policy making. The Committe e wishes 
that India should also endeavour  to imbibe creating potential for tourism in the very core of its 
policy making. Although tourism is an important activity in India, its share in global market is 
extremely small and the potential of tourism sector in India is yet to be unleashed. The actual 
implementation of tourist projects takes place at State/UT level but in most of the States/UTs, the 
outlay for Department of Tourism is meager. The Committee, therefore, recommends that in 
order to give policy push to the tourism industry, a National Tourism Council chaired by the 
Prime Minister and composed of Chief Ministers or Tourism Ministers of all States should be 
established. This National Council should be an empowered legislative body on the lines of GST 
Council. This will enable fast -track Centre-State level tourism decision making, leveraging and 
utilizing full synergies of India's tourism potential across all our States. 
(Para 31)

IV) IMPACT OF COVID -19 PANDEMIC ON TOURISM, TRAVEL AND

Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes that Finance Act, 2020 which was announced just before the start 
of COVID -19 crisis, inter alia, came up with new insertion of Tax Collected at Source (TCS) 
provisions under Section 206C (1 G) (a) of Income Tax Act, 1961 pertaining to TC S @ 5% on 
foreign remittance through Liberalized Remittance Scheme (LRS) and under Section 206C 
(1G)(b) pertaining to TCS@5% on selling of overseas tour packages by tour operators. The 
Indian Tour Operators face challenges to match the prices offered for o utbound tours in 
comparison to foreign tour service providers due to additional burden of taxes which include 
GST and newly inserted TCS provisions under Section 206C of the Income Tax Act, 1961 
because overseas agents and Online Travel Agents (OTAs) do no t charge the same since their 
base is out of India. The Committee is of the view that the above TCS provisions will not only 
increase the cost of packages sold by Indian tour operators, they will also shift all sales of 
outbound tourism to overseas suppliers, thereby denying the Government of income tax and GST 
revenue. These newly inserted TCS provisions, therefore, are detrimental to tourism business in 
India. The Committee, therefore, recommends that in order to allow domestic tour operators a 
level playing field in comparison with foreign tour operators in the market of outbound tourism, 
the above mentioned TCS provisions be rolled back. The Committee is of the view that once TCS 
on outbound tourism is withdrawn, it will enable the Indian Travel Agents and Tour Operators to 
stage a recovery post the pandemic. 
(Para 70)

Their Reply is awaited.

Schemes as per the Para 18 of the 318 th Report on Demands for Grants (2022 -23) of the 
Ministry, and there is no assurance that these UCs were successfully submitted or their 
amounts were fully cleared. The Committee desire s the Ministry to furnish a clear reply as 
regards the remaining UCs which were shown pending under its various Schemes and 
whether their pendency has been brought down by the Ministry. 
 (Para 1.4) 
III) CONTRIBUTION OF TOURISM TO GDP 
 The reply of the Ministry does not address the issue. The Committee has time and 
again raised the matter of inclusion of Tourism in Concurrent List in its previous 
recommendations (refer to Para 4.2 of the 298 th Report and Para 72 of the 288 th Report of 
the Committee). The Committee is of the view that inclusion of Tourism in the Concurrent 

51 
 
 
List will help in simplifying the issues of the pandemic -hit Indian Tourism Sector since 
tourism is a multi -sectoral activity and inclusion of tourism in the Concurrent List will 
play an  important role in facilitating the issues involved with multiple Ministries/ 
Organisations at Central level as well as with the States/Union Territories to create 
convergence and synergy of actions across multiple agencies and programmes. The 
Ministry should inform the Committee whether any action has been taken by the Ministry 
on this longstanding recommendation of the Committee. 
(Para 2.2) 
 The Committee believes that „Vision without action is a daydream, and action 
without a vision is a nightmare.‟ Mere ly drafting a National Tourism Policy is not 
sufficient for the development of Indian Tourism Sector, which requires resolving issues of 
the industry stakeholders. The Committee believes that vision combined with action can 
bring a huge change and therefor e reiterates that a National Tourism Council should be 
created in the line of GST Council to directly make recommendations to the Union and 
State Governments on various issues of the Indian Tourism Sector and its stakeholders. 
The Committee also desires to  be apprised of the action taken by the Ministry regarding 
views/comments received in inter-ministerial consultations in this regard. 
(Para 3.2) 
(IV) IMPACT OF COVID -19 PANDEMIC ON TOURISM, TRAVEL AND  
HOSPITALITY SECTOR 
 The Committee would like to be informed in detail of the specific action taken by 
the Ministry and of the State/UT Govts with regards to the recommendation in the NCAER 
Study Report. 
(Para 4.2) 
 The Committee notes that the Indian Hospitality Industry has faced a severe dent 
due to the pandemic and according Indian Hospitality Industry infra status with Capex 
above Rs. 25 crore (excluding land) to the sector will reduce the operating costs for 
hospitality players through subsidized rates of electricity and water charges, property tax, 
development tax etc. and also attract investments in the Sector. The Committee is confident 
that this move will fuel the Indian economy to achieve „atmanirbharta‟ in the post -
pandemic future. 

52 
 
 
(Para 5.2) 
 The Ministry may further clarify the matter and the co mmunication received from 
the Department of Revenue. 
(Para 6.2) 
 The Committee applauds the initiative taken by the 8 states - Maharashtra, 
Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Kerala, Karnataka, Punjab, Rajasthan and Uttarakhand in 
according “Industry Status” to the Hospitality projects, and recommends the Ministry to 
track progress status of the initiative in these States and ensure its successful 
implementation. However, there‟s still a long way to go, given that the remaining 20 Indian 
States are yet to take up suc h an initiative. The Committee desires to know whether any 
thoughts/ views on granting “Industry Status” to Indian Hospitality Sector have been 
conveyed by the remaining States/ UTs to the Ministry. 
(Para 7.2) 
 The Committee observes that the objective of introducing the Service Exports from 
India Scheme (SEIS) is to promote the export of notified services in the international 
market. The Committee is of the view that since the Indian Tourism Industry has faced one 
of its worst phases over the past year -and-a-half and endured „debilitating hardships,‟ the 
SEIS benefit would have provided some financial succour and help tide over the crisis. 
Capping the SEIS rates during the recovery period may or may not be a right decision. 
The Committee is confident that t here must be some other benefits that can be introduced 
by the M/o Finance for Indian Services Exporters, about which the Committee may be 
apprised. The Committee also desires to know whether any cost -benefit analysis has been 
done in this regard for withdrawal of the SEIS benefits from 7% to 2%. 
(Para 8.3) 
V. INTEGRATED DEVELOPMENT OF TOURIST CIRCUITS AROUND SPECIFIC  
THEMES (SWADESH DARSHAN) 
 The Committee desires to be apprised of the reasons for slow progress in both 
physical and financial areas. The Com mittee also suggests the Ministry to take the 
advantage of the regional, national and international linkages developed in North Eastern 
States so far in the tourism front and also follow a market -oriented approach in promoting 

53 
 
 
the North-Eastern Circuit tourism across the country and at international level. 
(Para 9.6) 
 The Committee notes that against the sanctioned amount of Rs. 737.01 cr., only Rs. 
501.94 cr. has been released for the projects under the Spiritual Circuit. The Committee 
desires to be apprised of the reasons in this regard. 
(Para 10.6) 
 Spiritual Tourism owns a prodigious canvas in Indian States of Kerala, 
Maharashtra, and Rajasthan harbouring splendid and far -famed pilgrimage sites, 
magnificently built temples, powerfully acclaimed religious  places. The Committee notes 
that while Kerala has been given a meagre Rs. 3.88 cr. contrary to the sanctioned Rs. 69.47 
cr., Rajasthan and Maharashtra have been given Rs. 68.24 cr. and Rs. 24 cr. against the 
sanctioned amounts of Rs. 89.93 cr. and Rs. 47.53 cr. The Committee desires to be apprised 
of the reasons for the low amount release as regards the State of Kerala and why approx. 
22 crores have been reduced from the sanctioned funds for the States of Rajasthan and 
Maharashtra. 
(Para 10.7) 
 The Committee reiterates its desire to be apprised of the details of projects which 
have had cost escalation and time overrun. 
(Para 11.3) 
VI. THE NATINOAL MISSION ON PILGRIMAGE REJUVENATION AND  
SPIRITUAL AUGMENTATION DRIVE (PRASHAD) 
The Committee notes in the Annexure-III furnished by the Ministry that in projects 
sanctioned five years ago or before 2017 -18, the „ Development at Hazratbal‟ in Jammu & 
Kashmir and „Infrastructure Development at Puri, Shree Jagannath Dham – Ramachandi 
- Prachi River front at Deuli  under Mega Circuit‟ in Odisha have achieved lesser progress 
rates than expected, i.e. 68% and <5%, the latter being a more concerning matter for the 
Committee, needs a valid reason from the Ministry for an inordinate delay in its 
completion. The Committee  is of the view that projects taking longer than five years may 
incur high cost and schedule/time overruns, which will put extra financial burden and 
resource crunch on the Ministry and implementing agencies involved. The Committee 

54 
 
 
recommends the Ministry to devise adequate monitoring mechanisms to ensure the timely 
completion of these projects. 
(Para 12.2) 
 The Committee applauds the Ministry‟s efforts in achieving 100% completion rate 
for 19 projects under the PRASHAD Scheme. The Committee hopes that the Ministry will 
achieve full progress of the remaining projects with more than 60% completion rate in 
stipulated time through its meticulous efforts and planning, and recommends the Ministry 
to keep it informed about the progress achieved in this regard. 
(Para 12.3) 
VII. DEVELOPMENT OF ICONIC TOURIST DESTINATIONS 
 The Committee desires to be apprised of the status of fund allocated for the Scheme, 
“Development of Iconic Destinations,” reason for delay in getting approval and steps taken 
by the Ministry to speed up the approval process. The Committee notes that cooperation is 
necessary to maintain the convergence among Ministries and ensuring a proactive role of 
all the Ministries involved in the said Scheme. The Committee desires to know whether any 
master plan has been chalked out by the Ministry to ensure better cooperation of all the 
Ministries at the execution stage after the Scheme gets approved. 
(Para 13.2) 
IX. DOMESTIC PROMOTION AND PUBLICITY (DPPH) SCHEMEINCLUDING  
MARKET DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE 
 The Committee desires to be apprised about the action taken in detail by the 
Ministry to promote the abovementioned areas of Niche Tourism. 
(Para 14.2) 
 
 
 
 The Ministry has not addressed the specific issue of Night tourism in its reply. 
Promoting Night Tourism  and nightlife in a way, would boost overall tourism of the 
country. A 24 -hour city status renders the daylight hour variation across the world less 
relevant and tourists struggling to adapt to new time zones on a tight schedule may also 
find it convenient  to visit a city which makes it easy for them to shop, dine and go 
sightseeing in night as well. Alongside permanent illuminations of the monuments across 
the country, the Committee recommends the Ministry to promote light/lantern festivals, 

55 
 
 
all-night art festivals, floating illuminated boats/yachts, candle -lit processions, and 
multimedia projections etc. which have already become popular in various countries. The 
Committee is of the view that lack of awareness is one of the reasons why night tourism has 
not taken off in the country yet. The Committee recommends the Ministry to take 
appropriate steps to aggressively promote Night Tourism in India and adopt initiatives to 
provide concessions/relaxation in fares/duties to night-time convenience stores/24X7 shops. 
(Para 15.2) 
X HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
 The Committee would like to know the status of new proposals received from the 
State Govt.s/UT Admn.s which have been considered under the Scheme of Financial 
Assistance to the HMs/FCIs/IITTM/ICI/NCHMCT. The Committee may also be apprised 
of the number of Private Institutions affiliated with the NCHMCT to train manpower in 
the field of travel and hospitality. 
(Para 16.4) 
 The objective of Foo d Craft Institutes is to provide instructions and training in all 
the Craft and skills, both theoretical and practical, and all the organizational and 
management techniques, required for the efficient functioning of Catering Establishments, 
Restaurants, Cruise Lines, Airlines, Entrepreneurship or industrial establishments etc. The 
Committee recommends the Ministry to employ modern techniques and speed up the 
development of three Food Craft Institutes at Balaghat, Dhar and Shahdol (all in Madhya 
Pradesh). The Committee is of the view that these FCIs may become an important source 
of revenue , and will prove  beneficial for the tourism and hospitality sector, and thus, 
recommends that such FCIs be encouraged in each Indian State in order to bring out the 
best opportunities for the Indian youth in the field of food crafts and skill enhancement. 
(Para 17.2) 
 The Committee is of the view that Indian Hotel and Tourism is rapidly expanding, 
given the surging demand from travellers, sustained efforts of government and private 
travel agents and creation of employment opportunities  simultaneously to boost the 
market. Today‟s highly competitive and dynamic environment requires a skilful 
workforce, specially trained in handling the modern challenges in the competitive game of 
the industry. A Curriculum enriched with new learning paradigms, modern methodologies 
and attributes for Staff Training at Hotel Industry will serve as a strong service -based 
philosophy in achieving customer satisfaction and business success.  The Committee desires 

56 
 
 
to be apprised of the outline of the new curriculum IHMs designed after obtaining inputs 
from Industry Academicians/Experts. 
(Para 18.3) 
 Skills and competencies are a function of the economic development and social 
development of any country and bring advancement and excellence to a country like India, 
which needs to achieve the twin target of economic growth and inclusive development 
through GDP growth of 8% to 9%. The Committee if of the view that a credible, sound 
and aspirational national system is needed to facilitate skill development in the country and 
would like to know the status and efficacy of the norms and guidelines stipulated by the 
MSDE for the placement of training programme to Institute(s). 
(Para 19.3) 
 With the government‟s agg ressive campaigning of „Make in India‟ and the 
accelerated growth in the economy, the demand for skilled manpower in the country has 
risen. The Committee is constrained to note that against the target of 63,600, only 20,729 
persons have been trained/certified so far. The Committee is of the view that training adds 
structure to an organization/industry‟s learning and development of employees and 
shortage in the trained and skilled workforce may lead to lower customer satisfaction of 
the tourists. The Committee recommends the Ministry to adopt appropriate mechanisms to 
achieve the set target and utilize the „demographic dividend‟ through vigorous branding 
and facilitating the active involvement of PPP since there is a huge scope of generation and 
supply of skilled workforce in India. 
(Para 20.3) 
XI. ASSISTANCE TO CENTRAL AGENCIES FOR TOURISM INFRASTRUCTURE  
DEVELOPMENT 
 The Committee may be apprised of the status and outcome of the meeting of the 
Task Force constituted under the Chairmanship of the Secretary, M/o Tourism and the 
steps taken by the Ministry to address the various issues related to tourism as per the 
recommendations of the SGoS for Tourism Sectoral Plan. 
(Para 21.4) 

57 
 
 
 The Committee applauds the Ministry‟s efforts in developing wayside amenities 
under the Swadesh Darshan Scheme since India is fast evolving as a potential economic 
trigger with the development of wayside amenities along the highways and byways across 
the country, consisting of retail fuel outlets, electric re -charging, eating joints, food courts, 
public conveniences and other commuter friendly services like drive -through food pick up 
points, which will not only support small businesses, create jobs, but will also give a big 
boost to the local economy. The Committee would like to know t he percent progress 
achieved in the Wayside Amenities 2018-19 project - „Development of wayside Amenities in 
Uttar Pradesh and Bihar at Varanasi - Gaya - Kushinagar in collaboration with MoRTH,‟ 
and whether more wayside amenity projects have been taken up in remaining Indian States 
and whether any cooperative mechanisms have been created with other Ministries for the 
same. The Committee also desires to know the status of „State Perspective Plan.‟ 
(Para 22.6) 
MISCELLANEOUS 
 The Committee observes that Asian countries - specifically India, China and the 
Caribbean islands are primary hotspots in the adventure tourism industry right now, apart 
from middle-eastern Europe. India having vast amount of adventure locations and a lot of 
potential in development and ex pansion of the Adventure Tourism, taking initiatives for 
Adventure Tour Operators to enable them to operate without much hassle will go a long 
way. However, competitive market pressures may force the Adventure Tour Operators 
(ATOs) to cut corners and operate “close to the edge” in order to remain financially viable, 
which indicates the short -term perspective for the industry. The Committee therefore 
recommends the Ministry to bring out some mandatory accreditation system to ensure 
adequacy of their infrastr ucture to strengthen safety of tourists in the adventure tour 
locations, especially the high -risk adventure zones across the country.  The Committee also 
recommends formulating appropriate policies/guidelines to address issues of the adventure 
tour operators and so that this sector could have a long -term and sustainable future in the 
Indian tourism industry. 
(Para 23.4)

Introduction 
 The Indian Civil Aviation sector is one of the fastest growing sectors of the country as 
well as of the world today. In terms of domestic air passenger traffic, India is the third largest 
aviation market. The unprecedented growth of the Civil Aviation industry can be gauged from 
the fact that in the domestic routes the number of domestic passengers carried by scheduled 
domestic Indian Carriers has witnessed a growth of 48.9 percent in the year 2022, as compared to 
the previous year 2021 (up to 31 st December, 2021) and while in the International Routes during 
the period January to December , 2022 a total of 43.4 million passengers were carried by 
Scheduled India/ foreign carriers as against 17.2 million in the corresponding period in 2021, 
thereby witnessing a growth of 152.7%.   The number of aircrafts registered in the Civil Aviation 
sector is also likely to reach a figure of 1200 in the next few years from the current figure of 744.  
The freighter aircraft deployed by Indian airlines have increased from 7 (2018) to 28 during the 
last three years (2021). 
2.       The Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation highlighted the following vision and objectives of 
the Ministry:- 
 To c reate an environment where the a viation industry is sustainable; affordable; safe;  
internationally competitive; and connects to all parts of India and the World;  
 To expand airport capacity more than five times to handle one billion trips a year; 
 To e nhance the availability and affordability of regional air connectivity the Regional 
Connectivity Scheme – Ude Desh Ka Aam Naagrik (RCS-UDAN); and 
 To ensure that airport tar iffs, taxes on fuel, landing charges, passenger services, cargo and 
other charges are determined in an efficient, fair and transparent manner. 
Mandate of the Ministry 
3.       The Ministry of Civil Aviation is responsible for the formulation of national policies and 
programmes for the development and regulation of the Civil Aviation sector in the country. It is 
responsible for the administr ation of the Aircraft Act, 1934;  Aircraft Rules, 1937 ; and various 
other legislations pertaining to the aviation sect or in the country. In addition to the primary 
functions of framing of policies, the Ministry provides guidance to the organizations in the 
implementation of policy guidelines ; monitors and evaluates their activities ; and also provides 
their interface with Parliament. It also supervises the implementation by the organizations of 
special programmes of the Government, particularly those intended for weaker sections of 
society.

allocation has been steadily decreasing from Rs. 6,602.86/- crore (2018-19), to Rs. 4,500.00/- 
crore (2019-20), to Rs. 3,797.71/ - crore (2020-21), to Rs. 3,224.67/ - crore (2021-22), barring

account of disinvestment of Air India ., and now the lowest at Rs. 3,113.36/ - crore for B.E.

inflation in the country, which implies that the effective allocations are ever lower. Even

Surge in Air Fares and Rationalisation 
65. The Committee also took up the issue of affordability of air tickets for the common man 
and enquired into the reason for removal of upper price cap on airfares. The Committee pointed 
out that by doing so, no extra revenue is being generated for the Governm ent or the airport 
operator and only the airline operators benefit at the cost of the passengers, who have to pay for 
the surge in flight tickets.  
66. The Committee during its deliberations expressed concerns about the high fares 
charged by the private ai rlines in the domestic sector. The Committee also pointed out the 

Page 27 of 108 
 
wrong information published by the private airlines on their websites, regarding the 
number of seats left in the flight and the prices of the tickets. The level of misinformation 
can be gaug ed from the fact that even after the last tickets have been sold, the same 
number of seats show on the website, as indicated before the tickets sale. This indicates that 
airline operators are misguiding the public and forcing passengers to pay more. In vie w of 
the above, the Committee recommends that the Ministry should formulate appropriate 
guidelines regarding rationalization of fares and publishing the correct information on the 
website of the airlines.  
67. The Committee  also pointed that 'Predatory Pri cing' is being restored to by the 
domestic airlines sector. A particular airline may sell its air tickets at such a low level, that 
other competitors cannot compete and are forced to exit the market. A company that does 
this will see initial losses, but eventually it benefits by driving competitions out of the 
market and raising its prices again. The Committee desired to know whether the DGCA 
had at an y point of time, intervened to check the fares of air tickets. The Committee also 
expressed concern at the fact that in the domestic sector, private airlines are charging 
different fares for same sector, route and same direction of flights. This is specifically so for 
the NE Region and Hilly areas including Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh , where the prices 
of domestic sector tickets are, sometimes even more than the i nternational airline sector  
prices.  
68. The Ministry apprised the Committee that after repeal of the Air Corporation s Act, 1953 
in March , 1994, the Indian domestic aviation market has been deregulated. Consequently, 
airlines are free to induct capacity with any aircraft type for selecting whatever markets and 
network they wish to service and operat e with compliance of Route Dispersal Guidelines 
(RDGs) issued by Government across the country. Thus, it is up to the airlines to provide air 
services to/from any airport in country depending on their operational and commercial 
viabilities. 
69. After deregulation of airline sector, the airfare is market driven and is neither established 
nor regulated by the Government. Air ticket prices generally vary depending upon the market 
forces. Airline pricing runs in multiple levels {buckets or Reservation Book ing Designator 
(RBDs)} which are in line with the practice being followed globally. Due to dynamic fare 
pricing, the tickets bought in advance are much cheaper than those purchased near the date of 
travel. The airlines are free to fix reasonable tariffs un der the provisions of sub -rule (1) of Rule 
135 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937, having regard to all relevant factors, including cost of operation, 
characteristics of services, reasonable profit and the generally prevailing tariff.  Directorate 
General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) has a Tariff Monitoring Unit that monitors airfares on certain 
routes on monthly basis to ensure that the airlines do not charge airfares outside a range declared 
by them. The airlines are compliant to the Sub Rule (2) of Rule 135 of the A ircraft Rules, 1937, 
as long as fare charged by them is in line with fare displayed on their website. 

Page 28 of 108 
 
70. The Director General, Directorate General of Civil Aviation stated that the Ministry does 
not regulate the fares, however, in compliance with the Airc raft Act, 1934, the Ministry 
exercised regulation of fares during the Covid pandemic, which was later withdrawn. The 
Secretary also apprised the Committee that as per international norms, fare buckets are created 
by the airlines and the Ministry only makes them publish their fares on the website. 
71. The Committee takes note of the fact that after the repeal of the Air Corporations 
Act, 1953, the airfare is market driven and depends on market fares, and is neither 
established nor regulated by the Government. It notes the DGCA ’s comments that the 
airfares were regulated for a fixed period during the COVID pandemic in compliance with 
Aircraft Act, 1934 and the regulation was withdrawn as the COVID pandemic abated and 
that airlines are free to fix reasonable tariffs under the Aircraft Rules, 1937, with regard to 
cost of operation, services, reasonable profit and generally prevailing tariff. 
72. The Committee is fully aware that the Indian domestic Aviation sector is growing in 
an open market and acknow ledges that the private airline operators should be given a free 
hand to decide the air fares as they are governed by competition and depends on market 
fares. It also notes that there is a provision in the Aircraft Rules, 1937, which inter-alia has 
a provision for fixing the air fares after considering ‘reasonable profit and generally 
prevailing tariff’ amongst other factors. The Committee observes that presently the surge 
in air fares does not reflect any sort of mechanism on part of the Minist ry to control the 
fares, based on existing Aircraft Rules, 1937, as during surge in air fares the prices go 
beyond the acceptable or justifiable limits of 'reasonable profit and generally prevailing 
tariff'.  
73. The Committee notes that while on one hand Government plans to make air 
transport affordable for the common man and the air capacity is being increased, on the 
other hand there is no commensurate expansion of the capacity to  bring in aircrafts. This 
creates lack of airline tickets considering the h igh demand and leads to increase in  the 
prices. The Committee recommends that there should be a mechanism with the Ministry 
such as capping of upper and lower prices to stop the practice of 'Predatory Pricing' or the 
sudden surge in prices. The Committee is of the firm opinion that a perfect balance has to 
be maintained between the commercial interest of the private airlines and the interest of 
the passengers so as to enable the private airlines to grow and at the same time the interest 
of passengers should also be kept in mind, so that they are not fleeced in the garb of 
commercialization. The Committee feels that even though p rice buckets are being created 
as per international aviation norms, a close watch has to be maintai ned by the DGCA &  
the Ministry and a mechanism should be devised to monitor the websites of various airlines 
to prevent them from misguiding passengers.  And, in case the private airlines do not 
publish the correct information regarding fares, they should be penalized for it. The 
Committee observes that the Ministry of Civil Aviation has a responsibility to the travelling 
public and the nation at large to ensur e that predatory pricing mechanism are not adopted

by the airlines under the cloak of free market economy. The Committee recommends the 
Ministry should formulate a pricing mechanism for air fares to ensure that passengers are 
not charged exorbitant prices.  The Committee also recommends that DGCA may be 
empowered to regulate tariffs based on the data generated by their monitoring Department 
or otherwise. Further, the passengers may also be  given an option to approach the said 
Department with their grievances.

Use of GEO Augmented Navigation (GAGAN)  
191. GAGAN is the acronym for Global Positioning System (GPS) Aided Geostationary Earth 
Orbit (GEO) Augmented Navigation, which has been jointly developed by the Indian Space 
Research Organisation (ISRO) and the Airports Authority of India (AAI). The GAGAN uses a 
system of ground stations to provide necessary augmentations to the GPS St andard Positioning 
Service (SPS) navigation signal. A network of precisely surveyed ground reference stations i.e., 
Indian Reference Stations (INRES) is strategically positioned across the country to collect GPS 
satellite data. Using this information, the master control centre i.e., Indian Master Control Centre 
(INMCC) generates messages to correct any signal errors. These correction messages are then 
uplinked through Indian  Land Uplink Station (INLUS) and broadcast through communication 
satellites (Geostat ionary) to receivers onboard aircraft , using the same frequency as GPS.   
192. The GAGAN is designed to provide the additional accuracy, availability, and integrity 
that may be necessary to enable users to rely on GPS, for all phases of flight, from enroute  
through approach for all qualified airports within the GAGAN service volume. GAGAN will 
also provide the capability for increased accuracy in position reporting, allowing for more 
uniform and high -quality Air Traffic Management (ATM). In addition, GAGAN w ill provide 
benefits beyond aviation to all modes of transportation, including maritime, highways, and 
railroads. 
193. The Ministry has informed the Committee that National Civil Aviation Policy (NCAP), 
2016 prescribes that new aircrafts being registered i n India from 1 st January, 2019 (subsequently 
revised to 1 st July, 20 21) will mandatorily have GAGAN -enabled GPS receivers onboard. 
However, exemption from GAGAN mandate has been given to Boeing -787 aircraft till 
31.12.2025 owing to major design changes to be made in the aircraft and subsequent approval of 
the State of Design i.e., Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). Moreover, five aircrafts of Air 

Page 69 of 108 
 
India, type B777-200 LR, have also been exempted from GAGAN Equipage for 42 months since 
the date of inception, subject to conditions.

14th July, 2022. Also, an amount of Rs. 774/ - crore was allocated for GAGAN Implementation 
from 2004 to 2014. However, the actual expenditure incurred so far is Rs. 792.70/ - crore. The 
difference between the sanctioned and actual expenditure is due to variations in Dollar vs. Rupee

The Committee during its deliberations expressed concerns about the high fares charged

seats left in the flight and the prices of the tickets. The level of misinformation can be 
gauged from the fact that even after the last tickets have been sold, the same number of 
seats show on the website, as indicated before the tickets sale. Th is indicates that airline

above, the Committee recommends that the Ministry should formulate appropriate 
guidelines regarding rationalization of fares and publishing the  correct information on the 
website of the airlines.  
(Para 66) 
The Committee also pointed that 'Predatory Pricing' is being restored to by the domestic 
airlines sector. A particular airline may sell its air tickets at such a low level, that other 
competitors cannot compete and are forced to exit the market. A company that does this 
will see initial losses, but eventually it benefits by driving competitions out of the market 
and raising its prices again. The Committee desired to know whether the DGCA had at any 
point of time, intervened to check the fares of air tickets. The Committee also expressed 
concern at the fact that in the domestic sector, private airlines are charging different fares 
for same sector, route and same direction of flights. This is spec ifically so for the NE 
Region and Hilly areas including Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, where the prices of 
domestic sector tickets are, sometimes even more than the international airline sector 
prices.
