know the reasons for the same.  
(Para 167) 
International Operations 
The Committee notes the Ministry’s reply with regards to granting ‘Point of Call’ status to 
International Airports in the country. The Committee feels that parity should be 
maintained between the international and domestic carriers for operating passenger 
services in the country. The Committee recommends that Ministry sh ould identify a 
balanced approach to liberalize the guidelines for granting of ‘Point of Call’ status to the 
Indian airports to ensure better air connectivity. The Committee opines that better 
connectivity to international airports in the country will give  passengers more options to 
choose from and increase the influx of international passengers. The enhanced number of 
international passengers/tourists will eventually boost the tourism prospects of the country 
and aid in economic development.  
(Para 170) 
Miscellaneous  
Sustainable Aviation 
The Committee welcomes Ministry’s vision to develop a sustainable Indian Aviation 
Industry through energy conservation, the adoption of sustainable practices, and 
improvements in emission measurement. The Committee notes that the Ministry has 
decided not t o participate in the voluntary phases of CORSIA. The Committee would like 
to know the reasons for India’s non -participation in the voluntary phases of CORSIA and 
how it benefits the Indian scheduled carriers with international operations. The Committee 
also notes that the offsetting requirement for Indian carriers under CORSIA, will start in 
2027. The Committee may be apprised of the Ministry’s plans with regard to the issuance 

Page 94 of 108 
 
of necessary guidelines to Airlines to motivate them to either use Sustainable A viation Fuel 
(SAF) or offset their emissions by purchasing carbon credits from ICAO approved scheme.  
(Para 173) 
The Committee notes that no funds have been allocated to the Ministry towards sustainable 
aviation and urges the Ministry to furnish the reason s for it. The Committee would like to 
know the present status of the Ministry’s Report containing its views on the 
recommendations of the Bio -ATF Programme Committee. The Committee may also be 
apprised of the details of the plan being formulated by the MoP &NG for production, 
supply and related issues of SAF for use in the aviation sector.  
(Para 174) 
The Committee recommends that the Government should encourage the use of Bio -ATF 
and formulate a policy in this regard. The Ministry should also assess the requirement of 
necessary technological innovations to ensure that the use of Bio -ATF is promoted. Th e 
Committee opines that the FUA will lead to optimal utilization of Indian airspace and 
result in reduction of flight time; fuel consumption; and carbon emission.  
 (Para 175) 
National Air Sports Policy 
The Committee is of the opinion that Air Sports have a huge potential for growth, in terms 
of tourism and employment generation, in the country. The Committee notes that under 
the head of Skill Development for Promotion/Development of Aero Sports, with an 
objective to provide Grants-in-Aid to Institutions in  the Civil Aviation Sector for 
Promotion/Development of Aero Sports, the projected demand was of Rs. 1.00/ - crore 
however, only Rs. 0.01 crore has been allocated in B.E. 2023 -24. The Committee would like 
to know the reasons for this token provision. The Co mmittee underlines the need for 
bringing in the latest technology; equipment; and infrastructure, to promote air sports in 
the country. The Committee is aware that the International Olympics Committee (IOC) is 
considering the inclusion of air sports in IOC -approved sporting events. In this regard, the 
Committee recommends the Ministry to popularize air sports and take concentrated steps 
in consultation with State Governments; the Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports; and the 
Ministry of Tourism, along with the Air Sports Federation of India.  
(Para 178) 
The Committee notes that with the formulation of the National Aero Sports Policy (NASP), 
2022, a great fillip is required towards the Aero Sports sector in the country. However, the 
Committee feels that the Aer o Club of India (ACI) which was the nodal organization and 
the National Aero Sports control authority designated under the Fédération Aéronautique 
Internationale (FAI), the equivalent of the International Olympics Committee, has not been 

Page 95 of 108 
 
positioned as the nodal body in the Policy, which could restrain the future of Aero Sports in 
India.  
(Para 179) 
The Committee also notes that the FAI has given recognition to the Aero Club of India 
(ACI), an autonomous body under the Ministry of Civil Aviation, for conduct ing, 
certifying, sponsoring and authenticating Aero Sports bodies in India. Hence, the 
Committee feels that the Policy may be fine -tuned to incorporate a provision to have the 
Aero club of India as the Nodal Aero Sports development centre for promotion of Aero 
Sports which it has been handling prior to and post-independence as well. 
(Para 180) 
The Committee would like to note that under the NASP, 2022, the Ministry is in the process 
of establishing the Air Sports Federation of India (ASFI), which shall be a n autonomous 
body under the Ministry of Civil Aviation, to represent India in the FAI and other global 
platforms related to Air Sports. However, the FAI recognizes the Aero Club of India as the 
longstanding autonomous body of the Ministry of Civil Aviation  which is audited by the 
CAG and the audit Report is submitted in Parliament, as the sole authority and authorised 
body of the FAI, as the National Aero Sports control authority in India. The creation of the 
new ASFI under the NASP, 2022 may not have the s ame legitimacy and as it may hamper 
the growth and development of Aero Sports in the country at the national and 
international level. 
(Para 181) 
Trans-Shipment Hubs  
The Committee is of the opinion that given India's strategic geographical location between 
Europe and Southeast Asia, it has the potential to become a leading air cargo trans -
shipment hub. The National Civil Aviation Policy, 2016 also envisages un -tapping this 
trans-shipment opportunity and also proposes setting up of Free Trade and Warehousing 
Zones to facilitate trans -shipment cargo. The Committee notes that after the SEZ Act, 
2005, only 8 FTWZs have been set up and out of these, 4 are non -operational. Th e 
Committee notes the low number of FTWZs set up since the Act was enacted in 2005 and 
desires to know the reasons for the obstacles and the steps taken by the Ministry to remove 
the bottlenecks.  
(Para 185) 
The Committee notes the various steps taken spec ifically the reduction of GST from 18% 
to 5% on air cargo, to simplify and reduce the charges to make India a more attractive 
logistics destination. The Committee also notes that AAICLAS has made budgetary 
allocation only for cargo terminals at Kolkata & C hennai and would like to know the 
reasons for the non-inclusion of other terminals/States. The Committee desires to know the 

Page 96 of 108 
 
present status of rolling out simplified single charges for domestic air cargo facilitated by 
AAICLAS and the status of the proposa l to the Ministry of Finance for exemption from 
Customs Cost Recovery charges.  
(Para 186) 
Issues of Cyber Safety and Security  
The Committee opines that the aviation sector is highly vulnerable to cyber security threats 
as most major airlines have reporte d incidents of cyber-attacks, putting air operations and 
passenger data at huge risk, in the past few years. The Committee is aware that recently 
several flights in the United States of America were grounded or delayed due to a possible 
cyber attack that i ncapacitated the airlines websites. The Committee notes the issuance of 
necessary circular/order for countering cyber attacks and protection of sensitive data in the 
Aviation Sector in India. The Committee appreciates Ministry’s move to seek Reports from 
Airport/Aircraft Operators on preventive measures taken to protect the Civil Aviation 
Sector from potential cyber security threats. The Committee recommends that the Ministry 
may expedite the replies from the concerned stakeholders and would like to be info rmed of 
the summary of all the cyber security measures taken by the Airport/ Aircraft Operators.   
(Para 189) 
The Committee also notes that in the last 5 years, 13 incidents of cyber -attacks have been 
reported with AAI. The Committee would like to know the  details of these attacks and the 
action taken by the Ministry, thereof. The Committee recommends the Ministry 
orchestrate a robust and comprehensive mechanism to counter cyber attacks/ terrorism. 
The Committee notes that AAI has utilized Rs. 51.80/ - crore for the implementation of 
Cyber Security in civil aviation from 2019 -2022. The Committee feels that the Ministry 
should make concentrated efforts to overcome the challenges viz., adoption of a 
multidisciplinary approach; data protection; and lack of skill ed manpower. The 
Committee further recommends that for proper monitoring of the challenges with respect 
the cyber security, the Ministry may explore the possibility of including a separate budget 
head and enhancing the budgetary allocations.  
(Para 190) 
Use of GEO Augmented Navigation (GAGAN)  
The Committee appreciates that India is one of the very few countries in the world, other 
than the USA and Japan, to have its own Satellite Based Augmentation System (SBAS) i.e., 
GAGAN. The Committee applauds Ministry’s as well as the ISRO’s coordinated efforts in 
this regard, which is a firm step towards ‘Atmanirbhar Bharat’. The Committee 
recommends that all out efforts should be made to ensure the installation of GAGAN in all 
registered Indian aircraft, in consultation with concerned stakeholders & expert agencies. 
(Para 195) 

Page 97 of 108 
 
The Committee notes that GAGAN will provide additional accuracy to the pilots, for all 
phases of flight, from enroute and through approach for all qualified airports within the 
GAGAN ser vice volume. The Committee would like to know the details of the airports 
identified for the GAGAN system and the basis for selection. The Committee feels that it 
should be implemented at all the airports in the country especially the ones which have 
difficult airstrips/runways to ensure smooth and safe take-offs and landing. The Committee 
may also be provided with a brief note on GAGAN including the details of INRES, INMCC 
and INLUS. 
(Para 196) 
The Committee further notes that the Ministry has successfully  tested GAGAN based 
approach procedures at the Kishangarh Airport, Rajasthan on 28 th April, 2022. The 
Committee notes that NCAP, 2016 mandatorily prescribes that new aircrafts registered in 
India will have GAGAN onboard. But, it also notes that the major c hallenge for GAGAN is 
that the design changes required to be made in the aircraft has to be approved by the 
concerned regulator of that country, before importing the aircraft in India for registration. 
The Committee feels that this issue is a major obstacl e to the complete implementation of 
GAGAN, as all the aircraft are presently imported. The Committee recommends that 
proactive steps may be taken by the Ministry to approach the foreign aircraft 
manufacturer and the regulator to resolve this issue.   
(Para 197) 
Promotion of Research and Development  
The Committee notes the progress of Research and Development initiatives that the 
Ministry has introduced with respect to access control and security at airports. The 
Committee appreciates that the Ministry has switched to a biometric enabled system from 
the earlier paper -based permits for the movement of employees in Indian airports, 
ensuring a paperless environment. The Committee would like to know the details of the 48 
airports which are planned to be covered under the Centralised Access Control System in 
the 1 st phase. The Committee desires to know whether the Ministry plans to cover the 
remaining airports in the subsequent phases and the details thereof. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry should devis e a foolproof mechanism to keep a check on the 
automated access control of employees and vehicles to ensure unauthorized intrusion in the 
airports. 
(Para 203) 
The Committee welcomes the usage of Radiological Detection Equipment (RDE) to prevent 
the entry/e xit of radioactive material which may be used to commit an act of unlawful 
interference and to eliminate the hazard generated by radioactive material substances by 
passenger, cargo and staff. The Committee desires to know the details of the 14 airports 
where RDE was installed in the 1 st phase and the 10 airports which are planned to be 

Page 98 of 108 
 
covered in the 2 nd phase. The Committee may also be apprised of the Ministry’s roadmap 
for installing and commissioning RDE at the remaining Indian airports.  
(Para 204) 
The Committee notes that the Ministry has under -utilised the budget allocated for CACS 
and RDE, over the years and desires to know the reasons for the same. The Committee is 
also aware that for B.E. 2022 -23, an amount of Rs. 20.00/ - crore was allotted under th e 
head of Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS) for 2022 -23 which included a provision 
for installation of RDE (2 nd Phase). The Committee recommends that the Ministry may lay 
its focus on more R&D projects and work towards making optimal utilization of funds 
allocated to them. 
(Para 205)

was allocated ₹ 9,363.70/- crores as Revised Estimates (2022 -23). O ut of this, the actual 
expenditure stands at ₹ 8065.54/- crores (till January, 2023) i.e. approximately 86% of the R.E. 
allocation.

the world. The number of domestic passengers in the country has increased by 48.9% in 2022 as 
compared to 2021. The number of registered aircrafts in the country is likely to reach 1,200 from 
the current 744, in the next few years. Post the conduct of ICAO Coordinated Validation Mission 
in November, 2022, India’s safety oversight ranking  has improved from 102 to 48, amongst  the 
193 countries in the world . Also, the implementation score has increased from 69.95% to 
85.49%.

till date. More than 2,19,000 flights carrying approximately 114.53 lakh passengers  have 
operated since the inception of the Scheme. As per the Output-Outcome Monitoring Framework

REPORT 
 
BRIEF BACKGROUND 
Indian culture and heritage is one of the oldest and richest in the world, dating back to 
several millennia. It is a diverse blend of various customs, beliefs, traditions, and values that 
have evolved over time and have been shaped by different religions, languages, and historical 
events. India's cultural and spiritual heritage is reflected in its architecture, literature, music, 
dance, cuisine, and festivals, which continue to fascinate and inspire people from all over the 
world. From the ancient Indus Valley civilization to the present day, Indian culture has 
witnessed numerous influences and transformations. This makes it a unique and dynamic 
tapestry of humanity's collective experience. 
2. Broadly, this Ministry is working on the protection, development and promotion of all 
types of Heritage and Culture namely, Tangible Heritage, Intangible Heritage and 
Knowledge Heritage. In addition, the Ministry also harbour s the responsibility of Gandhian 
Heritage and Commemoration of important historical events and centenaries of great 
personalities. 
3. Major programmes/activities of the Ministry of Culture relating to promotion, 
dissemination, preservation and conservation of the cultural heritage of the country are being 
implemented through a network of two attached offices, six subordinate offices, one statutory 
body, thirty-three Autonomous organisations and one charitable trust under its control. The 
Ministry also implements schemes for promotion and dissemination of Art and Culture under 
umbrella(s) namely; Centenaries & Anniver saries Scheme, Kala Sanskriti Vi kas Yojna, 
Development of Museum, Development of Libraries & Archives, Global Engagement & 
International Coopera tion and National Mission on Cultural Mapping and Roadmap. 
Activities of National Gandhi Heritage Site Mission are undertaken through Kala Sanskriti 
Vikas Yojna. The Ministry has no Centrally Sponsored Schemes.

9. The Committee noted that the allocation  for the Ministry of Culture is just 0.075% of 
the total budget this year. This is in sharp contrast to countries such as China, the UK, the 
USA, Singapore and Australia, which spend roughly 2 – 5% of their budget on the promotion 
of arts and culture.  
 
10. In response, the Ministry stated that it may not be tenable for a developing nation like 
India to allocate a considerable proportion of its public fund in the area of promotion of art 
and culture given the high disparity it experiences in elementary ru ral infrastructures like 
health, education and transportation etc. as against the countries in comparison. However, 
this Ministry has been consistently able to increase its budgetary outlays over the years 
except in the Covid pandemic period where priority  was given to other social sector 
ministries.  Though the approved budget outlay for the Ministry is a relative increase with 
respect to the previous financial year, the Ministry had projected around Rs. 3989 crore as a 
result of an overwhelming increase i n the number of activities by all organisations/offices 
under the ambit of Ministry of Culture. This is an achievable budget at RE 2023 -24 stage 
provided a good pace of expenditure is maintained in the next FY as well.  It may also be 
noted that apart from the union government spending on the promotion of arts and culture, a 
considerable part of the public spending is also made by the state governments in the field of 
art and culture which is not captured in the overall spent. 
11. The Ministry further menti oned that while a majority of the amount spent on art and 
culture is from the non -government sources for the counties in comparison, this may not be 
true for our county. Hence, the Ministry is trying and evolving innovative methods to 
maximise the particip ation of non -government organisations in the field of promotion and 
conservation of art and culture. Monument Mitra, NCF etc. are examples of such initiatives. 
This Ministry believes that Culture should be an area where a large part of expenditure needs 
to be sourced from non -government sources. Moreover, the Ministry of culture is taking a 
phenomenal role in supporting non -governmental organisations/voluntary organisations 
through its schemes/ organisations for participating in overall propagation, preserv ation and 
promotion of all forms of art and culture. This can be considered to have a ripple effect on 
the budget utilised by the Ministry.

development and promotion of the country's tangible as well as intangible heritage. 
Keeping this in mind, the Committee is convinced that the BE allocation of 3399.65 
crores for 2022-23 does not suffice the fund requirements of the Ministry. This is likely 
to adversely affect the vital projects, activities and schemes planned by the Minis try for 
2023-24.

2022-23 and ~1 percent higher than RE 2022 -23. However, the Committee notes that 
the increase of 1 percent as compared to RE 2022 -23 is not sufficient to c over the 
impact of inflation. The spending power of the Ministry will actually decrease in 2023 -
24.

allocation of the Ministry. The budget of the Ministry has increased from ₹2169 crores

underscore the importance of its mandated duties to the Ministry of Finance for higher

and museums in the country. It would also help India become a more attractive tourist

conducting archaeological research projects through its Circles, Museums, Excavation 
Branches, Prehistory Branch, Epigraphy Branches, Scienc e Branch, Horticulture Branch, 
Building Survey Project, Temple Survey Projects and Underwater Archaeology Wing.

Operating Procedures (SOPs) are in place to ensure that the maintenance and 
revamping of the monuments are in line with the standards set by ASI and other 
professional bodies. The procedures should include regular inspections, monitoring and 
reporting mechanisms. It must be ensured that any new structures that might be set up 
by the private partners in or near the monuments, complement the architecture and 
design of the particular monument.  
(Para 245) 
 The performance of the private sector entities should be regularly reviewed to 
ensure that they are fulfilling their obligations as per the agreement. This would ensure 
that the adopted monuments are being maintained properly and are provid ing a good 
experience to visitors.  
(Para 246) 

Page 88 of 142 
 
Measures taken towards cultural diplomacy 
 The Committee observes that India is well -known across the world for its rich, 
diverse and vibrant culture and heritage. It is important to build soft power and good 
will through cultural diplomacy, which can help further India’s larger political, 
economic and foreign policy goals. The Committee is, therefore, pleased to note the 
steps being taken towards enhancing India's cultural diplomacy efforts.  
(Para 250) 
 The C ommittee recommends that the Ministry should focus on signing more 
Cultural Agreements & Cultural Exchange Programs with different countries to 
increase people -to-people contact and foster better understanding of each other's 
cultures. The Global Engagement Scheme should be expanded to showcase not only folk 
art but also contemporary art, music, dance, literature, and cuisine to showcase the 
diversity of Indian culture. India should leverage digital platforms to reach wider 
audiences and engage with people around the world by creating more virtual events, 
online exhibitions, and webinars to promote Indian culture. The Ministry should 
establish more collaborations and partnerships with international museums to promote 
the exchange of knowledge, resources, and expertise.  
(Para 251) 
 The major challenges faced in cultural diplomacy efforts are language barriers, 
lack of awareness and understanding of Indian culture, and limited resources. India 
needs to address these challenges by investing in language training  programs, cultural 
awareness campaigns, and increasing funding for cultural diplomacy initiatives.  
(Para 252) 
 The Committee notes that in the past five years, Rs. 85.69 crore has been spent 
on activities under the Global Engagement Umbrella scheme. However, the Ministry 
can allocate more funds for more cultural diplomacy initiatives to achieve better results 
and e xpand its soft power and goodwill across the world. Doing so would promote 
Indian culture abroad, strengthen international relations and create opportunities for 
increased overseas trade and investment.  
(Para 253) 
Fostering community participation and public awareness 
 The Committee recommends that the Ministry should encourage local 
communities to come forward and participate in cultural preservation projects by 
providing them with information about NCF's mission and objectives. It should develop 
targeted campaigns and outreach programs that engage local communities and raise 
public awareness about the importance of cultural heritage preservation. These 

Page 89 of 142 
 
campaigns can be run on various media platforms and social media to reach a broader 
audience. This is cr ucial to enable more potential donor individuals and institutions to 
know more about the NCF platform.  
(Para 257) 
 The Committee further recommends that the Ministry/ ASI should involve local 
communities in decision -making processes related to cultural pr eservation projects. 
This will help build trust and foster a sense of ownership among local communities, 
thereby promoting long -term sustainability. It should create opportunities for local 
communities to participate in the preservation process through wor kshops, training 
programs, and hands -on activities. This will help build capacity among local 
communities and enable them to take a more active role in cultural preservation efforts.  
(Para 258) 
 The Ministry should focus on developing partnerships with lo cal community 
organisations, NGOs, and other stakeholders to promote community participation and 
public awareness for cultural heritage preservation. This will help to leverage local 
resources and expertise to achieve better outcomes.  
(Para 259) 
  The Ministry should also consider allocating a portion of the National Culture 
Fund towards promoting community participation and public awareness for cultural 
preservation. This will provide a dedicated budget for these activities and help to ensure 
their sustainability over the long term.  
(Para 260) 
Special measures to protect rural and tribal culture 
 The Committee appreciates the various initiatives being undertaken by the 
various organisations under the Ministry to protect rural and tribal culture. The 
Committee notes that the Anthropological Survey of India (AnSI) has been working on 
several projects related to the protection of rural and tribal culture, such as study on 
community health, study on de -notified, nomadic and semi -nomadic communities. 
Encouraging more research in these areas can help in understanding the culture and 
customs of these communities better, allowing the development of effective strategies 
for their preservation. IGRMS has been collecting ethnographic objects and 
documenting the tradit ional knowledge systems of rural and tribal communities 
through fieldwork, demonstrative workshops, and cultural performances. Promoting 
these knowledge systems can help in preserving the cultural heritage of these 
communities and generate awareness about their customs and practices.  
(Para 263) 

Page 90 of 142 
 
 Rural and tribal youth are often forced to move away from their cultural roots 
due to the lack of financial security. The Ministry should focus on organising cultural 
events showcasing their unique culture which wi ll empower them and give them a sense 
of pride in their cultural heritage. This can help in preserving the cultural traditions of 
these communities.  
(Para 264) 
 The Committee notes that VMH has organised various events such as Chhau 
dance theatre and inte ractive sessions on empowering regenerative livelihood in Santal 
tribal communities. These events can be replicated in other parts of the country to 
create awareness about rural and tribal culture and customs. IGNCA has been 
organising webinars and documen taries on various aspects of rural and tribal culture. 
Using technology to document and showcase the cultural heritage of these communities 
can help in preserving their traditions and reaching out to a wider audience.  
(Para 265) 
 
Creation of a mobile platform for classical dancers 
 A Member of the Committee noted that the various classical dances have a 
glorious history of being performed in temples and courts. In light of this, the 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may consider the creation of mobile  
platforms on which the classical dancers can showcase their rich heritage gracefully 
during the Republic Day programme and other similar events. 
(Para 266) 
 
Financial Assistance to Artisans who manufacture Aranmula Kannadi (Mirror) 
 The Committee recommen ds that the Ministry may extend financial assistance 
to the families which have been keeping the traditional art of making Aranmula 
Mirrors alive for centuries. The Committee also recommends that the Ministry should 
take initiative to popularise the Aranmula Mirrors through various publicity measures.  
(Para 269) 
 
Delay in providing salary to staff in Uttarakhand 
 The Committee notes that some persons employed by ASI who take care of 
many temples in the State of Uttarakhand have not received wages for more than a

year. The Committee recommends that ASI may urgently look into the issue and ensure 
timely payment of the salary dues to its personnel.  
(Para 270) 
 
Grant of permission for worshipping at temples under ASI 
 The Committee desires to be apprised of th e policy regarding permitting 
religious activities at religious historical monuments under the protection of ASI.

Image Capturing/enhancement/OCR - Records have been scanned with 300 -600 DPI

specifically, text documents are scanned at minimum 300 DPI (in case of legibility 
issues it has been scanned with 400 dpi).Treaties and manuscripts have been scanned 
with minimum at 600 DPI.Original scanned rec ords have captured in TIFF v 6.0 
format with LZW compression (ISO 12234 -2:2001).The Optical Image enhancement 
activities have carried out to remove bleed through, removal of black border, 
curvature correction, light equalisation, brightness and contrast en hancement, de -

Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Manav Sangrahlya (IGRMS) is an ethnographic museum which 
documents, collects, conserves and displays various facets of cultures of India. Major challenges 
faced are as follows :- 
1. Deviation of rural and tribal youth from their cultural roots as they don’t get financial 
security to cater their daily requirements. 
2. Culture is dynamic in itself and keeps changing due to impact of modern technology 
and various develo pment measures. Not only the cultural elements, which were significant, are 
disappearing or vanishing rapidly, even the bearers of those traditions are also migrating. 
IGRMS has been making systematic efforts to meet such challenges by generating and 
spreading awareness via its various programmes and activities to ensure participation of rural youth 
including tribals. Such steps include development of open air exhibitions and acquiring of raw 
material from the  respective areas, collection of ethnographic o bjects, organisation of cultural events 
to create awareness about the traditional culture, giving due recognition by addressing them ‘artists’ 
so that they should have a proud feeling.

Centre for Cultural Resources and Training (CCRT) has been working as an autonomous 
organisation under the aegis of Ministry of Culture, Govt. of India, since 1979. CCRT organ ises 
Orientation Courses and Thematic Workshops at National Level for In -service Government and 
Government-aided School Teachers and Teacher Educators throughout the year, for preservation and 
promotion of Indian Culture by training them for incorporating the cultural component in classroom 
teaching. These programmes help in preservation and development of diverse culture, tradition 
thereby creating awareness of rich heritage in all parts of the country. These Training Programmes 
introduce the participating  teachers/students to the rich fabric of our artistic and cultural 
heritage.CCRT Regional Centres are also established in Tribal dominated areas i.e. Regional Centre

under its Community and Extension Feedback Programme which incl udes, Educational tours to 
Monuments, Museums, Art Galleries, Craft Centre, State Emporia, Zoological Parks, Nature Gardens, 
Camps on Conversation of the Natural and Cultural Heritage, Camps on Learning Crafts using low 
cost locally available resources, Le ctures and demonstration by artists and crafts person in schools, 
Slide-lectures supplementing classroom teaching . CCRT is  also implementing scholarship and

which is being manifested through various performing literary and visual art forms.  There were 
certain difficulties which were faced during COVID – 19 w.r.t. the training programmes /workshops 
and other physical cultural activities . But  CCRT has de veloped online virtually interactive digital 
training programmes during the pandemic period to mitigate all the major challenges & hurdles in 
switching over from On Campus to Online programmes . 
IGRMS, VMH, IGNCA and CCRT being the autonomous organisations of the Ministry of 
Culture, receives annual grants for its regular activities. 
Seven Zonal Cultural Centers are set up by the Ministry of Culture to organise various 
cultural programmes/activities throughout the year on a regular basis in their member States for 
protection of various folk arts and culture including rural and tribal culture. Artists from all over India 
which also comprises rural and tribal artists are engaged by these ZCCs to showcase their talents 
during these cultural programmes. These artists are paid honorarium, TA/DA, boarding & lodging 
and local transportation which help them to earn their livelihood. All the seven ZCCs implement a 
number of schemes viz. Award to Young Talented Artistes, Guru Shishya Parampara Scheme, 
Theatre Rejuvenation Scheme, Research & Documentation Scheme, Shilpgram Scheme, OCTAVE, 
J&K Festivals and National Cultural Exchange Programme (NCEP) for promotion of rural and tribal 
culture. Besides this, Ministry of Culture also organi ses Rashtriya Sanskriti Mahotsav (RSMs) 
through these ZCCs where a large number of folk, rural and tribal artists from all over India are 
engaged to showcase their talents. From 2015 onwards, thirteen (13) RSMs have been organised by 
the Ministry of Cultur e across the country. These ZCCs also organise a minimum number of 42 
Regional Festivals every year for protection of various folk arts and culture including rural and tribal 
culture. 
The major challenge faced by these artists is that they have to come fro m far flung areas to reach the 
programme venues at a very short notice as they are not able to get transportation easily. To overcome these 
challenges, from time to time these ZCCs have been asked to inform these artists well in advance to enable 
them to reach the venues before time.

next 25 years. The roadmap to achieve this vision is to leverage technology to broaden access to 
arts and culture.  He apprised the Committee about the major achievements of various divisions 
of his Ministry. Unde r the ‘Azadi Ka Amrit Mahotsav’ (AKAM) celebrations, more than 1.25 
lakh programmes have been done in India and abroad. The Museum Division completed the 
work on PM Sangrahalaya last year. The Akademis Division conducted various 
programmes. These include I nternational Literary Festival ‘ Unmesha’, International Dance 
Festival ‘Amritam Gamaya’ and Festival of unsung performers ‘Jyotirgamaya’. 
17. The Secretary informed the Committee that the Ministry has brought back 229 antiquities 
to India since 2014. The Ministry will bring 300 more antiquities from New York. UNESCO has 
added three new Indian sites to its World Heritage Tentative List in the last year. These are 
Lepakshi Temple, Living Bridges of Meghalaya and rock paintings found along Konkan Coast. 
Under the Har Ghar Tiranga program, citizens hoisted about 23 crore flags across India. 
18. The Ministry highlighted that as part of the G20 Summit, it will conduct four theme -
based exhibitions at the four venues of Cultural Working Group meetings across India. The 
Ministry will curate a G20 Digital Museum by creating a digital walkway of artefacts from all 
the G20 countries.  

146

B.E. 2023 -24 stage. The budget expenditure of t he Ministry is about 95 -97 percent of the 
allocation in the last two years. It has spent about 75 percent of the allocation till mid -February 
this year. On a query regarding lack of allocation under the Head 'Capital', the Secretary 
informed that expenditure done by autonomous bodies is classified as revenue expenditure even 
though many of these bodies spend money for capital works. The total amount spent on capital 
purposes is around Rs. 750 crores during 2022-23.

State having one Culture College affiliated to it.

REPORT 
 
Shipping is the life  blood of the global economy. Shipping‟s ability to transport goods 
cheaply, in large volumes and with the minimum environmental footprint is unmatched by any 
other mode of transportation. Around 80% of the international trade in goods is carried by sea. 
The importance of maritime trade has been underscored in recent times by the Covid Pandemic 
which disrupted suppl y chains and shipping networks.  The trade loss due to delay s in cargo 
shipments, higher shipping costs and lower m aritime connectivity lead to higher inflation and 
shortage of food and adversely impact the  world economy. Maritime Transport is a critical 
infrastructure for the economic development of a country. It influences the pace, structure and 
pattern of development.  
2. The Maritime sector in India comprises Ports, Shipping, Ship Building, Ship Repair and 
Inland Water Systems. India has a long coastline of about 7,500 kilometers spread on the western 
and eastern shelves of the mainland and also along  the islands with 12 government-owned major 
ports and approximately 200 minor and intermediate ports dotting the coastline.  Around 95% of 
the country‟s trade by volume and 68% by value is moved through Maritime Transport.  India is 
also endowed with 14500 kilometers of in land waterways in the form of rivers, canals, 
backwaters and creeks. The geographical location of India is at the centre of the Indian Ocean 
which is the epicenter of economic activity due to key international trade routes  which give 
strategic advantage to  India. Shipping is therefore a vital part of the Indian economy. As Prime 
Minister Narendra Modi summed it up succinctly, the blue chakra or wheel in India's national 
flag represents the potential of Blue Revolution or the Ocean Economy and that is how ce ntral 
the Ocean Economy is to India.

Coastal Shipping & IWT 
129. The MoPS&W, under its Sagarmala  Programme, has embarked on developing an 
ecosystem for promotion of Coastal Shipping and RORO/Ro-Pax Ferry waterway transportation 
in the country. This mode of transportation  has proved to have multiple benefits over other 
modes of transportation such as improved  cargo delivery and passenger travel time, reduced risk 
of accidents, improved operational speed, low-cost transportation, lower fuel consumption, lower 
congestion on roads and rail,  lowered air, noise and land pollution, along with providing 
seamless travel to passengers, and vehicles. 
130. To promote coastal shipping, Ministry  of Ports Shipping & Waterways has  undertaken 
following initiatives.  
 To encourage a modal shift, Coastal vessels are being provided  a discount of 40% in port 
charges over foreign going vessels.  
 reduction of GST on bunker fuel from l8% to 5%,  
 Cabotage relaxation for cargo vessels, integration of inland and coastal cargo. 
 Subsidy support to Indian shipping companies  
 Green channel clearance for coastal cargoes and priority berthing for coastal vessels at 
major ports  
131. Under the Sagarmala Programme, currentl y two Ro-Pax ferry services are operational  in 
the country on the Gogha- Hazira route in the state of Gujarat and Mumbai- Mandwa route in the 
state of Maharashtra bringing the travel time to 3 hours and 45 minutes with an  estimated carbon 
(CO2 emissions) reduction of 24MT per day and l3MT per day  respectively. These two services 
itself have benefited  more than 24.15 lakh  passengers and around 4.58 lakh passenger vehicles 
and 0.36 lakhs trucks till December 2022  and is continuously getting overwhelming pub lic 
response. 
132. Further, 9 projects including the above two have already been completed and  are 
expected to commence the services soon, and 35 more projects are under various stages of  
development and implementation. Moreover, dedicated berths for the movement of goods and  
passenger are being developed under the Coastal Berth Scheme. Five dedicated Coastal  Berths 
have already been constructed and another six are under development. 
133. Coastal Shipping is a competing mode for road and rail transport however with o nly less 
than 7% modal share of water transport.  India's transport modal share is relatively more skewed 
towards road and rail. Both road and rail transport are s ubsidised by various Government 
policies, however currently, no such benefit is available for the passenger and freight transport 
by Coastal Shipping i n order to reduce the burden on the operations of the Coastal/RORO/ Ro-
Pax ferry urban waterway transportation which are currently on the verge of unavailability due to 
above stated challenges/ issues and for augmenting this newly emerging ecosystem towards  
sustainable operations to compete with the copiously subsidised modes of transportation in  the 
country. Therefore in the Bu dget 2023 -24 to promote coastal shipping VGF guidelines  which 
shall be issued by Ministry of Finance will be followed to promote coastal shipping.

142. The efficiency of a port directly affects the economy of the country since the major share 
of the global trade is carried by sea . Ports handle around 90% of EXIM Cargo by volume and 
70% by value. During the pandemic, freight rates reached record highs. Surges in freight rates 
can affect the prices of goods and  impact global food security.  Ports are  therefore vital to the 
economy. 
143. Port performance indicators are measures of various aspects of a port‟s performance. 
Total cargo traffic handled and Turnaround time are good measures of a port‟s financial and 
operational productivity respectively. Turnaro und time is the total time spent by a vessel at the 
port from the time of its arrival to its departure. The Average Ship Berth Day Output (OSBD) is 
the total cargo handled by vessels/total stay at working berth.

expansion of Port Capacity has been accorded the highest priority through implementation of 
well-conceived infrastructure development projects. The government has given a strong push to 
port modernisation and d igitalisation, with a number of ease of doing business initiatives. 
National Logistics Portal - Marine has been developed to facilitate "Ease of Doing Business" by 
bringing all stakeholders (viz.,  Terminal operators, Shipping line agents, Banking, Exporters, 
Importers, Customs/Cargo clearing authorities, PGAs, logistics service providers etc.) onboard to 
enable seamless exchange of information/ documents in digital format through this portal. This 
Portal has been formally inaugurated by Hon‟ble Minister of P orts, Shipping & Waterways on 
27.01.2023. Direct Port Delivery and Direct Port Entry have been implemented in all Major 
Ports which has significantly reduced cost and dwell time.

security in the maritime sector.

 MoPS&W, Government of India  has taken various measures like appointing  Chief Information 
Security Officer (CISO) at each port, Various technology trainings on Cyber -attacks and its 
threat analysis, Security Audit & Drills, Cyber Security Advisories from NCIIPC, Analysis of

advisories received from NCIIPC, CERT -in, IB. There is no dedicated fund allocated for cyber

huge potential to affect the safety of the crew, vessel, cargo and even ports. Ships are

conduct business. In addition, critical vessel systems required for the safety of navigation, 
power supply and cargo management are increasingly digitized and connected to the

CONTAINER MANUFACTURE 
233. The Committee had queries the Ministry regarding the number of containers   locally 
manufactured and imported in the last 5 years.  The Committee had also asked the Ministry to 
give details of the steps taken to boost container manufacturing in India.   
234. The Ministry has stated that the number of shipping containers manufactured in India is 
not readily available with this Ministry and may be available with the Department of Revenue 
(Customs) or the Department of Commerce. The Ministry has enumerated the following steps 
taken to boost container manufacturing in India -  
235. BIS has issued amendment no. 1 Aug 2022 to the corresponding 
Indian Standard IS 11587:1986 Structural Weather Resistant Steels, incorporating CORTEN A, J
IS G 3125:2021 equivalent Steel grades in IS 11587:1986 and the same has also been established 
through gazette on 18th August, 2022.  
236. MoPS&W has funded to IIT , Delhi a   Research and Development Project   namely 
'Design and Manufacturing of Sea borne 20 ft containers in India'. The project is under 
implementation stage with 'detailed drawings' have been released. 
237. Ministry of Steel has already intimated the steel producers to apply for BIS License for 
the Indian Standard  at the earliest  to enable them to produce the said steel. M/o Steel 
is following up with the steel producers on the progress of obtaining BIS license for  the 
aforementioned BIS Standard. 
238. All approv ed Ship Classification Societies in India have been authorised by DG 
(Shipping) to carry out testing and certification of Containers. 
239. The Ministry also informed that a  PLI scheme for manufacturing shipping containers is 
currently under consideration in MoP S&W. This Ministry has circulated the EFC note for inter 
ministerial consultations with respect to the draft PLI Scheme. Accordingly, the comments 
received from various stakeholders have been sent to DG Shipping with a request to examine the 
above comments  and accordingly conduct consultations with the stakeholders and submit the 
revised comprehensive PLI Scheme after due deliberations to this Ministry. 
240. The Ministry also informed that the key challenges in augmenting container 
manufacturing capacity were as follows :- 
 Low volume of domestic demand, primarily due to the huge cost difference between 
domestically manufactured containers and the imported ones. 
 Poor availability of CORTEN steel plates, extruded sections and corner pieces used for 
manufacturing shipping containers. 
 Steel manufacturers require a minimum order quantity of CORTEN steel in each pour, 
for the production cost to be viable; whereas one TEU container unit requires less than 3 

Page 58 of 93 
 
tons of steel materials only.  Ordering a lesser quantity of steel will considerably increase 
the price of CORTEN steel. Hence the container manufacturing industry will be viable 
only if bulk orders are received. 
 High investment in automated machinery for steel works (eg. Sheet roll forming machine 
for Corrugation of l arge steel plates, automatic welding sets etc). Automation will 
considerably reduce the production time of containers. 
 The Ministry also stated that the shipping container manufacturing industry is at a 
nascent stage and would require initial support from policymakers.  
241. The Committee observes that India requires about 3.5 lakh containers every year. 
There is no container production in India and the country has to depend mainly on C hina 
which is a global producer.  
242. The Committee notes that „Aatmanirbhar Bhar at‟ is the motto of the Government 
and „Make in India‟ is the major principal governing the manufacturing sector. The 
Committee recommends that private participation may be encouraged to achieve India ‟s 
goals in Container production, by giving various incentives.

The Committee appreciates the improvement in the port capacity, average 
Turnaround Time and Cargo Handling Capacity of major ports.  However, the Committee 
notes that the increase in Capacity and productivity still falls far short of International 
standards.  For instance, the Average Turnaround Time for all Ships has decreased only 
marginally from 52.80 hours in 2014 -15 to 50.01 hours in December, 2022. Only f or 
Container Ships the Turnaround time has decreased from 32.39 to 27.29 hours By contrast, 
the Turnaround time in Norway is only 10 hours. Singapore has 32 lakh TEUs per month 
and its port capacity is 65 lakh. In India it is only 8 lakh.

among the top 20 ports in the world on any performance index. India scores low on the

largely on its transport connectivity. The turnaround time of the Major Ports of India has 
increased but still lags much behind the top international ports.  The Maritime India

2. At the outs et, the Chairman welcomed the Members of the Committee and the senior 
officers of the Ministry of Ports, Shipping & Waterways to the meeting. The agenda of the 
meeting was deliberations on the Demands for Grants (2023 –24) of the Ministry. The Chairman 
noted that the B.E. allocations in 2023 -24 were significantly higher as compared to the 
allocations in the preceding three years and the increase was mainly in the Capital outlay. He 
sought to know the plans of the Ministry to utilise the enhanced Capital Outl ay. He   desired to 
know the performance of various schemes of the Ministry in both financial & physical terms. He 
also desired to know the reasons for slow progress under Port Modernization and the initiatives 
taken by the Ministry for promotion of coastal shipping mode of transportation.  
3. The Secretary informed the Committee that the Ministry has already attained an 
expenditure level of 75% in the allocations under R.E. 2022 -23. The Secretary then expounded 
on the major initiatives of the Ministry: 
 Promotion of Landlocked model of port development through PPP partnerships  at Major 
Ports 
 Development of Vadhavan Port in Maharashtra under the PPP model which is at the stage 
of environmental clearance 
 Development of International transhipment hub at Great Nico bar Island for which 
  Expression of Interest has been invited  
 Promotion of coastal shipping as an energy -efficient and low -cost mode of transport and 
increased cargo movement of 30 % on National Waterways in 2022. 
 Initiatives for promotion of Ease of doi ng business (EoDB)  including launching of a 
 single-window platform - National Logistics Portal -Maritime -   to enable end -to-end 
logistic solutions for maritime stakeholders for EoDB at ports, the promulgation of Major 
Ports Authorities Act, 2021, Marine  Navigation Act, 2021, Inland Vessels Act, 2021. 
 Other legislations like the Merchant Shipping Bill, the Indian Ports Bill and the Coastal 
Shipping Bill are expected to be introduced in Parliament shortly.   
 
4. Through his presentation, the Secretary briefed the Committee about the Gross Budgetary 
Support (GBS) and Internal & External Budgetary Resources (IEBR) Outlay of the Ministry. 
While the GBS for 2023 -24 was Rs. 2218.74 crores, the targeted Internal and Extra -Budgetary 
resources (IEBR) was Rs. 3633.21 crores.  The Secretary informed that the unique feature of the 
Ministry was that the IEBR was nearly 65% higher than the GBS. The ports were not being 
given any GBS but the Inland Waterways, still in a nascent stage of development, was dependent 
on GBS. Si milarly, Cochin Shipyard and Shipping Corporation of India were not given 
budgetary support except for R&D in case of Cochin Shipyard and specific programmes in case 
of the Shipping Corporation.  The Secretary also informed that while Cochin Shipyard and i ts 

97 
 
subsidiaries were under the Ministry, all other shipyards in India were under the Ministry of 
Defence. 
5. The Chairman queried about the reason the income of an independent, public limited 
company, the Cochin Shipyard Limited (CSL) was being shown as the I EBR of the Ministry. 
The representatives of the Ministry stated that the revenue earned by the Corporation is being 
invested back in the projects of the Corporation. The Chairman stressed that the income of an 
independent company could not be included in t he budget of the Ministry under internal 
resources. 
6. The Ministry informed the Committee about its achievements in the port sector and the 
initiatives proposed for the FY 2023-24: 
 The capacity of major ports in the country has increased by 83% in the last s even years - 
from 871 Million Tonnes Per Annum (MTPA) in 2015-16 to 1597 MTPA in 2022-23; 
 The traffic handled at Major Ports during the period April, 2022 to January, 2023  
has increased by 9.31% in the FY 2022-23 on year-to-year basis. 
 Turnaround time for containers has reduced from 31.43 hours in 2017 -18 to 27.1 hours in 
  2022-23; 
 Average Output per Ship Berth day has improved to 17,026 tonnes in 2022-23. 
 52 PPP projects worth Rs. 37,200 Cr. have been completed and have contributed to the 
growth in port c apacity to the tune of 550 MTPA. 20 projects are under implementation 
and are expected to add 150 MT capacity. 
Proposed initiatives for 2023-24 
 Efforts of all Major Ports to lessen the carbon footprint 
 Green Hydrogen Hubs to be developed at three major por ts, namely, Paradip, Kandla and 
Tuticorin; 
 20 PPP projects of Rs. 6,760 Cr. will be awarded 
Achievements under Sagarmala Programme – 
7. The Ministry informed the Committee that the themes under the flagship programme of 
Sagarmala, which was started in 2015 , were port modernisation, port connectivity, coastal 
community development, coastal shipping and inland water transport. 

98 
 
 45 projects worth Rs. 2,829 Cr. have been completed while 55 projects worth Rs. 6,353 Cr 
are under implementation and 51 projects worth Rs. 3,146 Cr. are under development.    
 17 Sagarmala grant-supported projects of Rs. 1,122 Cr. are also initiated in the FY 2022 -
23.   
 2 Ro-Pax ferry projects - Gogha-Hazira route and Mumbai-Mandwa route are successfully 
operating with 24 lakh passenger movement and nearly 5 lakh vehicle movement till 
December, 2022, resulting in reduction of 37 tonnes in CO2 emissions. 
 Completion of setting up of National Technology Centre for Ports, Waterways and Coasts 
(NTCPWC) under the Sagarmala Scheme, to provide in novative and applied research -
based solutions in Indian maritime sector. 
Proposed initiatives for 2023-24 
 14 NTCPWCs are proposed to be set up and 53 projects of Rs. 1,051 Cr under Sagarmala 
are to be developed in the FY 2023 -24.  44 projects will be taken  up under PPP during the 
next two Financial Years. Guidelines for RoRo and RoPax ferry services will also be 
developed.

of Shipping in the Financial Year 2022-23: 
Inland Waterways sector 
 The world’s longest river cruise MV Ganga Vilas was flagged off on 13.01.2023 from 
Varanasi (NW-1) to Dibrugarh (NW 2) covering a distance of approximately 3200 Kms; 
 Under the Jal Marg Vikas Project (JMVP) (NW -1 Ganga), Multimodal Termi nal at 
Haldia worth Rs. ₹ 482 Cr. of total cost inaugurated in January, 2023 
  Traffic movement in inland waterways has increased from 55 MMT in 2017 -18 to 109 
MMT in 2021-22; 
 Arth Ganga (JMVP- 2) - 11 Community Jetties inaugurated & foundation stone laid f or 5 
jetties. 
 Projects Sanctioned for 2023 -24 - Development of 16 new NWs, Ship Repair Facility, 
Elevated road to MMT Pandu & Procurement of Catamaran Vessels for ₹ 784 Cr. 
sanctioned 
 Indo-Bangaldesh Protocol route (IBP) route cargo movement increased 51% from 3.58 
MMT in FY 2021-22 to 5.43 MMT in FY 2022-23 traffic; and 
 Under JalMarg Vikas Project in NW -1, Fifty one community jetties, five pairs of Ro -Ro 
terminals and modernization of existing Navigation Lock, Farakka are to be taken up   
 as well as awarding of O&M contract for Sahibganj and Varanasi MMT.

 The development objects for the next financial year, for the North -Eastern Region, are 
the Jogighopa Terminal; elevated road and ship repair facility construction at Mult i-Model

 CSL delivered two Autonomous/ unmanned Electric Vessels to M/s ASKO Maritime,

Indian Maritime University 
 Admission for marine programmes 94% & overall admission 78% ;

 10 training programmes for Port Officials;

 Increase in number of employed seafarers by 21.5%

 Conduct of various grades of proficiency exam through remote proctoring;

9. The Committee was further informed that out of the pending 12 CAG Paras, only 3 Paras 
pertaining to Jawaharlal Nehru Port and the Vizag Port Authority are still pending against the 
Ministry as on 16.02.2023.   Action note for one Para has been uploaded on the Audit Para 
Monitoring System (APMS) portal. Action Notes for the remaining 2 Paras  will be uploaded as 
soon as the Regional Labour Commissioner and the Conciliation Settlement Committee   (CSC) 
give their awards 
10. A Member enquired about the green initiatives taken by the Ministry to reduce carbon 
emissions. The CMD of the Cochin Shipy ard briefed the Committee about the 23 fully electric 
hybrid buses for the Cochin Water Metro designed and engineered by the Cochin Shipyard and 
the fully battery powered KMLR vessels being delivered to a Norwegian supermarket chain. He 
informed about the Corporation’s work in development of India’s first hydrogen fuel cell vessel 
with the support of CSIR and a private Indian tech company, KPIT technologies. He further 
informed the Committee about contracts secured by the Corporation from German clients for  the 
construction of Construction Support Offshore Vessels (CSOV) to service off -shore wind power 
farm units, a milestone achievement in green energy. An MoU has been signed for production of 
all-electric vessels to be launched in four Indian cities. A Memorandum of Intent has been signed 
with a Norwegian company for the production of the world’s first hydrogen fuelled 
containerships. A National Centre for Excellence for Green Ports and Shipping has been set up at 
TERI campus in Gurgaon which will be the fulcrum for all of India’s green shipping initiatives. 
11. The representatives of the Ministry also informed the Committee about the green 
initiatives taken by the Major ports particularly Tuticorin port. Solar energy is a major initiative 
across all the por ts.  In Tuticorin, a 5MW ground based solar power project is ongoing along 
with a 2MW windmill project and a rooftop solar project,   all of which will make the port 100% 
green by the end of the year.   Another initiative is harnessing wind energy as certain  belts in 
India like Tuticorin and Kandla are very good for wind energy. This initiative is being carried 
out with the help of the National Institute of Wind Energy (NIWE) and the projects will be of 

101 
 
PPP model. The third major initiative is the Offshore Wi nd Programme in which studies are 
being conducted for exploiting offshore wind. Other green initiatives by ports include using 
LEDs, electric vehicles and electric cranes, production of green hydrogen, shore -to-ship power 
etc. 
12. A Member enquired about t he future plans of the Ministry in developing landlord port 
model on PPP basis.   The representatives of the Ministry informed that JNPA has become the 
first port to adopt the landlord model fully. Port is a sector where international competitiveness is 
needed and landlord model has the advantage of private sector efficiencies in the operations part. 
The landlord model is the way forward and most ports will follow this model. 
13. A Member enquired about the status of development of National Waterways NW -8, NW-
9, NW-13 and NW-59 and whether the DPRs have been shared with the State Government.  He 
emphasized that development of these Waterways should be on priority basis since they act as 
feeder routes to NW -3 which is also planned to be extended further.  A Me mber enquired 
whether the hundreds of ships plying below the Digha Bridge in Bihar were under the control of 
the Ministry. Another Member asked about the Ministry’s plans for development of Inland 
Waterways and whether any study had been done regarding Chi na’s transportation of cargo 
through its waterways.   The Member commented that the Ministry must make all efforts to 
promote waterways as this mode of transportation was the cheapest.  The Member suggested that 
if the GBS was not sufficient, the Ministry should think of the PPP model.  He also desired status 
on the Buckingham canal issue. 
14. The representatives of the Ministry informed that the NW -8, NW-9, NW-13 and NW-15 
waterways were notified in 2016 and the feasibility studies were conducted in 2019 an d shared 
with the State Government. Certain projects like construction of pontoon, dredging of waterways 
etc. have been taken up.   Issues relating to increasing the height of bridges and availability of 
land to keep the dredging material and terminals are being sorted out by the State Government 
for the development of waterways in Kerala.  Under the Inland Vessels Act, enacted in 2021, the 
control of survey, certification and registration is with the State Government. The vessels plying 
in the Digha Bridge have been registered with the State Government. Regarding the Ministry’s 
plans for Waterways, there is a Vision Plan of 2030 and a Vision Plan of 2047.   The long term 
plan is that the cargo has to increase to 200MT by 2030 which is expected to be achieved by 
2025 because in 2022, cargo of 109 MT has been achieved. Regarding the Buckingham canal, 

102 
 
the major issues are increasing the height of bridges and encroachments and the same have been 
taken up with the State Governments of Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. 
15. The Member also stated that Cochin Shipyard, a profitable PSU producing strategic ships 
should be promoted and should take up all Union and State Government projects wherever the 
Corporation is capable of providing vessels. Appreciating that the Corpo ration has delivered the 
indigenous Aircraft Carrier, INS Vikrant to the Indian Navy,    making India only the 6 th country 
in the world to design and build its own aircraft carrier, the Member stated that such profitable 
PSUs should not be disinvested.  Citing the example of Shipping Corporation of India (SCI), 
another Navratna Company under strategic disinvestment, he commented that the scheme of 
arrangement for demerger of and transfer of non -core assets of SCI into another entity SCILAL 
(Shipping Corporation of India Land and Assets Limited) would countermine the Company.   He 
also raised the matter of non -payment of increments to seafarers despite a Kerala High Court 
order for setting up a tribunal on the issue. The representatives of the Ministry stated t hat the 
rationale behind disinvestment of a profitable PSU is the market interest and better value for the 
Government. 
16. A Member enquired whether the reduced budgetary support for Sagarmala was sufficient 
in view of the new projects proposed by the Mini stry.  He also enquired whether the Ministry 
would be financing projects under Sagarmala through PPP mode. The representatives of the 
Ministry informed that the schemes under Sagarmala are appraised every five years based on the 
expenditure made in the pre vious five years.   The expenditure was on the low side in 2019 -20 
due to Covid and also due to some issues in implementation of projects.   Therefore only Rs. 
1800 crore was allotted for the next five years which means Rs. 360 crores per year. The 
representative further informed that there are 55 under construction projects under Sagarmala 
and 51 projects under tendering. Money is released in three tranches, 50% at the time of award of 
tender, 40% upon completion of 50% physical progress and 10% upon complet ion of 100% 
physical progress. The representative also informed the Committee that with more than 100 
projects in the pipeline, the Ministry is confident of spending the budgetary estimates. Further, 
budgetary support is given only to those projects like c oastal community development which are 
not viable under PPP. Most projects of cargo handling in major ports are taken up under PPP 
mode. 
17. A Member suggested that the Central government should take up the cost of 
modernization and connectivity of non -major ports since it would not be possible for the State 

103 
 
Governments to invest huge outlays on such ports.   The Chairman also asked the Ministry about 
its plans for modernization of ports and the time span in which all major ports would be 
modernized. A Membe r asked about the increase in port capacity and whether the key 
achievements of Indian Ports in Turnaround Time, Ship berth day output etc. equalled 
international standards. The representatives of the Ministry submitted that the total capacity of all 
Major ports was 7,50,000 containers per month out of which 4,00,000 containers are being 
handled by the JNPT and 1,500 -1,800 containers by the Chennai port and rest by other ports. 
One Member pointed out that Singapore has 32 lakh TEUs per month and the capacit y is 65 lakh 
while India the capacity is only 8 lakh.   The Secretary replied that once Vadhavan port is 
developed, the port capacity of India would definitely increase. 
18. A Member asked whether a lighthouse was being constructed in Goa. The Chairman 
commented that lighthouses, being outdated technology, were basically being used for tourism 
purposes and enquired from the Ministry whether it was viable to invest crores of rupees in 
construction of lighthouses.    The representatives of the Ministry informed  that there are three 
lighthouses in Goa and proposal to construct more but the land falls under ASI.   The Ministry 
further informed that Directorate General of Lighthouses is a self -sustained organisation with its 
earnings mainly coming from charges levie d on container ships.   While lighthouses are one of 
the oldest technology based communication, the Ministry also has the latest advanced satellite 
technology including 23 DGPS stations and the biggest network of vessel traffic system.   
However lighthouses are also necessary since service to marine navigation is an international 
obligation for Government of India under IMO Convention. 
19. A Member raised the issue of stoppage of outer anchorage crew change at Vizhinjam port 
as significant revenue had been ea rned through the same.  The Committee was informed that the 
issue had been taken up with the Ministry of Home Affairs who had not agreed to the request and 
the State Government of Kerala had been informed of the same. The issues of crew change and 
customs clearance would be taken up if a fresh request is made. 
20. The Chairman commented that container manufacturing is very important but despite 
having the Container Corporation of India Company, India is presently dependent on container 
imports from China. T he representatives of the Ministry informed that manufacturing of 
containers is at a very nascent stage. The Ministry has drafted a PLI scheme for container 
manufacturing and the DG (Shipping) will be holding stakeholder consultations with the 
shipping sector. 

104 
 
21. The Chairman also enquired about the transshipment hubs planned by the Ministry 
especially the one in Great Nicobar island and commented that 75% of India’s transhipment 
cargo is presently handled at ports outside India, i.e. Singapore, Colombo an d Klang. The 
representative of the Ministry informed that Expression of Interest (EOI) has been floated for the 
transhipment hub and DPR is at draft stage. 
22. The Ministry was asked their plans for development of Andaman & Nicobar Islands to 
promote touri sm in that area. A Member enquired the Ministry’s plan of action regarding 
clearing the wrecked and rusted ships lying in the islands. 
23. A Member commented that the shipping industry creates many jobs for both skilled and 
unskilled people and asked whether the Ministry has a programme similar to the ‘Pradhan Mantri 
Kaushal Vikas Yojana’ (PMKVY).  
24. A Member also commented that there are 21 Dry Ports in the country but none within 
250 kms of Delhi.  The Member asked if the Ministry had any plans for Dry Ports near Delhi as 
it would be convenient to distribute containers from the port to inland. 
25. The Chairman also raised issues of cyber security in ports and the status of the six lane 
road project connecting Vishakhapatnam sea port to Bhogapuram airport  under Sagarmala.    He 
also enquired about the Polavaram dam project and how the Ministry proposes to ensure free 
passage of internal waterways ships while crossing the dam as the locks proposed in the dam 
were smaller. 
26. The representatives of Ministry responded to some of the queries raised by the Members 
and took note of the suggestions made by the Members. The Chairman directed that written 
replies to the points which had not been answered may be sent within a week.

BRIEF BACKGROUND 
An efficient, robust road network is a critical infrastructural requirement that enables the 
efficient movement of goods, people, and services across a region. It connects businesses to 
markets, workers to jobs, and people to vital services like healthcare and education. A well -
maintained road network can also help to reduce traffic congestion and improve safety, saving 
lives and time for commuters. The development of road networks has been shown to promote 
economic growth, as it fac ilitates trade and commerce, encourages investment, and boosts 
productivity. In rural areas, road networks can also connect isolated communities, providing 
access to critical resources and services. Overall, the importance of a well -connected, efficient 
road network cannot be overstated, as it plays a vital role in shaping the economic and social 
fabric of any society. 
2. India has the second largest road network in the world of about 63.32 lakh km. This 
comprises National Highways, Expressways, State Highw ays, Major District Roads, Other 
District Roads and Village Roads as under: 
 
Introduction and Mandate of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways 
3. The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways was formed in 2009 by bifurcating the 
erstwhile Ministry of Shipping, Road Transport and Highways into two independent Ministries, 
i.e., Ministry of Road Transport & Highways and Ministry of Shipping. 


 
Page 2 of 137 
4. The tasks and responsibilities of the Ministry encompass, inter alia , construction and 
maintenance of National Highways (NHs); administration of the National Highways Act, 1956; 
National Highways Authority of India Act, 1988; National Highways Fee (Determination of 
Rates and Collection) Rules, 2008; Motor Vehicles Act, 1988; and Central Motor Vehicles Rules 
1989, a s also formulation of broad policies relating to road transport and automotive norms, 
besides making arrangements for the movement of vehicular traffic with neighbouring countries. 
5. The associated offices under the Ministry are as follows:- 
National Highways Authority of India 
The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) was set up through an Act of 
Parliament, namely the National Highways Authority of India Act, 1988. The NHAI is 
responsible for the development, maintenance and management of the Natio nal 
Highways entrusted to it and for matters related or incidental thereto. The NHAI became 
operational in February, 1995. 
National Highways & Infrastructure Development Corp. Ltd. (NHIDCL) 
The Cabinet, in its meeting held on 13 March, 2014, approved the s etting up and 
operationalization of a new corporate entity, the NHIDCL, under the Ministry of Road 
Transport and Highways to exclusively carry out the task of construction/up -
grading/widening of National Highways in parts of the country which share interna tional 
boundaries with neighbouring countries in order to promote regional connectivity on a 
sustainable basis. 
Indian Academy of Highway Engineers (IAHE)  
IAHE is a registered Society under the administrative control of the Ministry. It is a 
collaborative body that was set up in 1983 with the objective of fulfilling the long felt 
need for training of Highway Engineers in the country, both at the entry level and during 
their service period. 
Indian Roads Congress (IRC) 
IRC was formally registered as a Societ y on 24 September, 1937 under the Societies 
Registration Act of 1860 for the periodical holding of road conferences to discuss issues 
related to road construction, maintenance & development. IRC has over 16,850 registered 
members comprising engineers & pro fessionals of all stakeholders of the road sector, 
from Central and State Governments; Public Sector; Research Institutions; Academic 
Institutions; Local bodies; Private sector; Concessionaires; Contractors; Consultants; 
Equipment manufacturers; Machinery manufacturers; Material producers & suppliers; 
Industrial Associations; and Multilateral & Institutional organisations like World Bank, 
ADB, JICA, JRA, IRF etc. 

 
Page 3 of 137 
National Highway Logistics Management Limited (NHLML)  
NHLML is a 100% owned subsidiary company  of NHAI. It is a Special Purpose Vehicle 
(SPV) company incorporated by the Ministry in the year 2020 with the intent of 
spearheading the development and inter -departmental coordination pertaining to the 
Multi-Modal Logistics Parks (MMLPs) for Cargo Traffi c and first/last mile Port 
Connectivity Road projects under the Bharatmala Pariyojana. NHLML has also been 
delegated by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways for the development of other 
allied highway infrastructure such as Inter -modal Stations for passenger traffic and 
development operations and management of Way -side amenities along National 
Highways, Utility corridor along NH. NHLML has been pivotal in accelerating the pace 
of coordination with various State Governments and Partner Government Agen cies in 
terms of on -boarding them as equity stakeholders for development of MMLPs and 
signing of MoUs with various agencies. Since its inception, the organisation, under the 
supervision of Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, has prioritised action on fast-
tracking first/last mile direct road connectivity for various major and non -major ports and 
Inland Waterway Terminals under Bharatmala Pariyojana, while coordinating with the 
Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways and various Port agencies.

Focus Areas of the Ministry for the year 2023-24 
12. The Ministry informed the Committee that its focus areas for the year 2023 -24 are as 
follows: 
(i)     Green Field Expressway and Access-Controlled Corridors :-  
● 27 Expressway and Access -Controlled Corridors are being developed by the 
Ministry with a length of 9,860 km at a total capital cost of about Rs. 4,08,000 Cr. 
● Out of this 9,860 km, 6,235 km has been awarded till 31 st Jan, 2023 at a total 
capital cost of Rs. 2.83 Cr. Out of this, 383 km has been awarded in the current financial 
year. Further, 1,667 km will be awarded in next two months. 
● In addition, the remaining 1,958 km will be awarded in the ne xt financial year 
(FY 2023-24) 
● As of 31 st Jan, 2023, 2,475 km out of the total 6,235 km awarded has been 
constructed. The entire length is expected to be completed by FY 2026-27 
● 574 km will be dedicated to the nation in FY 2022 -23 and ~1,350 km is planned 
to be dedicated to the nation in FY 2023-24 
In addition, multiple sections of other Expressway and Access -controlled corridors are 
planned to be initiated for development by FY2023-24 
(ii) Multi-Modal Logistics Parks (MMLPs) 
MoRT&H has identified 35 locati ons for the development of Multi Modal Logistics 
Parks (MMLPs), in order to enhance logistics efficiency across the country. Out of these 
35 MMLPs, 15 are prioritised for development under Phase -I of Bharatmala Pariyojana. 
Within these 15 MMLPs, the MMLP a t Jogighopa is currently under development with a 


 
Page 8 of 137 
total cost of Rs. 694 Crores and will become operational in FY 2023 -24. Jetty work has 
been awarded separately and that work shall also be completed in 2023-24. 4 MMLPs are 
planned to be awarded in FY 2022-23. Out of these 4 MMLPs, the MMLP at Chennai has 
been awarded in November, 2022 for development at a total cost of Rs. 1,424 Crores and 
3 MMLPs (Nagpur, Bengaluru and Indore) have been tendered. Furthermore, 5 MMLPs 
(Pune, Anantapur, Coimbatore, Hyderabad , Jammu) are planned for award in FY 2023 -
24. 
(iii) Parvatmala: National Ropeways Development Programme 
MoRT&H is implementing the Parvatmala Pariyojana for the development of ropeways 
to improve accessibility & convenience for passengers and to promote to urism in hilly 
regions. Along with hilly areas, ropeways are being developed as an alternate mode of 
transportation to ease traffic movement in congested urban areas e.g., Varanasi, Ujjain. 8 
ropeway projects have been planned for award during FY 2022 -23, out of which the 
ropeway project at Varanasi has been awarded and bids for 7 projects (Kedarnath, 
Hemkund Sahib, Ujjain, Gwalior Fort, Bijli Mahadev, Shivkhori and Doshi Hill) have 
been tendered. Furthermore, 20 additional ropeways are planned for award in  FY 2023-
24. 
13. The Committee notes the various focus areas of the Ministry for the year 2023 -24. 
The Ministry has awarded 383 km of Expressway and Access -Controlled Corridors in the 
ongoing year. It will award 1667 km in the next 2 months and the remaining 1958 km in the 
next financial year. The Committee desires to be apprised of the slow pace of award in the 
ongoing financial year. The Ministry may inform how it plans to ensure that the remaining 
length is awarded by the next financial year. 
14. The Committee observes that the MMLPs offer a significant boost to the regional 
and overall economy through enhanced connectivity and improved efficiency. The Ministry 
has prioritised 15 out of the 35 locations identified for development of MMLPs. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may come up with a clear targeted timeline for 
awarding the remaining 20 MMLPs. 
15. The Committee feels that it is the responsibility of the Ministry to enable 
transportation access to the remotest areas of the country. The Mini stry should work out a 
balance between the transportation  needs of both remote areas and tourist spots while 
planning projects under the Parvatmala programme. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry may lay due focus on enha ncing connectivity through ro peways as last mile 
connectivity to remote areas and hamlets in hilly regions. This would help the local 
residents to contribute more to the local economy, besides improving their quality of life.

Development Projects (NHDP). In addition to the Government Budgetary Suppor t, NHAI has

Resources) to meet its target fund requirement as per the limits approved in the Union Budget.

servicing liability has already started and as per present situation there shall be no further 
increase in the debt liability of NHAI at least till 31st March, 2024.

● Role of citizens 
185. The Ministry highlighted that citizens can report the lack of safety provisions on National 
Highways or any other issues related to road safety through both online and offline mediums. 
Online mode : Citizens can submit reports/grievances via online mode through 
CPGRAMS (Centralised Public  Grievance Redress and Monitoring System). It is an 
online platform available to the citizens 24x7 to lodge their grievances to the public 
authorities on any subject related to service delivery. The status of the grievance filed in 
CPGRAMS can be tracked w ith the unique registration ID provided at the time of 
registration of the complainant. CPGRAMS also provides appeal facility to the citizens if 
they are not satisfied with the resolution by the Grievance Officer. After closure of 
grievance if the complain ant is not satisfied with the resolution, he/she can provide 
feedback. If the rating is ‘Poor’ the option to file an appeal is enabled. The status of the 
Appeal can also be tracked by the petitioner with the grievance registration number. 
Further, Complain ts are also being registered by citizens online through Sukhad Yatra 
mobile application, 1033 Helpline telephone no., “feedback/report an issue” option on 
NHAI website and via e-mails and social media platforms (like Instagram, Twitter etc.). 
Offline mode: Reports can be submitted via offline mode at Ministry’s official address. 
Further, Complaints can be registered offline through visiting field unit offices, contact/ 
address details of which can be obtained from NHAI / Ministry website, nearby toll 
plazas or 1033 Helpline number.
