23. The Chairman then asked the Ministry to brief the Committee about the roadmap of 
the Ministry in the near future and the coordination mechanis ms employed by the MoCA, 
AAI and DGCA to develop the projected target of 220 airports by year 2025. He further asked 
the MoCA, DGCA and AAI to put forth their views regarding various Greenfield/Brownfield  
airport projects facing inordinate delays and other issues which were pointed out by the 
Members in the earlier meeting. 
 
24. The Chairman asked the DGCA to brief the Committee about its functions and 
responsibilities handled by it in the Indian aviation sector with specific reference to the 
subject under examination. He also inquired about the reasons for the undue delay in the 
grant of  clearances to new aircraft for operating in the country, construction of the 
Greenfield/Brownfield airports/Civil Enclaves projects that have been delayed for more than  
five years due to site clearance, license process or in-principle approval by the DGCA 
and concerned agencies and whether any steps have been taken to tackle such delays. The 
Chairman also desired to know the reasons for delay/denial of clearance in cases where States 
are willing to allocate land for the construction of airports.  He also pointed out that replies to  
the questionnaires sent by a Member of the Committee and some questions sent by the 
Secretariat, have not been received and desired that the replies may be expedited. 
 
25. The Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation, assured the Committee that the replies to 
the remaining questions would be sent shortly. He then shared with the Committee two recent 
important developments in the Indian aviation sector, the first being the recent inauguration 
of the Hollongi Airport in Arunachal Pradesh adjacent to Itanagar, its capital city,  by the 
Hon’ble Prime Minister and the second being the elimination of the necessity of filling up the 
Air Suvidha form, due to declining Covid cases, by international travelers to India which is 
believed to further facilitate the inward flow of international tourists.  Referring to the issues  
raised by the Committee in its earlier meeting and in the questionnaires, the Secretar y stated 
that the Heads of the attached offices of the Ministry would address the issues concerning 
their organizations. 

122 
 
 
26. The Chairman, Airports Authority of India (AAI) addressed the issues regarding 
operational airports, nigh-landing facilities, profitability of airports, use of renewable energy 
in airports etc. He informed that presently there are 134 operational airports out of which 119  
airports are carrying out scheduled operations and 15 airports are carrying out non -scheduled 
operations and the figure keeps changing slightly due to operational reasons.  Out of the 119  
airports, 28 are run on Visual Flight Rules (VFR) and 90 use Instrument Flight Rules (IFR)  
procedure. He further informed that there are 43 airports which have CAT -I facility, 16  
airports with CAT -II facility and 6 airports have CAT -III facility. The AAI is trying to 
convert many of  the VFR airports into IFR airports but the problem arises due to lack of 
space as most of the old VFR airports are in congested areas. As regards Night Landing 
Facility, the Committee was  informed that out of the 134 airports, 89 airports have Night 
Landing Facility and 45 airports, presently do not have this facility. For Night landing facility 
the airports needs to be an IFR  airport and sufficient  land should be available for lighting 
arrangement and the Ministry is in discussion with the State Governments to provide land for 
installation of said facility at airports which do not have it. He further added that AAI is in the 
process of procuring of 34 Instrument Landing System (ILS) from Russia. Informing the 
Committee of the profitability of  the airports, the representative of AAI informed that out of 
110 odd airports,  only 10 -15 airports are consistently making operational profits. On the 
issue of airstrips, the Ministry  informed that as per the records of DGCA, there are 452 
airstrips, including the airports  mentioned before, some of which are owned by the State 
Governments and Defence authorities while some of the airstrips are also owned by the 
private owners. The Ministry  further informed that wherever land becomes available and 
opportunity arises, efforts are being made to convert airstrips into proper airports. 
 
27. The Committee was further informed by the AAI that there are 17 Flying Trainin g 
Organisations (FTOs) which are operational and 9 FTOs have been approved on AAI land in  
phase-I and are on the verge of becoming operational within next 6-8 months. Thereafter, 
in the next phase, FTOs are going to be setup at 6 more airports. Regarding use of renewable 
energy, the AAI informed that efforts are being made to convert all its 100 odd airports for  
renewable energy by December, 2024, either installing by solar plant or by procuring renewal 
energy through the distribution companies. 
 
28. The Director General of Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) while 

123 
 
informing the Committee of the aviation safety aspects, stated that India is a signatory to the  
Chicago Convention, 1944 which has set the international standards for civil aviation and  is 
followed by 193 countries across the world. There are 11,000 safety standards in the said  
Convention and it is obligatory for all the signatory countries to follow those standards, 
failing which a country may be declared an “outlaw”. He further informe d that this had 
happened once in a limited way to India in 2013 but India has now got 70 per cent rating and 
is going up to  85% rating consequent to the recent successful audit of the International Civil 
Aviation Organisation (ICAO).  India is now comparabl e to the rating of New Zealand, 
Belgium etc, thus, which indicates the significant strides made by India in this regard. The 
Director-General then informed the Committee that the primary role of DGCA was to 
implement the ICAO  SARPS (Standards and Recommended Practices).  There are eight 
critical elements in safety  oversight, namely Primary Aviation Legislation, Specific 
Operating Regulations, State Systems, Qualified Technical Personnel, Technical Guidance 
Tools, Licensing Certification,  Authorisations and Approval Obligations, Surveillance 
Obligations and Resolution of Safety  Issue. The Committee was informed out of the eight 
parameters, there are issues only regarding insufficient number of Flight Operating Inspectors 
(FOIs) which are being looked into. As  regards the certification of an airport, the DGCA 
informed that the process is slightly time  consuming as all the 350 check points as per the 
ICAO document have to be certified. Similarly for aircrafts certification, there is a detailed 
procedure involving numerous parameters and manuals that has to be followed and it takes 
time to grant clearance to a new  aircraft. However, the Ministry has implemented the e-
Governance of Civil Aviation (eGCA) to reduce  human interface which has considerably 
reduced the delays.

airport infrastructure projects which have long gestation periods.   Comparing the gestation 
period of 50 years for the DMRC at   low interest rates, it was suggested that participation of

Corporation of India (LIC), etc. be allowed/ facilitated to provide long -term financing at

Schedule of the Indian Constitution.

sectoral policies, if any, will automatically stand amended and modified to the extent of

development of airports, which is the constitutional obligation of the Central Government. He 
highlighted the contradictory requested them to apprise the Committee about the republishing of 
the 2008 Guidelines for setting up of Greenfield Airports in December, 2016, after the National

any instances wherein land has been provided by Airports Authority of India (AAI) since the 
introduction of NCAP 2016.  The Committee desired to know the rationale behind mandating 
State Governments to provide land for development of airports free of cost without any equity. 
24. DG, DGCA informed the Committee that land for development of airports is not being 
provided by the State Governments  in all cases . He highlighted the examples of  Cochin and 
Sabarimala airports which have bee n developed by crowdsourcing of funds while Pakyong 
airport is completely funded by the Central Government. On a query of the Committee regarding 
whether State Governments can be forced to provide land for development of airports, he 
informed that the idea is to pool resources and that NCAP is an executive order suggestive in 
nature, which nudges the State Governments to provide the land for development of airports. He 
confirmed that the NCAP is not binding on the State Governments.  
25. A Member of the Committee highlighted various provisions of the Airports Authority of 
India Act, 1994 and 2008 Guidelines for setting up of Greenfield Airports and stated that the 
2016 NCAP is in contravention of the Act and the Union List of the Constitution . In response to 
a query of the Committee, Law Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs informed the Committee 
that 2016 NCAP is legal and valid as per the provisions of the AAI Act and the Constitution.

prosecuting the unruly passenger.

installation of Instrument Landing System (ILS) at Pasighat Airport, etc.

6.         Thereafter, the Chairman welcomed the representatives of the Ministry of Civil Aviation, 
Department of Expenditure (Ministry of Finance), Department of Economic Affairs (MoF), 
Department of Revenue (MoF) and NITI Aayog to the meeting. He informed that the agenda of 

151 
 
the meeting was to seek the vi ews of the Ministry/Departments on certain specific aspects 
pertaining to National Civil Aviation Policy (NCAP), 2016 as part of the  examination of the 
subject ‘Development of Greenfield and Brownfield Airports and Issues Pertaining to Civil 
Enclaves in Defence Airports’.   
7. The Chairman asked the representatives of the Departments and NITI Aayog to elaborate 
on the views furnished specifically with regard to Para 13(a)(iii) of the NCAP at the stage of 
consultation on the Policy. He sought to know whether  any financial difficulties were being 
observed in the implementation of ‘Guidelines for setting up of Greenfield Airports, 2008’ which 
stated that land for Greenfield airports has to be provided by AAI. He also sought their views on 
possibly amending the NCAP, 2016 to remove the mandate for State Governments to provide 
land free of cost and without equity for the development of airports. 
8.         The Finance Secretary & Secretary (Expenditure) began his deposition by informing the 
Committee that the Depa rtment had not offered any comment on Para 13(a)(iii) of the NCAP at 
the time of consultation on the Policy. He added that the Department did not have any objection 
to it. He stated that the said paragraph envisages cost sharing with the State Governments,  which 
is not adverse to the objectives of the Department.  
9. The Finance Secretary observed that the lists of subjects given in the Seventh Schedule of 
the Constitution have been interpreted as demarcating the legislative and executive powers over 
the sector, not necessarily as an exclusive realm for financial matters. He cited the examples of 
Central Government Schemes viz., Modernization of Police Forces and Police Infrastructure, 
Modernisation of Prisons, Swachh Bharat Mission and so on, even though Pu blic Order, Prisons 
and Public Health are subjects under the State List. He stated that there is no bar on State funds 
in Central subjects. 
10.         The Finance Secretary stated that theoretically, value capture mechanism can be looked 
into as a potential source of funding for airport projects. 
11.         The Chairman enquired whether, under the federal system of democracy, the Central 
Government can frame a policy without consulting the State Governments compelling them to 
contribute land free of cost without expecting any equity. The Finance Secretary opined that it is 
desirable to consult State Governments in such cases. He added that the Government is often 
able to take up individual cases in a slight deviation from the policy because the policy is n ot a 
law.  
12.   A Member of the Committee enquired as to why the policy is then invoked to reject 
requests for the development of an airport even if there is desirability or possibility of the Central 

152 
 
Government to build the airport. The Finance Secretary  stated that the policy is binding on the 
Ministry of Civil Aviation and Ministry of Finance but the Union Cabinet can go beyond the 
policy. 
13.       The Secretary, Department of Economic Affairs stated that all fairly viable airports can 
be taken up by the private sector but beyond big cities, there is an issue of viability. He informed 
the Committee that adding the cost of land to the project would result in a large number of 
projects becoming unviable. He cited the example of railway projects wherein hu ndred per cent 
cost of the land for any new line to be constructed, is to be borne by the State Government, along 
with 50 per cent of the project cost. He added that the Department of Economic Affairs had not 
commented on Para 13(a)(iii) of the NCAP at the time of consultation regarding the policy.  
14.     A Member of the Committee stated that the Policy mandates the State Governments to 
provide land even in case an airport project is viable. Another Member highlighted the issue of 
almost all airports in t he North -Eastern States being unviable and sought to know about the 
resolution for the same under the NCAP. The Chairman opined that the Ministry of Civil 
Aviation should ask for viability gap funding in case of unviable projects, not force upon the 
State Governments to provide land free of cost. 
15.       Director General, NITI Aayog informed the Committee that NITI Aayog had not given 
any specific comment about Para 13 when it was referred. He stated that the promotion of 
competitive and collaborative federalism is one of the cornerstones of NITI Aayog which is why 
it did not offer any comment on Para 13. He opined that it is an operational matter of the 
Ministry. He was of the view that the policy is not only a nudge; it makes it mandatory for the 
State to provide land. The Chairman requested the DG, NITI Aayog to furnish replies to a 
questionnaire on Para 13(a)(iii) of the NCAP, at the earliest. 
16.       The Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA) stated that the Ministry will consider 
whatever recommendations the Committee would make on this subject with an open mind. He 
submitted that the NCAP is a direction of the Cabinet and the Ministry is bound to comply with 
the directions of the Cabinet. He added that the Ministry would consider any varyin g views 
opined by the Committee. He informed the Committee that fares are not regulated in any manner 
and that airlines have fare buckets that fill up depending on passenger interest. He shared that 50 
per cent of the seats are offered at a reduced fare un der the RCS routes while balance seats are 
unregulated. He highlighted that one or two airlines are defaulting on operationalisation in many 
sectors because of their financial condition.  

153 
 
17.   The Secretary, MoCA informed the Committee that Air India has placed a large order for 
aircraft induction over the next six years, which would help improve the situation of shortage of 
flights. He further informed that many aircraft of many airlines are grounded for want of engines 
which would be resolved on easing of global supply chains. 
18.       Members of the Committee raised queries pertaining to the lack of flights from various 
airports across the country such as Kushinagar Airport, Darbhanga A irport, Itanagar Airport, 
Kannur International Airport and Calicut Airport. The Committee highlighted the issue of the 
Darbhanga sector being auctioned to SpiceJet for operations under RCS. SpiceJet is flying less 
number of flights from Darbhanga and the s ector cannot be operated by anyone else as per the 
policy in this regard. 
19.       Members of the Committee raised various queries pertaining to the following issues:- 
 discontinuation of cargo operations from Patna, Bhubaneswar, Pune, Jammu, Vizag and 
Coimbatore due to non-compliance with BCAS requirements; 
 need for an upper limit for charging fares for flights; 
 amount of funds spent in Civil Aviation under the package announced for Bihar by the 
Hon’ble Prime Minister; 
 lack of facilities for people coming to receive family/friends at Darbhanga airport and for 
passengers waiting to board flights; 
 land-related issues regarding the development of the airport at Mehsana (Gujarat); 
 the targeted date of operationalisation of Gorakhpur airport extension in Bihar; 
 status of operationalisation of Gondia airport in Maharashtra; 
 lack of development of Advanced Landing Grounds (ALGs) in Dirang, Daporijo and 
Anini in Arunachal Pradesh; and 
 delay in the development of Sabarimala airport. 
20. The Secretary, Ministry of Civ il Aviation stated that the volume of cargo at various 
airports where cargo operations have been discontinued is low. He added that there is a viability 
issue and it is not making commercial sense for the cargo terminal operator to invest money to 
arrange additional machines and screeners at these airports. A Member of the Committee 
highlighted the need for AAI Cargo Logistics and Allied Services Company Ltd. (AAICLAS) to 
invest money in these airports to meet the BCAS requirements so as to permit the 
operationalisation of cargo operations thereat.

Report 
Culture is the soul of any nation, and it is our duty to preserve, nurture, and promote our rich 
cultural heritage. In India, we are blessed with a diverse tapestry of cultures, languages, traditions, 
and art forms that have been passed down through generations. It is essential that we ensure the 
proper functioning of our cultural institutions, such as the various Akademis, which play a crucial 
role in preserving and promoting our cultural legacy. 
2. The primary mandate of the Ministry of Cult ure (MoC) is the preservation and conservation 
of ancient cultural heritage and the promotion of tangible and intangible heritage. MoC through its 
organizations is engaged in  the development of the country's rich heritage including art, music, 
dance, theat re, literature, and handicrafts as well as recognition of excellence in these fields. The 
Akademi Bureau of MoC has the overall administrativ e supervision of the following a utonomous 
bodies viz. Sangeet Natak  Akademi, Sahitya Akademi, National School of Dr ama, Lalit Kala 
Akademi, Centre for Cultural Resources and Training, Indira Gandhi National Centre for Arts a nd 
Kalakshetra Foundation. 
3. The Cultural Akademis are the most prestigious in the country and yet there is a growing 
apprehension that they have failed to fulfil their original mandate and have been ineffectual in 
popularising the arts among the  general population. The Committee notes that the promotion of arts 
and culture through Akademis and other Cultural Institutions lacks an integrated approac h since 
there are a host of overlapping functions. This results in duplication of efforts and prevents the 
optimum utilisation of resources. Allegations of administrat ive mismanagement and financial 
irregularities have been levelled against some of the Aka demis. Further, the issue of 
bureaucratisation of the functioning of cultural Akademis which stifles their creative dynamism 
arises from time to time. 
4. The Committee decided to examine these premium Cultural Institutions to understand their 
functioning a nd how to make them more accountable, effective, visible and relevant, without 
impairing their autonomy in any manner. During the course of the examination, the Committee heard 
the Ministry of Culture, Administrative Heads, and elected Heads of National Akademis and other 
Cultural Institutions in its meetings held on 9th May, 2023 and 29th May, 2023, respectively.

Objective and Mandate of the National Akademis and Cultural Institutions 
5. Mandate of the National Akademis and Cultural Institutions 
Sangeet Natak Akademi (SNA), was set up in  1952 as India's national ac ademy of music, dance 
and drama. It is  functioning as the apex body in the field of performing arts in the country, 
preserving and promoting the vast intangible heritage of India's diverse culture.  
Sahitya Akademi  (SA), India’s National Akademi of Letters , established in 1954 by the 
Government of India is the central institution for literature, literary dialogue, publication and 
promotion of literature in the country and the only institution that undertakes literary activities in 24 
languages including English. Sahitya Akademi confers 24 awards for original and creative writing 
every year.  
Lalit Kala Akademi  (LKA) which was inaugurated in 1954, is the N ational Academy of Art and 
Culture and focuses its activities in the field of visual arts  such as sculpture, graphics, ceramics and 
painting. It is an autonomous body, fully funded by the Ministry of Culture.  
The National School of Drama  (NSD) is one of t he foremost theatre training institutions in the 
world and the only one of its kind in India. It was set up by the Sangeet Natak  Akademi as one of its 
constituent units in 1959 and in 1975 became an independent, autonomous organisation fully 
financed by the Ministry of Culture.   
Centre for Cultural Resources and Training  (CCRT), established in 1979 is one of the premier 
institutions working in the field of linking education with culture. CCRT conducts a range of training 
programmes for in-service teachers, educators and administrators across India. 
The Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts (IGNCA), established in the year 1987 is a major 
resource centre for arts and functions as a centre for research, academic pursuit and dissemination in 
the field of arts.  
Kalakshetra, as the name suggests, is a centre for artistic endeavour. Founded in 1936 by the vibrant 
visionary Rukmini Devi Arundale, the institution stands testimony to her dream of creating a space 
where the essence of Indian thought would find e xpression through artistic education, an institution 
she established with the vision “of imparting to the young the true spirit of Art, devoid of vulgarity 
and commercialism.”

The Ministry submitted the following  with regard t o the efforts and ende avours of the Akademis in 
pursuance of their respective mandate: 
Sangeet Natak Akademi (SNA), has been working relentlessly to achieve its mandate to preserve and 
promote the performing art forms of the country. It has successfully achieved its goal by promoting the 
performing arts through audio -video documentation, publications, and by supporting and promoting as 
well as recognizing the artists by giving production and publication grants, by organizing festivals, 
seminars, etc., at various levels, and through Akademi Fellowships and Awards for artists of all age

The Lalit Kala Akademi (LKA) is an institution that has rendered service to the nation in the sphere of 
arts long before the world woke up to the global impact of Indian art.  Central to the Akademi’s mission 
is the encouragement of a deeper understanding and enjoyment of modern and contemporary art by the  
diverse local, national and international audience that it serves.  It is involved in a wide range of 
activities related to the promotion of art and artists through programmes and strategic partnerships by 
organizing Camps/ Workshops / Lecture s/ Seminars/Art Festivals/Exhibition/ Residency 
Programme/Cultural Exchange Programme/ Competition /Film Shows/Slide Shows etc. 
The Centre for Cultural Resources and Training (CCRT) has the mandate of propagation of Culture 
in Schools and Colleges and has provided training to 2,13,659 teachers across the country. The institute 
also ensures its presence in every corner of the country, under its District Resource Person (DRP) 
Scheme by appointing its trained teachers as DRP s who ensure the dissemination of art and culture at 
the grassroots level. Till date , CCRT has trained 10,11,497 under the “Extension Services and 
Community Feedback Programme”. 
The National School of Drama (NSD) has already trained over 1200 theatre Postgraduate Diploma 
students in the performing arts, not only in India but throughout the globe. Beside s regular teaching and 
training programmes, the premier drama institute also engages in extension activities and reaches to the 
nooks and corners of the country by extending support to theatre practitioners and theatre workers. NSD 
has consistently produced thespians and popular artists of silver screen and most of the students get 
employed in the respective fields of direction, production, acting and lighting etc.

Election and Tenure of Heads of the National Akademis and Cultural Institutions 
16. The Ministry informed the following with regard to the election and tenure of the Heads of 
the National Akademis: 
Sahitya Akademi (SA) 
The President of the Sahitya Akademi  is selected by the new General Council from a max imum 
three-person’s panel to be forwarded by the outgoing Executive Board. The outgoing Executive 
Board selects the panel from the names forwarded by the outgoing General Council. The President 
continues in office until the election of the new President by the new General Co uncil at its first 
meeting. The General Council has 100 representatives from different sources. The State 
Governments and Union Territories send three nominations each.   The Ministry also receives 
nominations of three names each from all 350 Central and St ate Universities where Humanities are 
being taught,  out of which representatives of twenty universities are selected on a rotation basis.   
There is also a provision for 24 language representatives and about 10 ex -officio members like Joint 
Secretary etc. The authority vests in the General Council of the Akademi which also elects the 
President of the Akademi for a period of five years. 
 
Lalit Kala Akademi (LKA) 
The Lalit Kala Akademi  is an autonomous body, fully funded by the Ministry of Culture. It 
comprises of the General Council and Executive Board for three years and the term of the Chairman 
is for three years.  Chairman, Lalit Kala Akademi is appointed through a 3 -Member Search 
Committee, (one member is nominated by the General Council of the Akademi and the other two 
members shall be nominated by the Pre sident of India; and one out of three members may be a 
woman). The Search Commit tee submits recommendations of three  names to the President of India.  
The President of India appoints one out of the three names for Chairmanship. The General Council 
of the Akademi consist s of 65 Members.  The term of the members of the Executive Board as are 
elected by the General Co uncil or nominated by the Government of India or the Chairman for 
membership of the Executive Board is three years.

Lalit Kala Akademi informed the  Committee that its administration was taken over by the Government 
of India in 2015. The government took over in order to form the General Council, Executive Board, 
Finance Committee and Programme Committee as there was no General Council or Executive Board in 
2013. The government handed over the administration to Lalit Kala Akademi in 2018 and  the Chairman 
was appointed. Thereafter, the General Council, the Executive Board and the Finance Committee were 
formed following due process. Now, all these Committees are in place. 
 
Sangeet Natak Akademi (SNA) 
The Chairman, Sangeet Natak  Akademi, is appointed by the  President of India for a period of five 
years. The Sangeet Natak Akademi has 72 M embers, with one representative nominated by each S tate 
Government in addition to e xperts, Government nominees and E x-officio Members. The management 
of the Akademi is vested in its Governing Council which is elected for a period of five years. 
 
National School of Drama (NSD) 
In the case of the National School of Drama , Chairman is appointed by the President of India and the 
tenure of the appointment is four  years. NSD has a Society of 14 M embers to run the Akademi.  The 
Members of the Society are nominate d by the Central Government, Ministry of Culture/ Ministry of 
Information and Broadcasting. 
 
IGNCA 
IGNCA has a Board of Trustees and an Executive Council  drawn from the Board of Trustees.  The 
Executive Council is headed by  the President who is appointed by the Trustees  from amongst 
themselves. The tenure of appo intment of the President is ten years. The number of Members in the 
Governing Council ranges fr om 7 to 21.   The Members of the Executive Committee are  drawn from 
among the Trustees and function under a Chairman. 
 
CCRT  
The Chairman of CCRT is appointed by the Gov ernment of India, Ministry of Culture for a period of 
four years.  The Vice Chairman of CCRT is appointed by the Society, CCRT  from amongst its 
members. The Members are nominated by the Central Government, the Ministry of Culture  and their 
total number is 18.

held, etc.   Also, there are no people’s representatives in the Governing Council of the Akademis. 
18. The Committee observes that there are different parameters for different Akademis.  In 
Committee’s view, this lack of uniformity is not desirable as it leads to administrative and 
organisational inconsistencies among the various Akademis and Institutions. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends Government to formulate a policy emphasising uniformity among all the 
Akademis in terms of the tenure of the  Chairman/President, representation and election of the 
General Council, and the minimum number of meetings to be held each  year. If required, 
legislation governing the Akademis/ Institutions may be amended to ensure uniformity among the 
Akademis and their functionaries. 
19. Committee, further, suggests that  one Member of Parliament should be included on the 
Governing Board of each of the Institutions on the lines of All India Institute of Medical Sciences 
and other such institutions to assist the working of Akademis and to provide ground report s to the 
Akademis.  
20. The Committee also recommends that there i s a need to increase the involvement of States 
in the overall functioning of the National Akademis and other Cultural Institutions and this may 
be done by giving representation to all States in the administrative set -up and through 
collaboration with cultu ral bodies at the state level.  In this regard, proper consultations must be 
conducted with all States.

The Ministry should evolve a well -designed digitization program that includes not just digital 
capture, but also appropriate care and repair of original materials, and long-term management of 
the digital files it produces.

2.         At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Members and informed them that the 
agenda of the meeting was to deliberate on the subject of “Functioning of National 
Akademies and other Cultural Institutions”. The Chairman also informed the Members 
that as the Secre tary, Ministry of Culture had sought exemption, the Committee would 
instead hear the Joint Secretary of the Ministry along with the administrative heads of all 
the National Cultural Akademies. 
(After the witnesses took their respective seats) 
3.           The Chairman noted that the Akademies have been given autonomous status to 
ensure their freedom of expression but issues of bureaucratisation of the cultural 
institutions which hampers their creative dynamism arise from time to time.   The 
Chairman asked that the Committee may be briefed on this issue as well as the challenges 
faced due to lack of infrastructure, manpower shortages and bureaucratic hurdles. He 
asked the Ministry and Akademies to elaborate on the measures taken to promote and 
preserve cultural traditions in the digital age.  The Chairman also noted that there were 
allegations of administrative and financial irregularities in the functioning of some of the 
Akademies, especially the Lalit Kala Akademi and desired that the Committee may be 
briefed in this regard. The Chairman asked the JS whether the budgetary support provided 
by the Ministry to each institution/Akademi is adequate to meet their needs and whether 
any financial assistance is provided to artists/scholars by the Akademies/Ministry.   Citing 
an article in a newspaper  wherein Ministry officials were quoted as stating that Cultural 
Akademies should mobilize funds only from non -governmental sources and not depend 
on government funding, the Chairman enquired about the legality of such proposals.    
4. The Joint Secretary informed the Committee that there were seven Cultural 
Akademies, the oldest being Kalakshetra Foundation (founded in 1936), then the Sangeet 
Natak Akademi (established 1952), the Sahitya Akademi and the Lalit Kala Akademi 
(both established in 1954), the National School of Drama (NSD) (established 1959), the 
Centre for Cultural Resources and Training (CCRT) (established in 1979) and the newest 
being the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts (IGNCA) (established in 1985).  

92 
 
5.         The mandate of the Kalakshetra Foundation is mostly   Bharatnatyam and Carnatic 
Music while the Sangeet Natak Akademi promotes the intangible heritage of dance, 
music, and drama.   The Sahitya Akademi   promotes literature, including   children's 
literature. The Lalit Kala Akademi   is  working on tribal traditional arts and ceramic art.   
The NSD is working in the field of theatre. The CCRT is working for educating   school 
children on culture. The IGNCA works as a repository of all the art forms in the country 
and does a lot of research and documentation..   
6.         In response to a query by a Member, the representative of the Ministry informed 
that the tenures of Chairmen/ Presidents are different for different Akademis. In the case 
of Lalit Kala Akademi, the tenure is three years. The NSD and the CCRT are having four 
years tenure. IGNCA has the longest tenure of ten years while the remaining three 
Akademis have a tenure of five years.   Each Akademi, since they are autonomous bodies, 
has its own General Council and an Executive Board. 
7.         In response to another query about the election of the Chairman/President of the 
Akademies, the representative of the Ministry explained that the process was again 
different for different Akademies.  The Chairman of Lalit Kala Akademi is a presidential 
nomination chosen from a list of 3 -4 experts in the field of art picked out by a  Search-
cum-Selection Committee, which is appointed by the Ministry.   The General Council has 
65 members drawn mostly from the n ominations received from each State/ Union 
Territory as well as the nomination of 5    members from the Government of India and ex -
officio members like the Joint Secretary (Akademis) and the Finance Member.   All the 
members have voting rights and decisions are taken on majority vote.  
8.         The President of the Sahitya Akademi, usually a person of eminence in the literary 
field, is elected by the General Council. The General Council has 100 representatives 
from different sources. The State Governments a nd Union Territories send three 
nominations each.  The Ministry also receives nominations of three names each from all 
the about 350 Central and State Universities where Humanities are being taught,   out of 
which representatives of twenty universities are selected on a rotation basis.  There is also 
a provision for 24 language representatives and about 10 ex -officio members like Joint 
Secretary etc.   Upon a query by a Member, it was informed that there were only 20 
members in the University category and car e was taken during selection to include all 
States on a rotation basis since some states had only one university.  

93 
 
9.       The Sangeet Natak Akademi has 72 members, with one representative nominated 
by each State Government in addition to experts, governm ent nominees and ex -officio 
members.  
10.       The National School of Drama and Kalakshetra are mainly training institutes. The 
Chairman of the NSD is appointed by the President while the NSD Director is a 
Government appointee.   Both are appointed by the Government from among three 
candidates selected by a search cum selection committee.    
11.  The Chairman remarked that there are different parameters for different Akademies 
and there is a need to bring uniformity among all the Akademies in terms of tenur e of 
Chairmen/President and representation and election of General Council members.    The 
representative of the Ministry acknowledged that as most Akademies have been   in 
existence  since the 1950s, there is a need to change the age -old systems and the Ministry 
has  taken cognizance of the same 
12.     The representative of the Ministry also informed that the IGNCA has   9 centres 
across the country, the Lalit Kala Akademi (LKA) and the Sangeet Natak Akademi 
(SNA) have 7 each, and the Sahitya Akademi and the  NSD have 5 each while CCRT has   
4.  Upon query by Members about the reason for no centres being in states like 
Rajasthan, the Ministry informed that Zonal Cultural Centres cater to cultural needs in 
places which do not have Regional Centres. Besides, the Akademies and CCRT conduct 
shows and workshops even in places where are no centres.   
13. A Member enquired about the mechanism of preservation and promotion of the 
intangible culture of India. He gave examples of artists from around the country, the lack 
of recognition of their work and the ways to promote their work. The Ministry elaborated 
on their efforts to promote the unsung heroes of India like the event of Jyotirgamaya of 
Sangeet Natak Akademi in Rajasthan which comprised 350 artists for five days. 
Similarly, an event in Delhi focussed on instrument making. Upon further discussion and 
observations by some Members about the lack of visibility of the programmes and 
workshops conducted by the Ministry, the representative of the Ministry stated that the 
entire information about the last three years of the programmes, workshops and other 
activities done in Rajasthan and other states would be provided   institution-wise.  A 
Member suggested that  a meeting can be held once in three months in the State Capital  

94 
 
about the working of the Akademies to which    Members of Parliament   can also be 
invited.    
14. Upon a Member’s query whether the Akademies have tribal members the JS informed 
the Committee that the Ministry promotes all States’ art forms and any tribal art expert 
nominated by the State Government, is taken as a member.  
15.       The Committee was further informed about the achievements of the various 
Cultural Akademies - 
 the Sahitya Akademi held   India’s largest international literature festival – 
UNMESHA in Shimla under the Azadi Ka Amrit Mahotsav (AKAM) , that hosted 
64 events featuring more than 400 writers and scholars and the Festival of Letters 
in New Delhi which featured more than 400 writers, hosted 40 events and 
promoted 60 languages.      The Akademi also maintains the   archives for Indian 
literature and every year conducts more than 50 regional, national and 
international seminars and 100 symposiums and about 400 literary gatherings in 
every language. 
 the Kalakshetra Foundation inaugurated a 'Bharata Kalakshetra Auditorium,"    
free-of-cost dance classes for children in low socio -economic strata, Seminars and 
workshops to propagate craft, culture and education,  Kalanubhava, a First-ever art 
exhibition by  Rukmani Devi College of Fine Arts and a cultural festival at 
Mahabalipuram in presence of Hon’ble President of India and His Highness King 
of Netherlands etc.  
 Achievements of the NSD included the International Theatre Festival of India 
(Bharat Rang Mahot sav) where 100 theatre groups from India and abroad 
participate every year in February since 1999, National Theatre Festival organised 
for children (Jashn -e-bachpan & Bal Sangam), organises Indian Classical Drama 
Festival since 2016, Poorvottar Natya Samaroh since 2009 
 the achievements of the IGNCA   included the National Mission of Cultural 
Mapping, New Parliament artwork and the Vedic Heritage Portal,   Mera Gaon 
Meri Darohar (MGMD) initiative to document 6 lakh+ villages on various cultural 
parameters, lik e documentation of Devnarayan Phad tradition, the revival of the 

95 
 
art form of Ramman in a Joshimath village and in instrument making, the revival 
of original Tanpuras in Dharwar and many instruments of the North-East.  
 the achievements of the LKA included o rganising art camps and exhibitions and 
workshops and award of fellowships to artists selected from all over the country. 
 the achievements of the   Sangeet Natak Akademi Awards includes, organising the 
15th Sattriya Sangeet Samaroh to increase awareness ab out the Sattriya Music 
tradition, four-day music/dance/drama festival-Amrit Yuva Kalotsav for recipients 
of the Yuva Puruskar, organizing Jyotirgamaya where artists can register 
themselves on the SNA website with proof of their talent.   
  Under the CCRT’s initiatives  2,13,659 teachers have been trained since inception 
till date and 10,11,497 students were trained under ‘Extension Services & 
Community Feedback Programme.’ 14,637 and 1,908 scholarships were awarded 
under Cultural Talent Sea rch Scholarship Scheme (CTSS) and Scholarships to 
Young Artistes (SYA) Schemes respectively. 2,142 Junior/Senior fellowships 
were awarded from 2014 to till date. CCRT has also produced 57 publications and 
46 documentary films.  
16. The Committee was also i nformed that all the Akademies were contributing 
substantially for the Azadi Ka Amrit Mahotsav (AKAM).   A programme called Kalanjali 
is being held regularly at the Central Vista where there are performances of various art 
forms and music bands.

REPORT  
 
 
Ports play a pivotal role in the economic developme nt of a country. They serve as 
important gateways for international trade, facilit ating the movement of goods and 
commodities between countries. The main functions o f the early ports were cargo handling 
and storage, gradually expanding to packaging and d istribution. The role and function of 
ports have evolved over time along with the evoluti on of maritime transport technology. The 
development of container transportation in the earl y 1980s witnessed a sea change in the role 
of ports from traditional services to value-added l ogistics services, eventually leading to the 
emergence of a new intermodal transport system.   
 
2. A modern seaport is not merely a transit area bu t a crucial link in a global supply 
chain ecosystem. Today, ports compete for seamless integration in supply chains to create 
added value to the cargo passing through the port. The share of the major and non-major 
ports of India in cargo traffic reflects the realit y of the changing roles of the Ports. The Major 
Ports of India are facing stiff competition from th e ports styled as Minor Ports though the 
distinction is only in terms of jurisdiction. The major ports a re under the direct administrative 
control of the Central Government  and fall in the Union List in the 7 th  Schedule of the 
Constitution. Ports other than the major ones are u nder the jurisdiction of the respective State 
Maritime Board and fall in the Concurrent List.  
 
3. Though port traffic in India registered a steady  rise year after year, reflecting the 
country’s growing international trade, yet the shar e of non-major ports in the handling of 
overall traffic has been steadily increasing compar ed to the major ports. Of the total traffic 
handled by all Indian ports, the Major Ports handle  55% whereas the Minor Ports handle 
45%. The impressive performance of the non-major po rts is reflective of the greater 
operational efficiencies, freedom to fix tariffs, a vailability of vast storage space at nominal 
prices, longer concession periods, low waterfront r oyalties and so on. In contrast, the major 
ports suffer from old and inadequate infrastructure , low draft depths and poor hinterland 
connectivity. Further, major ports under the Tariff  Authority for Major Ports (TAMP) regime 
earlier and various other regulatory controls strug gle to sustain in the tough competition vis-
à-vis non-major ports . 
 
4. To enable the Major Ports to be competitive with  the private players in the sector and 
to infuse professionalism and transparency in the g overnance of the Ports, the Major Port 
Authorities Act, 2021 was passed which bestowed on the Major Ports greater autonomy. As a 
result, the control of TAMP has been diminished and  the Port Authority (erstwhile Port 
Trust) now has the power to enter into contracts an d fix the tariffs as per the market 
conditions, enabling them to compete with the priva te players. Further, to harness the private 
sector's potential, the Government has formulated p olicies to attract them for infrastructure 
development through Public Private Partnerships (PPP). 

2 
 
5. The Major Port Authorities Act and the Indian Po rts Act are the two principal statu tes 
in the sector, which provide for the constitution o f the major port authorities and the 
administration, control and management of the ports . The Indian Ports Act also contains 
provisions for the operation, pilotage and other related issues for the non-major ports.   
 
6. The earlier Major Port Trusts were administered by their respective Board of Trustees 
headed by the Chairman, and the Members of the Boar d were nominated by the Government 
of India from various stakeholders of the port. Con sequent upon the enactment of the Major 
Port Authorities Act 2021, the board for each major  port will now include representatives 
from the state government, the Ministry of Railways, the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of 
Customs, and the Department of Revenue as members. In addition, the board will have a 
government nominee member and a representative of t he employees of the Major Port 
Authority. 
 
7. There are 12 major ports and about 213 non-major  ports along India's vast coastline, 
which is approximately 7,517 km. Six Major Ports, viz.,  Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port 
(SMP), Kolkata, Paradip Port, Visakhapatnam Port, K amarajar Port (Ennore), Chennai Port 
and V.O. Chidambaranar Port, are on the east coast and the other Six Major Ports, viz., 
Cochin Port, New Mangalore Port, Mormugao Port, Mum bai Port, Jawaharlal Nehru Port 
(Sheva, Navi Mumbai) and Deendayal Port (erstwhile Kandla) are on the west coast.  
 
8. The oldest Major Port of India is the Kolkata Po rt, now called the Syama Prasad 
Mookerjee Port. It is also the country's only Major  Riverine port. The second oldest port, 
Mumbai Port, is also India's largest Natural port a nd harbour. Out of the 12 Major Ports, the 
Kamarajar Port or the Ennore Port in Tamil Nadu is the only corporatized port registered as a 
Company.  
 
9. To study the impact of the various policy initia tives taken by the Government on the 
functioning of the Major Ports, the PPP partnership s entered into by the Major Ports and the 
technological advancements introduced to improve po rt performances, the Department 
Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transpo rt, Tourism and Culture decided to 
take up the subject "Functioning of Major Ports in the Country" for examination and report 
thereon. As a sequel to an examination of the subje ct, the Committee called for Background 
Notes and Replies to Questionnaires formulated to o btain exhaustive information on the 
relevant topics relating to port performance and de velopment. The Committee heard the 
views of the Secretary, Ministry of Ports, Shipping  and Waterways on the subject in its 
meeting held on the 24 
th   April 2023, the representatives of the Indian Por ts Association and 
the Indian Private Ports and Terminals Association on 17 th   May 2023,  the representatives of 
the Minor private ports, the Gujarat Pipavav Port a nd the JSW Jaigarh Port, Maharashtra on 
the 16 th  June 2023 and the representatives of Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation of India 
Limited (DFCCIL) on the 26 th  June, 2023.

lack of proper evacuation facilities, old flotilla, to name only a few.

Average Output per ship berth day (OSBD): The average OSBD 
measured in tonnes of cargo.

Annexure-I details the origin, location, type of cargo, numbe r of container terminals,

various Performance Parameters of the individual Ma jor Ports and comparisons with global

TRAFFIC HANDLED BY MAJOR PORTS  
12. The Ministry informed that the total traffic ha ndled by all ports, both Major and 
Minor, was 1445 MT against a total capacity of 2627  MT per annum. The Committee 
observes that the total traffic handled by the Major Ports in 2022-23 was 796 MT, an increase 
of 10.41% over the preceding year of 720 MT, while the traffic handled by Minor Ports was 
650 MT. In all, the share of Major Ports in total c argo handled was 55% and that of Minor 
Ports was 45%. In his deposition, the Secretary inf ormed the Committee that this incremental 
increase of 10% in the total traffic handled by the  Major Ports is the highest ever increase in 
cargo handling. The Secretary also informed that in  2022-23, the Major Ports had reversed 
the trend of their declining market share as in 2021-22, major ports handled 54 per cent of the 
total cargo, and the non-major ports, all combined, handled 46 per cent.   
 
13. The Committee observes that the cargo handling of the Major Ports has been 
steadily increasing over the years, and only in the last year has there been an increase of 
10%. On a query by the Committee, the Ministry repl ied that to augment the volume of 
cargo handling, the Port Authorities have also expl ored the possibility of generating 
new cargo to reduce the gap between the actual traf fic and the capacity. Major Ports 
also organize trade meets to attract traffic from t heir hinterland/region. Several steps 
have also been taken to boost coastal shipping.   
 
14. The Committee also observes that the increase o f 10% has come primarily due to 
JNPA’s impressive performance, followed by Paradip and Deendayal Port. There is

by the remaining nine Major Ports and recommends th at the Ministry come out with a 
focused and calibrated strategy to raise the cargo handling performance of such Major 
Ports .

th  position globally regarding 
container traffic handled. Massive Container Ships invariably require deep drafts, and

CAPACITY OF MAJOR PORTS  
16. There are no two views that the capacity of Maj or Ports has increased over the years. 
However, the capacity utilisation was only around 4 9%. The Ministry informed the 
Committee that the total capacity of both major and  non-major ports in the country is 2627 
million tonnes per annum, of which about 1,600 mill ion tonnes per annum is the capacity of 
the major ports, and the other 1000 million tonnes per annum is the capacity of the non-major 
ports. The capacity utilisation of the major ports is about 49 %, and that of the non-major 
ports is around 64%. 
 
17. The Secretary, while responding to a query duri ng deposition before the Committee 
said that in the Ports Sector, 70% of capacity util isation is considered to be saturation and the 
beginning of congestion in the ports. The Major Por ts continuously augment their cargo 
handling capacity to meet the ever growing needs of  the economy. In 2015, the capacity was 
only 872 MT and in 2022, it has grown to touch 1,60 0 MT. The Secretary further elucidated 
that had the capacity not been expanded by nearly 8 00 MT in the last eight years, the ports 
would have reached 90% of their capacity and got ch oked. There are ports in which the 
capacity utilisation has touched even 70 per cent, but, on average, the capacity utilisation is 
around 49 per cent for the major ports. The only ex ception is the Goa port which has only 
27% capacity and is in a negative growth trajectory . The future target of capacity addition is 
to achieve 2000+ MTPA by 2030. Several capacity aug mentation projects are already under 
implementation, like the mechanisation of berths, m odernisation of facilities, improving 
productivity and efficiency, bringing in best practices at the ports, etc.  
 
18. The Committee observes that while port capacity  is considered to be saturated at 
70-75% of capacity, some of the Major Ports are fun ctioning far below the mark. 
Mormugao operates at only 27% capacity, while Chenn ai and VoCA operate just at 
32%.  
 
19. The Committee observes that there is still much  untapped potential to be 
harnessed so as to increase the capacity of most of  the Major Ports. The Committee 
points out that the capacity utilization of the Non -Major Ports in India has remained at 
64%, which is much higher than the average capacity utilization in the Major Ports and 
recommends that the Major Ports may set targets to increase the utilization of their 
existing capabilities to an optimum level.

DRAFTS OF INDIAN PORTS VERSUS FOREIGN PORTS  
32. Maritime India Vision 2030 has suggested that 1 6 meter deep drafts would be 
essential to improve the cargo handling capacity of  Indian Mega Ports. Most of the Major 
ports have already achieved a draft of 14 meters, a nd some other ports, namely Kamarajar, 
Paradip, Deendayal and Cochin, are striving to achi eve much deeper drafts of up to 18 
meters. To ensure the smooth movement of ships, the  Ports regularly take up maintenance 
dredging of channels and berths. 
 
33. The Committee observes that the world over, the  shipping industry is moving 
towards mega-size vessels with ships of 20,000 TEU and above. While a Capesize vessel 
requires upwards of 18m draft, the draft at Indian ports is in the range of 14-16 meters 
only, owing to siltation. The Committee observes th at the geographical and 
topographical limitations are identical for both th e public and private ports in India, 
but the private  ports have been able to develop drafts matching wi th world-class ports 
whereas the public ports have lagged behind. The Gu jarat Pipavav port has a draft of 
18.5 metres and plans to extend it to 20.5 metres. The Committee, while acknowledging 
the high dredging costs, underscores that the ports  drafts must be in sync with the 
growing size of the ships in the interest of maximi zing the benefits of large ships in 
cargo handling. 
 
34. Ports must increase draft according to the resp ective cargo profile. Indian 
container terminals must target an 18m+ draft.  Wit h the evolving ship types and 
increasing port parcel sizes, loading and discharge  rates must be enhanced. The 
Committee also emphasizes that greater ship sizes a nd container loads need increased 
mechanization at Indian ports to improve the loadin g and unloading ecosystem. Dual-
cycle cranes and Automated Guided Vehicles (AGVs) m ay be introduced in ports to 
ensure incremental productivity.  
 
35. The Committee observes that the Indian Private Ports and Terminals 
Association (IPPTA) had stated in its deposition be fore the Committee that most of the 
tugs deployed by major ports had outlived their eff ective life and are operating beyond 
economic conditions. The service levels rendered by  them do not match the Industry 
Standards. Private Tug Companies should be encourag ed to render towage services at 
Major Ports in line with the international practice s. The Committee calls upon the 
Ministry to consider this issue on merit.

III. PORT MECHANIZATION AND MODERNIZATION 
67. The level of mechanisation at Indian ports, par ticularly major ports, is limited, and 
most of the commodities are handled by conventional  means. This has meant significantly 
higher turnaround time and cargo dwell time at thes e ports than the international standards, 

15 
 
thus, high overall logistics costs. Increased mecha nisation of berths equipped with high-
capacity cranes, conveyor systems, grab unloaders, etc. have the potential to  improve overall 
productivity. The Major Ports, however, are also co nstrained by the non-availability of funds 
to bring in large-scale mechanisation at their exis ting berths and depend on stevedores 
(persons employed at docks to load/unload cargos) t o handle cargoes. Further, the cargo 
throughput should reach a threshold value for the m echanisation of berths to make the 
investment a viable proposition. Some ports have ou tsourced the requirement by inviting the 
private sector to invest, install and operate mobil e harbour cranes, etc. while other ports have 
adopted the PPP route to achieve this objective. Annexure-V shows the status of 
mechanisation of berths at Major Ports.  
 
68. The Ministry informed that the mechanisation of  berths is a continuous process, and 
complete mechanisation of all berths in most of the  Major Ports is expected to be completed 
by 2030. As a part of the National Monetisation Pip eline Plan, Ports and the Government 
have proposed privatization of the existing berths.  Under this Plan, 31 port projects involving 
mechanisation and modernisation have been identifie d to be developed on PPP basis with an 
estimated capital cost of Rs. 12,828 crores to be completed by 2024-25. 
 
69. The Committee observes that only 35%  of total berths are mechanised in the 
Major Ports. Only Kandla port has all of its berths mechanised.

IV. DEVELOPMENT OF MEGA PORTS, NEW PORTS AND TRANSH IPMENT 
HUBS 
74. Across the world, mega ports are cropping up, w ith better infrastructure, faster 
operations, lower operational costs, and higher cap acity to handle large cargo volumes and 
mega-ships.  
India needs to have mega-port and terminal infrastr ucture to handle Ultra-large ships, that 
seek speedy unloading of the large volumes they car ry. Ports need a higher draft, several 
large cranes, better yard management capability, in creased automation, more extensive 
storage facilities, more inland port connectivity and enhanced labour productivity. 
 
75. The Ministry informed that India has 05 Major P orts and 2 Non-Major Ports with over 
100 MTPA capacity. Two existing Major Ports i.e. De endayal Port and Paradip Port, have 
been identified to be transformed into Mega Ports h aving cargo handling capacity of 300+ 
MTPA. A new Vadhavan Port will also be developed as  the country’s Mega Port, having a 
cargo handling capacity of about 300 MTPA. 
 
76. The Ministry informed that the key challenges i n creating mega ports are Land 
Acquisition, Environmental Concerns, and Financing and detailed the various steps to 
address these challenges:- 
• Identifying locations which are possessing natural drafts up to 24 m with the 
availability of huge land banks and scope for devel oping industrial complexes close by 
and the required ecosystem like Special Economic Zo nes, Industrial Zones, Free Trade 
Warehousing Zones, Container Freight Stations, etc. 
• Stringent environmental policy/regulation is enforc ed to minimize the impact of port 
development on ecosystems. 
• Huge investments are required for developing such m ega ports, and the viability of 
developing such ports has to be established with gr ants/viability funding from the 
Government. 
• The Government has prioritized the development of p ort infrastructure, including the 
creation of deep draft channels, the construction o f modern berths, and the 
establishment of storage facilities.  
• Connectivities by water/rail/road to the hinterland  need to be established. Linkage 
through dedicated rail freight corridors will be of help. 
 
77. The Committee observes that the economies of sc ale in maritime trade have 
given rise to Mega ships or Capesize Ships, which n aturally require larger terminals 
and ports. Indian ports presently lack the infrastr ucture to deal with Capesize ships 

17 
 
which are vital to international maritime trade. As  Indian ports are gearing up to 
handle these giant ships by increasing their draft depths and modernizing the ports, 
India should also plan for developing Mega Ports to  handle the ever-increasing size of 
vessels and Containers. The Committee also recommen ds that while planning for the 
mega port, the Ministry may also arrange for linkag es with the local economy, creating 
industrial clusters to be economic drivers for the region.

DEVELOPMENT OF TRANSHIPMENT HUBS  
83. The Committee observes that Indian Ports handle  only 25% of Indian transhipment 
cargo, and international ports such as Colombo and Singapore handle the rest, leading to loss 
of revenue opportunities for India. The transhipmen t at ports outside India mostly happens 
regarding container traffic generated on India's So uth & East Coast. Colombo accounts for 
48% of Indian international cargo, Singapore 22% and Malaysia's Port Klang 10%. 
 
84. Ports on India's west coast are mostly gateway ports that send cargo containers 
directly to destinations. In contrast, those on the  east coast rely on transhipment at nearby 
hubs. Only a few ports in south India have the wate r depth to match global cargo handling 
efficiencies and function as a transhipment hub. Th e main ports currently handling the 
transhipment cargo are Jawaharlal Nehru Port, Cochi n Port, V.O. Chidambaranar Port, 
Kamarajar Port, Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, and Mumbai Port.  
 
85. Exporters and importers in south India incur an  additional charge of 
/Rupee 5,000- /Rupee 6,000 
per TEU due to extra port handling at transhipment hubs, making them less competitive, 
adding huge costs to the economy and resulting in I ndian ports losing as much as /Rupee 1,500 
crore per year in business. India is also losing th e opportunity to become a large hub for 
Asia–Africa, Asia-US/ Europe container traffic trade. 
 
86. The major challenges in developing Indian ports  as transhipment hubs are as follows: 
(i) Lack of sufficient drafts at Indian ports is one of  the main reasons why big ships 
carrying transhipment containers cannot call at Ind ian ports. The shipping industry is 
moving towards mega-size vessels and above. 16 – 18 m drafts are required to handle 
these vessels, while a Capesize vessel requires 18m+ draft.  
(ii) Absence of modern and highly sophisticated equipmen t like Dual Cycle Cranes and 
AGVs -which can deliver incremental productivities in less time. 
(iii) Many Indian ports do not enjoy the locational advan tage like Colombo Port which 
enjoys a highly critical location advantage due to the proximity to the East-West Trade 
route, which is only 19 nautical miles away from the main route. 
(iv) With efficient cargo services and high operational performance, Colombo Port offers 
competitive Terminal Handling Charges, which makes it an attractive Hub in the 
region.   
 
87. With the focus on self-reliance from a cargo tr ade perspective, Maritime India Vision 
2030 (MIV 2030) has set the target of achieving 75%  of the total transhipment volumes at 
Indian Ports. Developing a transhipment hub in Indi a will create new revenue streams and 
solidify the presence of Indian ports on global maritime routes.

VII. LOGISTICS AND EASE OF DOING BUSINESS  
125. Upon query by the Committee regarding the high  Logistics costs in India, currently 
constituting 13-14% of India’s GDP, as compared to 9% in China and 8% in US and Europe, 
which drive up the overall cost of doing business i n the Indian shipping sector, the Ministry 
informed that National Logistics Policy has been la unched by DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce 
and Industry (MoCI) with an objective to lower the cost of logistics from its current 14% of 
GDP to less than 10% by 2022. The policy aims at ma king Indian goods more competitive 
while also promoting economic growth and expanding job possibilities. The Policy 
establishes a broad, multi-jurisdictional, cross-sectoral framework for the growth of the entire 
logistics ecosystem to address concerns of high cost and inefficiency.  
 
126. In this respect, various interventions are bei ng taken up by MoRTH including 
continued expansion of the National Highways networ k in the country and Bharatmala 
Pariyojana Phase 1 Project where approx. ~34,800 Km s road network is under Development. 
Bharatmala scheme is reviving the entire road devel opment scenario and providing the 
required impetus for speedy implementation of new a ge highways and expressways thereby 
enhancing the speed of cargo movement across the nation. 
 
127. Additionally, 35 Multi-modal Logistics Parks ( MMLPs) on PPP have been identified 
by MoRTH for implementation. The MMLP at Chennai ha s already been awarded, and bids 
invited for MMLPs in Nagpur, Indore & Bengaluru; wi th another 10+ awards to be made by 
FY2025.  
 
128. Moreover, Ministry of Railways is preparing co mprehensive plans for multimodal 
connectivity to MMLP and Rail Gati Shakti Terminals . This will provide the much-needed 
impetus towards establishing cost efficient and sea mless multimodal network for cargo 
movement in the country. 
 
129. To bring down the overall cost of doing busine ss, most of the major ports have taken 
steps such as concessions in vessel and cargo relat ed charges and installation of RFID based 
access control system at gates for faster movement of trucks. Ports are also undertaking 
extensive mechanization of berths. Further, under E ase of Doing Business (EoDB), the ports 
have taken various measures in the areas like Infra structure improvement, simplification of 
process and digitalization to reduce overall logistics time and cost. 
 
130. The Committee observes that the main reasons f or high logistics cost in India are:– 
• The highly fragmented and unorganized nature of the  Indian logistics sector especially 
in Tier II and III cities. Lack of big players to o ffer cost advantage of scale drives up 
the logistics costs, along with hampering the free movement of trucks and price 

26 
 
settlements. 
• Absence of automation in logistics also leads to poor productivity. Unorganized players 
in the logistics market prefer to utilize the easil y available high amount of labour rather 
than invest in technology and automation. The unorg anized sector and lack of 
automation leads to low supply chain visibility and  no means to reduce the waiting 
times.   
 
131. In the ports sector the High Vessel related ch arges in the Major Ports were also 
related to higher maritime logistics cost - 
 
132. The Committee was informed by the IPPTA in its  deposition that the vessel related 
charges at Indian major ports are very high when co mpared to the charges at nearby non-
major ports and foreign ports. The share of non-maj or ports in the traffic handled gradually 
increased from about 10% in the beginning of this c entury to about 45% now. Much of the 
cargo was the diverted cargo from nearby major ports.  
 
133. High port tariffs make Indian ports uncompetit ive compared to their global peers in 
their bid to attract more large-size direct calls. Rival foreign transhipment hubs of Colombo, 
Sri Lanka; Jebel Ali, United Arab Emirates; Singapo re; and Port Klang, Malaysia, apply 
substantially lower marine charges than those at Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust (JNPT), Cochin, 
Chennai, Visakhapatnam, etc. 
 
134. Another charge which adds to the vessel relate d charges is the Light House Dues 
(LHD) – which is also very high compared to ports/h ubs in neighbouring countries. A 
comparison of the LHD between Cochin & Colombo is given at Annexure – X. 
  
135. The Committee observes that reduction in port charges is essential if maritime 
logistics costs are to be reduced. The Committee fu rther observes that the Port Call costs 
for India and the Light House Dues are nearly four times than that of the ports of other 
countries. The Committee has been informed that Ves sel Related Charges (VRCs) can be 
reduced only by reducing the Operating Expenses but  due to the salary payments, legacy 
pension payments and the requirement of discount of  50% in case of cruise vessels for 
promotion of cruise tourism, most ports have very l imited leeway of reducing the 
operating expenses. Therefore, reduction in Vessel Related Charges is an unsustainable 
proposition for ports.

155. The Committee notes that the United Nations Cl imate Change Conference (COP21) 
held in Paris adopted by 196 Parties, including Ind ia, on 12 December 2015 regarding 
globally agreed goals for action on climate change,  aims to keep the global surface 
temperature rise well below 2 
/uni2009°C above pre-industrial levels, while pursuing effo rts to keep

156. Shipping plays a central role in global supply  chains and is a significant source of 
Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions. The industry curren tly accounts for about 3% of CO2 
emissions but the enormous scale and volume of mari time transport means that its 
contribution to global CO2 emissions would continuo usly increase in the next decade. 
Decarbonization of the sector must receive top poli cy priority if the world is to achieve net 
zero emissions by 2050.    
 
157. The International Maritime Organisation (IMO) Initial Strategy on the reduction of 
GHG emissions from shipping has the goals as -  
• Cut annual greenhouse gas emissions from internatio nal shipping by at least half by 
2050, compared with their level in 2008, and work towards phasing out GHG emissions 
from shipping entirely as soon as possible in this century.  
• The Initial GHG Strategy envisages a reduction in c arbon intensity of international 
shipping (to reduce CO2 emissions per transport wor k), as an average across 
international shipping, by at least 40% by 2030, pu rsuing efforts towards 70% by 2050, 
compared to 2008.

XI. ACTS AND LEGISLATIONS, MODEL CONCESSIONAIRE AGR EEMENT 
AND THE ISSUES IN PRIVATE PUBLIC PARTNERSHIPS  
181. The Committee had been informed in its meeting s with the stakeholders that one of 
the most crucial issues impacting the viability of PPP projects is their inability to use tariff 
mechanism to face the ever-increasing competition i n the port sector from competing 
facilities both within the major ports as well as n earby non-major ports. Till recently, tariffs 
for PPP operators were being regulated by the Tarif f Authority for Major Ports (TAMP). The 
unviable rates fixed by TAMP have affected the viab ility of many of the PPP Projects 
governed under the Tariff Guidelines issued in 2008 , 2013 and 2019. This has led to 
negativity in the investor’s perception and is one of the main factors for the lukewarm 
response in the bidding process in the port sector over the last few years.  
 
182. Keeping the above facts in mind, the Governmen t has abolished TAMP and provided 
market-based tariff freedom to PPP Operators throug h enactment of Major Port Authorities 
Act, 2021 which made some key changes like the intr oduction of the Landlord Port Model of 
Development and accordance of market-based tariff f reedom to the new concessionaires 
under Public Private Partnership Mode. The role of TAMP has ceased in fixation of 
tariffs/SoRs. However it may be associated in advis ory capacity and resolution of past cases 
of tariff fixation as the MPA Act 2021 is not applicable with retrospective effect  
 
LANDLORD PORT MODEL 
 
183. The landlord port model is a port management m odel in which both public and private 
sectors are engaged in the management of the port.  The Port Authority retains ownership of 

37 
 
the land and leases the infrastructure particularly  the terminals to private companies which 
handle the port operations .  In June 2022, Jawaharlal Nehru Port Authority port became the 
first 100% Landlord Major Port of India.  The Landlord Port Model aims at - 
/head2right decentralizing decision making to infuse profession alism in governance of Major 
Ports.  
/head2right imparting faster and transparent decision making be nefiting the stakeholders and 
enhance the project execution capability.  
/head2right reorienting the governance model in central ports i n line with the successful global 
practices.  
/head2right bringing transparency in operations of Major Ports.  
The Ministry also informed the Committee that to fu rther complement the landlord 
port model, the Public Private Partnership mode is being promoted in infrastructure 
projects aimed for expansion, modernization and up- gradation of Major Ports in the 
country with a view to keep the ports abreast with new technologies. 
 
184. The following  policy related reforms have also been done initiate d for strengthening 
and encouraging PPP in port sector: 
(1) Revision of Model Concession Agreement (MCA), 2 021  
MoPSW has announced the revised Model Concession Ag reement (MCA) - 2021 on 18th 
November, 2021. It has not only provided more clarity for the responsibilities and obligations 
of authority and private party, but also introduced  clauses related to the termination payment 
prior to Commercial Operations Date (COD), change i n cargo due to unforeseen 
circumstances as well as change in law. These claus es among others should enhance Ease of 
Doing Business (EoDB).  
(2) Formulation of Tariff Guidelines, 2021  
In December 2021, new tari 
ﬀ guidelines have been issued which allow the conces sionaires at 
Major Ports to set tari ﬀs as per market dynamics and sharing of revenue wit h the Port 
Authority as per the bid condition and Concession Agreement.  
(3) Formulation of the Guidelines for dealing with stressed public private 
partnership Projects at Major Ports  
 On 10 th  May, 2022, the Ministry of Ports, Shipping & Water ways has issued the 'Guidelines 
for dealing with stressed PPP Projects at Major Por ts’ for reviving the stuck projects and 
unlocking blocked capacity. 
(4) Establishment of the Society for Affordable Res olution of Disputes - Ports 
(SAROD-Ports)   
In order to seek speedy, a 
ﬀordable, just and reasonable redressal of dispute/d i ﬀerences 
between Major Port Trusts and Concessionaire/Contra ctor arising out of and during the 
course of execution of various contracts, a Society  for A ﬀordable Resolution of Disputes - 
Ports (SAROD-Ports) has been formed under the Socie ties Registration Act, 1860 on 30th 
January 2020. 
(5) Constitution of Conciliation and Settlement Com mittee for Major Ports 
succeeds in settling decade long commercial disputes.
