may be apprised about the staff requirement. The Co mmittee expresses the view that in case of 
any shortage, recruitment process must be rolled ou t. In the case of consultants, the Committee 
seeks to know the total number of consultants with the Ministries and the basis for their 
appointment. 
(Para 79) 
The Committee recommends that recourse be taken to five R's - (i)  Revive or create posts, (ii)  
Restructure the organization to bring in efficiency , (iii) Recruit young talent, (iv) Reframe 
policy/processes, (v) Refresh minds by giving inter im professional training and also to revive 
and create posts.   
(Para 80) 
Budgetary Allocation 
The Committee notes that the provisioning and utili zation of funds for the construction of 
ROBs/ RUBs could be better. There needs to be more co-ordination between the Railways and 
the State Governments in providing a budget and exe cuting the works. Further, the large chunk 
of unspent amount under the Setu Bharatam programme  is an overarching concern. There is a 
need for proper channelization and utilization of the earmarked funds. 
(Para 82) 
(ii) Road Safety related issues 
The Committee notes that the Motor Vehicles Amendme nt Act (MVAA), 2019 creates 
adequate accountability framework to ensure that ro ad-owning agencies, contractors and 
concessionaires are held accountable for faulty roa d design and construction. To 
operationalise this at the State level, the Act pro vides discretionary powers to States to 
create Rules under  Section 210D.  The Section 210 D authorizes State Governments to make 
rules for design, construction and maintenance stan dards for National Highways and roads 
other than National Highways, respectively. 
(Para 84) 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Minis try of Road Transport and Highways 
should persuade State Governments to frame such rul es under Section 210D of the MVAA Act 
at the earliest.  The Committee may also be kept apprised of the matter.   
(Para 85) 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Railw ays should relook into ‘Gate Mitra’ 
scheme and ensure that these personnel are being pr ovided with all basic amenities.  In the 
Committee’s view, proper implementation of the Gate  Mitra scheme will promote the safety of 
road users, besides generating employment. 
(Para 87) 
Damaged Pavement Surface 
The Committee recommends that timely repair and maintenance of damaged pavement surfaces 

60 
 
on service roads should be undertaken on priority i n the interest of road safety.  Routine 
inspection should be carried out at regular interva ls to identify and address any issues such as 
waterlogging, potholes, cracks, or uneven surfaces.  Adequate resources and manpower need to 
be allocated for timely repairs, including resurfac ing, relaying or patching of service roads as 
needed. The safety of all road users needs to be pr ioritized by maintaining smooth and well-
maintained service roads. 
(Para 90) 
Lane Drop 
 The Committee observes that lane drops with poorer  site geometrics have higher conflict rates.  
The Committee is of the view that there is a need t o revise existing guidelines/criteria to 
ensure that bridge sections are designed with consi stent geometry, including the same 
number of lanes, similar to those of the through ro ad for fast and long distance traffic.  
Lane drops must be designed properly from the outset, in as much as traffic control devices 
are not as effective in reducing conflicts as are proper site geometrics.  
(Para 92)  
Absent Shoulders  
The Committee recommends that the Ministry may re-e xamine the existing 
guidelines/criteria relating to paved and unpaved s ections of the road.  If needed, the 
Ministry should come out with revised guidelines/cr iteria to ensure that bridge sections are 
designed with shoulders so that they can be used fo r emergency stopping of vehicles.  
Further, these guidelines must be strictly followed during the construction of the roads. 
(Para 94)  
Inadequate Illumination  
The Committee takes note of the technological advan ces made in the field of streetlighting and 
recommends that installation of street lights, pref erably with automatic sensors, retro-reflectors 
may be undertaken for proper road illumination. In the case of power supply failure or damage 
to the street lights, the retro-reflectors act as r eliable visual guides, reflecting light from 
headlights and assisting drivers in manoeuvring safely and staying on the correct path. 
(Para 96) 
The Committee recommends conducting comprehensive l ighting audits to assess the adequacy 
of current lighting conditions on roads.  Areas wit h inadequate lighting should be identified and 
prioritized based on factors such as traffic volume, accident history, and visibility requirements. 
(Para 97)  
Inefficient Safety Barriers 
The Committee recommends that all measures should be taken to ensure that the safety barriers 
are appropriately designed and constructed to withs tand the impact forces generated by heavy 
vehicles.  Also, these should be provided with suff icient height to prevent them from breaching 
the barrier.  Increasing the height and capacity of safety barriers is essential for maintaining the 
integrity of the bridge and protecting the road use rs, thereby minimizing the risk of fatal 
crashes. 
(Para 99)  
             Absent Signage and Hazard Markings 
The Committee recommends that bridge infrastructure  planning and maintenance should 
prioritize the inclusion and proper maintenance of traffic signs and hazard markers to ensure the 
safety of road users, pedestrians, and cyclists. Re gular inspections, timely repairs, and routine 

61 
 
maintenance are essential to ensure that these vita l elements effectively communicate important 
information, guide road users, and mitigate potential hazards, thus contributing to safer and more 
organized bridge crossings. 
(Para 101) 
The Committee also recommends establishing standard ized designs for road signs that comply 
with national or international standards, such as t hose set by the Manual on Uniform Traffic 
Control Devices (MUTCD).  Also, there should be use  of clear and easily recognizable symbols, 
colours, and fonts to improve readability and comprehension. 
(Para 102) 
Inadequate Anti-glare Measures 
The Committee recommends for proper implementation of appropriate anti-glare measures 
on bridge sections to enhance visibility, reduce th e risks associated with glare, and ensure 
the safety of all road users, especially during night time. 
(Para 104) 
 
The Committee also recommends implementing advanced  technologies, such as adaptive 
lighting systems or intelligent transportation syst ems (ITS) in automobiles that adjust 
lighting levels based on real-time conditions. These systems can automatically dim or adjust 
lighting intensity to reduce glare during specific periods or in response to changing weather 
conditions. The Committee feels that the road autho rities can significantly enhance road 
safety and reduce the risk of accidents caused by blinding glare. 
(Para 105) 
Issue of vegetation/plantation 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that no plantation be done up to 25m at the median 
while approaching a crossing. Cuts in the median, and exit/ entry to or from service lane need to 
be ensured for clear visibility to avoid chances of crashes/accidents. 
(Para 110)  
Inadequate Pedestrian Facilities 
To ensure safe and comfortable walking conditions, the Committee recommends that it is 
crucial to provide hassle-free pedestrian facilitie s based on the requirement.  Places with 
high pedestrian traffic require wider footpaths. Pe destrian facilities should also consider 
accessibility requirements for individuals with disabilities or limited mobility. 
(Para 112)  
Absent Pedestrian Guard Rails 
To address the lack of pedestrian guardrails on ser vice roads, the Committee recommends the 
Ministry to perform thorough audits of high-trafﬁc areas, intersections, and road segments to 
identify locations where pedestrian guardrails are most needed.  Guard rails should be provided at 
all safety-critical areas with a higher concentration of vulnerable road users, such as near schools, 
hospitals, and areas with a significant pedestrian population. Additionally, it must be ensured that 
the guardrails are designed with appropriate standa rds, considering the height, strength, and 
visibility requirements for optimal pedestrian safety. 
(Para 114) 
There is also a need to conduct public awareness ca mpaigns to educate pedestrians and drivers 
about the importance of using designated pedestrian crossings, respecting guardrails, and adhering 
to traffic rules for pedestrian safety. 

62 
 
(Para 115) 
  Absent Pedestrian and Cyclist Facilities 
The Committee recommends including  pedestrian and bicycle facilities as a mandatory a nd 
integral part of bridged sections to accommodate th e requirements of all road users, promoting 
safety, accessibility, and sustainable transportati on options. Moreover, the mandatory 
inclusion of pedestrian and bicycle facilities on b ridges promotes social equity, providing 
equal access to all members of the community, regardless of their mode of transportation or 
physical abilities. 
(Para 117)  
Discontinuous Service Roads  
The Committee recommends that it is important for r oad-owning agencies to address 
discontinuous service lanes to ensure the safety of  local traffic and minimize the risks associated 
with merging the service lanes with the main highway. Continuous service roads offer a dedicated 
route for local traffic. This reduces the risk of c ollisions due to merging with the highway. Road 
planning and design should take into account the needs of the local traffic and ensure provisioning 
of appropriate infrastructure, including merging lanes, acceleration lanes, deceleration lanes, and 
proper signage. This will help minimize conflicts b etween local traffic and high-speed highway 
traffic, improving overall road safety. 
(Para 119) 
          Lack of designed U-turn facilities under the brid ges 
            The Committee recommends implementing U-turn facili ties under bridge sections where 
feasible. These U-turn facilities should have contr olled access points, clear signage, and proper 
lane markings, allowing motorists to make use of it safely. 
(Para 121) 
            Inadequate Treatment of Merging and Diverging Points 
            The Committee recommends for providing adequate length for acceleration and deceleration 
lanes, clear signage, and road markings. Consistent  lane designations and trafﬁc control 
measures, such as trafﬁc signals or yield signs, sh ould be implemented to guide drivers and 
minimize conﬂicts. Additionally, regular maintenanc e and periodic assessments of these points 
are essential to address any signage obstructions, pavement deterioration, or visibility issues. By 
implementing these recommendations, bridge sections  can facilitate smooth and safe transitions 
for merging and diverging trafﬁc, enhancing overall  trafﬁc ﬂow and reducing the risk of 
crashes. 
 (Para 123) 
           The Committee recommends that a robust m onitoring mechanism may be put in place not only 
to oversee the progress of ongoing ROB/RUB projects  but also to identify and address any 
bottlenecks in execution 
 (Para 126) 
            Inter-ministerial coordination mechanism 
The Committee notes that PM Gati Shakti- National M aster Plan for Multi-modal Connectivity 
has provided an excellent platform for integrated p lanning and coordinated implementation of 
all infrastructure projects, including ROBs/RUBs, w hether on a standalone basis or as part of 
corridor projects. 
(Para 131) 
The Committee recommends that the Government should  establish a Central Coordinating 

63 
 
Body or a Committee comprising representatives from  key ministries involved in road 
development, namely, the Ministry of Road Transport  and Highways, Ministry of Finance, 
Ministry of Environment, Forests and Climate Change , and Ministry of Railways. This body 
will facilitate regular communication, coordination , and decision-making among the Ministries. 
Such a step will also help overcome the delay in co nstruction due to waiting in approval of 
clearances. 
(Para 132) 
The Committee also recommends that the roles, respo nsibilities, and mandates of each Ministry 
involved in road development must be clearly defined. It must be ensured that there is clarity on 
the specific areas in which each Ministry is respon sible for and how they interact with other 
Ministries to ensure time-bound resolutions of issu es. This will minimize delay, overlaps, 
conflicts, and uncertainties in decision-making and implementation. 
(Para 133) 
The Committee feels that there remains a communicat ion gap among the Ministries, leading to 
avoidable delay.  The Committee, therefore, recomme nds establishing effective communication 
channels between the Ministries, such as dedicated focal points or inter-ministerial co-
ordinating officers. These officers can serve as a single point of contact for communication, 
coordination, and information exchange between the Ministries. 
(Para 134) 
The Ministries should establish mechanisms for info rmation sharing and data integration 
among the Ministries/ Agencies involved in road dev elopment. They can create a centralized 
repository or platform where relevant data, reports , and project updates can be shared among 
the concerned Ministries/authorities. This will ena ble Ministries to access and utilize 
comprehensive information for decision-making and project monitoring. 
(Para 135) 
Maintenance and upgradation 
The Committee is of the view that the Ministries sh ould conduct regular inspections of ROBs 
and RUBs to identify any signs of deterioration, st ructural issues, or maintenance requirements. 
These inspections should be carried out by qualifie d engineers and experts to assess the 
condition of the built infrastructure. The study as sessment should be placed in the public 
domain and MPs and MLAs of the concerned area may a lso be appraised about the findings of 
the inspection report. 
(Para 139) 
The Committee recommends the Ministries to evaluate  the load-carrying capacity of 
ROBs/RUBs periodically and consider structural upgr ades if required. This may involve 
strengthening the existing structure, modifying loa d limits, or implementing weight restrictions 
to ensure the safety and longevity of the infrastructure. 
(Para 140) 
 
The Ministries/ Agencies must ensure proper lightin g and signage along ROBs/RUBs for 
improved visibility and safety. Installation of ade quate lighting systems and prominent signage 
indicating height restrictions, speed limits, and o ther important information benefit the road 
users. 
(Para 141) 
With reference to encroachments, the Committee reco mmends that the Ministries should 

64 
 
conduct a comprehensive survey and mapping of the R OB/RUB area to identify encroachments 
and unauthorized structures by using modern surveyi ng techniques, such as drones or satellite 
imagery so that proper remedial measures can be tak en to get rid of encroachments around the 
infrastructure. 
(Para 142) 
The concerned authorities must ensure to take legal  actions against encroachers in accordance 
with relevant laws and regulations. They should ini tiate eviction proceedings and enforce 
penalties for unauthorized occupation. Adequate hum anitarian support and assistance should 
be provided to those affected by encroachment- induced eviction. 
(Para 143) 
Further, the Committee recommends that the engageme nt with the local community and 
stakeholders should be strengthened to obviate any future encroachments. The relevant NGOs, 
advocacy bodies and local opinion of leaders may al so be roped in to create awareness about 
non-encroachment of the public infrastructure spaces. 
(Para 144) 
The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the C RRI in the field of road development. 
However, the Committee is of the view that the CRRI  should also come up with binding 
guidelines for adoption of sustainable technology a nd materials for road development and the 
road designs keeping in view the national goals and aspirations. 
(Para 149) 
The Committee in this regard recommends that compli ance with IRC guidelines must be made 
a mandatory requirement for all road development pr ojects. Further, the Committee suggests 
that independent third-party audits should be condu cted to assess compliance with IRC 
guidelines. Engaging qualified auditors who are fam iliar with IRC guidelines can provide an 
unbiased evaluation of project compliance and ident ify any gaps or non-compliance issues that 
need to be addressed. 
(Para 162) 
The Committee further notes that effective implemen tation of Rule 166 of the Central Motor 
Vehicles Rules (CMVR) can ensure road safety. Rule 166 (dealing with road, design, 
construction, and maintenance standards) under the Central Motor Vehicle Rules, 1989 7, was 
added via G.S.R 584(E), dated 25th September 2020 ( w.e.f. 1-10-2020) to give effect to Sec 198A 
of the Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 2019. The rule states as follows: 
“(1)The design, construction, and maintenance of na tional highways shall be in accordance with 
the standards and speciﬁcations of the Indian Road Congress (IRC) as may be applicable, or any 
other instructions or guidelines issued by the Central Government from time to time…” 
           (Para 163)  
The Committee notes that the IRC guidelines are mam moth in nature, as there are over 200 
guidelines introduced and renewed by IRC since it w as established in December 1934. 
Currently, the IRC guidelines include a range of su bjects like the method of recording 
accidents, and practices for road users, apart from  the guidelines on road, design, construction, 
and maintenance. Therefore, for effective implement ation of the codes pertaining to road 
design, construction, and maintenance by the design ated authority, contractor, consultant, or 
concessionaire, it is imperative that such IRC guid elines be speciﬁcally called out under Rule 
166 CMVR, or else there will be chances on missing out important standards at any point while 
implementing road safety standards at all or any of the three stages. 

65 
 
(Para 164) 
 Fund allocation and support to IRC 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry may cons ider deputing some officers having 
interest and inclination toward standardization, R& D to work in the IRC.  Also, the Ministry 
may consider providing a reasonable amount of corpu s seed fund to the IRC to manage the 
function of its Secretariat, the modalities of whic h may be worked out in consultation with the 
IRC.  
(Para 166) 
 Further, since the Technical Committees, Apex Comm ittees, Highway Research Board and its 
Committees are involved in the preparation of initi al drafts, reviewing critically the draft 
prepared, state-of-the-art reports, explanatory han dbook on Codes with solved examples, etc., 
the Ministry may consider providing them support th rough budgetary allocation for their 
works including for bearing expenditure on intercit y travels, accommodation, local travel, and 
honorarium. 
(Para 167 ) 
The Ministry may provide budgetary allocation to th e IRC to organize workshops, seminars, 
and webinars in order to disseminate the knowledge on latest IRC guidelines to the practicing 
highway engineers in the interest of creating a lar ge pool of engineers with knowledge on the 
cutting-edge technology in the rapidly evolving road design and engineering sector. 
(Para 168)  
The Committee, accordingly, recommends that the Min istry must examine the feasibility of 
adopting and implementing the proposed design suggested at (b) which is based on international 
standards . 
(Para 172)  
Induction of new technologies 
The Committee notes the reply of RDSO, Indian railways that in most cases, India is at par with 
the advanced nations.  However, the Committee sugge sts adopting Building Information 
Modelling (BIM) technology which enables the creati on of detailed 3D models that integrate 
various aspects of the ROB/RUB development process,  including architectural, structural, and 
utility design. Further, Virtual Reality (VR) and A ugmented Reality (AR) technologies can also 
be used to provide immersive experiences and simula tions during the design and construction 
phases of ROBs/RUBs. They allow engineers and proje ct teams to visualize and interact with 
virtual models, facilitating better design review, construction planning, and stakeholder 
communication. 
(Para 178) 
The Committee also emphasizes on usage of Advanced Construction Materials such as fiber-
reinforced polymers (FRPs), high-performance concre te, and composite materials to enhance 
the durability, strength, and lifespan of ROBs/RUBs . These materials offer improved resistance 
to corrosion, seismic forces, and other environmental stress factors. 
(Para 179) 
 
Artificial Intelligence (AI) enabled Intelligent Tr ansportation Systems (ITS) technologies can be 
integrated into ROBs/RUBs to enhance road safety an d better traffic management. These 
include systems for automated traffic control, real -time monitoring of road conditions, traffic 
signalling, and vehicle detection. ITS can improve the efficiency of traffic flow, reduce 

66 
 
congestion, and enhance overall safety. 
(Para 180) 
 
Smart Sensors embedded in ROBs/RUBs can continuousl y monitor the structural health, 
detecting and alerting to any anomalies or signs of  deterioration. SHM systems provide real-
time data on the structural integrity, stress, vibr ations, and deformation of the infrastructure, 
facilitating proactive maintenance and preventing failures. 
(Para 181) 
The Committee also recommends the usage of Geospati al technologies, such as Geographic 
Information Systems (GIS) and remote sensing, to en able accurate mapping, analysis, and 
visualization of the project area. These tools assi st in land surveying, route planning, 
environmental impact assessment, and site selection for ROB/RUB development. 
(Para 182) 
Private Sector Participation 
The Committee is of the view that the Ministry shou ld conduct comprehensive feasibility studies 
to assess the viability of implementing PPP models for ROB/RUB development. The Ministry 
should evaluate factors such as project size, reven ue potential, market conditions, and potential 
private sector interest. Feasibility studies will p rovide valuable insights into the suitability of 
PPP and help in making informed decisions. 
(Para 184) 
 
The Committee recommends that an assessment of lega l and regulatory framework should be 
pursued to evaluate the existing legal and regulato ry framework and to identify any barriers or 
limitations to implementing PPP in ROB/RUB developm ent.  The Ministry should also identify 
necessary amendments or new legislations required t o facilitate PPP arrangements, ensure 
transparency, and provide a favourable business environment for private partners. 
(Para 185) 
The Committee also suggests that the Ministries sho uld establish transparent and competitive 
procurement processes to attract capable private entities. They should also implement a fair and 
competitive bidding process that encourages multiple private sector players to participate.  
(Para 186) 
 
The Ministry should engage with various stakeholder s, including local communities, transport 
authorities, private sector entities, and financing institutions, seeking their input and addressing 
any concerns or expectations they may have. The Min istry should also foster partnerships and 
collaboration to enhance the success and sustainability of PPP projects. 
(Para 187) 
Sustainable and environment-friendly roads 
The Committee appreciates the innovative efforts ma de in the direction of construction of 
environmentally sustainable roads. However, it feel s that given the national aspirations to 
gradually move towards a zero-waste circular econom y, more measures should be taken in this 
regard. The Committee suggests that the Ministries should adopt features like rain gardens, 
bioswales, and permeable pavements to manage stormw ater runoff and improve water quality. 
Green infrastructure can help recharge groundwater,  reduce the load on drainage systems and 
help enhance biodiversity in roadside areas. 

67 
 
(Para 192) 
 
The Ministries should also implement Sustainable Dr ainage Systems (SuDS) to manage surface 
water runoff from roads. SuDS techniques include infiltration basins, constructed wetlands, and 
detention ponds that mimic natural hydrological pro cesses. SuDS can reduce the risk of 
flooding, promote groundwater recharge, and improve water quality by removing pollutants. 
(Para 193) 
 
The Ministries should also encourage road design th at optimizes energy efficiency. This can 
include factors such as minimizing excessive grades , optimizing alignment to reduce vehicle 
energy consumption, and incorporating intelligent t ransportation systems (ITS) to improve 
traffic flow and reduce congestion-related emissions. 
(Para 194) 
The Committee also recommends that the Ministries c an explore opportunities to integrate 
renewable energy sources into road infrastructure. This can include incorporating solar panels 
into noise barriers or utilizing solar-powered ligh ting along roads. Renewable energy 
integration can help reduce dependence on fossil fu els and contribute to a more sustainable 
transportation network. 
(Para 195) 
The Ministries should enhance Environmental Impact Assessments for road projects to evaluate 
the potential ecological, social, and cultural impacts. Further, such assessments should be placed 
in the public domain. Assessment of the project's p otential effects on ecosystems, habitats, and 
natural resources should also be undertaken to deve lop appropriate mitigation measures to 
minimize negative impacts. 
(Para 196) 
 
Need for VUP/CUP   
The Committee reiterates that CRRI’s suggestion tha t wherever the highway passes through 
built areas, the need for VUP/ Light Vehicular Underpass (LVUP) must be built as part of Road 
safety Audit (RSA) report conforming to IRC: 84 (20 19) or IRC: 87 (2019), including the 
provision of half-subway, i.e. depressed Pedestrian Under Pass (PUP). 
(Para 198) 
            Good Samaritan Law 
The Committee recommends that first aid education f or every police personnel must be 
mandatory along with their regular training. All Po lice PCRs must be equipped with the 
requisite first aid equipments and items, etc.  
(Para 209) 
Further, the scope of the ‘Good Samaritan Law’ must  be enlarged beyond helping a road 
accident victim. Victims of natural calamities like drought and flood, fire incidents, or victims of 
any medical condition, etc. must be included in the  ambit of ‘Good Samaritan Law’, as the 
nature of helping victims of above situations, is i dentical with the road accident victims and 
hence must be part of Good Samaritan Law.  
(Para 210) 
 
The Committee feels that for reaping the best resul ts out of ‘Good Samaritan Law’; mass 
training and awareness is needed. ‘Scouts & Guide’ system which used to be in schools earlier 

68 
 
can be truly instrumental in this regard. ‘First Ai d Training’ and handling and assisting a 
person injured in a road accident or in any natural  calamity, is an essential part for every 
student trained under the ‘Scout and Guide’ System.  This needs to be resurrected in all schools 
and the Ministry should appropriately sensitise and  take up with the concerned authorities for 
building citizenship rooted in sublime values.   
(Para 211) 
 
The Committee also recommends sensitizing the polic e of its duties and 
 responsibilities during 
such a situation. Increased fund allocation to publ ic funded hospitals has the potential to 
establish robust emergency care units, besides crea ting adequate infrastructure. Police and 
judiciary must be adequately sensitized so that the y remain alive towards the protection of 
Good Samaritans. 
(Para 212) 
 
To provide for accountability of various Government  authorities and encouragement for Good 
Samaritans, the Committee recommends that a “Grievance Redressal Mechanism” be instituted 
nationally. The new section 134A of the MVAA 2019 p rotects the Good Samaritans but does not 
guide one over the breach of the obligations of the  police and the hospital. Sin ce these 
subjects are a part of state lists, the states must  be encouraged to come up with rules regarding 
the grievance mechanism in case of breach of compliance. 
(Para 213) 
 
Besides, campaigns to increase the awareness of the  rights of Good Samaritans must be 
undertaken to educate the public. Further, in pursu ance to the guidelines for Good Samaritans 
issued by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare mentioned therein, both public and private 
hospitals and police stations must publish the char ter on the rights of Good Samaritans. This 
will go a long way in encouraging the spirited public and help greater information dissemination 
on right of the good Samaritans. 
(Para 214)

Research Activity:  
IRC does not receive any grant or funding from Gove rnment department for road research. 
However, IRC has stimulated interest in road resear ch and taken active interest in setting-up of 
road research laboratories in the country way back as in 1944. Detailed scheme was worked out by 
one of its committees for setting-up Central Road R esearch Institute, New Delhi, and a chain of 
research laboratories in the States, in addition to  the work of gathering, correlating and 
disseminating information concerning road research within the country. 
In October 1973, the Highway Research Board (HRB) was set up under the auspices of the IRC for 
giving undivided attention to road research and dev elopment activities. The Board aimed to 
Identify highway research needs, recommend prioriti es and schedules of research, set up 
Committees consisting of experts who are concerned with the problems of roads and road 
transport.  Within its limited resources and capabi lity of IRC concerted efforts are also being made 
to summarise and make available the significant res ults of road research and to guide and 
coordinate road research work in our country with a view to avoid duplication of effort. 
Further, as per advice/ directive from the Hon’ble Court (one order by Madras High Court) and 
Vigilance agency (one case by Kerala State) IRC has  sent team of Experts for investigation of 
specific road and bridge project and submit its reports.  
IRC is also involved in preparation & revision of ‘ Specification of Road & bridge Works’ for 
Ministry of Road Transport & Highways and ‘Specification for Rural Roads’ for NRIDA, Ministry 
of Rural Development. 
Simultaneously, IRC provides technical inputs / ass istance to NDMA, NGT, BIS, Ministry of 
Environment, and forest, etc. whenever sought.

2.         Some concerns were raised by the Committee regarding the issue of entry passes to 
Research Assistant to the Chairman of the Committee and the postponement of the study visit of 
the Committee to Gangtok, Guwahati & Tawang from 15 th April to 19 th April 2023.   The

Speaker, Lok Sabha. Members were of the view that the Secretariat should restrict itself to the 
smooth functioning of the Committee.   Thereafter, the Committee authorized the Chairman to 
take necessary action in this regard. The Committee also desired that a brief note on issues to be 
discussed in the meetings may also be provided to the Members, henceforth. 
 
(After the witnesses took their respective seats) 
 
3.         The Chairman welcomed the Members of the Committee and the witnesses who were 
present. The Chairman informed that the agenda of the meeting was to hear the Additional 
Secretary, Ministry of Road, Transport & Highways and National Hig hways Authority of India 
on the subject 'Construction of Road -Over-Bridges (ROBs) and Road -Under-Bridges (RUBs), 
Service Roads, and Review of Road Survey Guidelines etc.'  The Chairman asked the Additional 
Secretary to brief the Committee on the following points: 
i. Details of ROBs and RUBs constructed in the country under PM Gati Shakti and the 
targets set by the Ministry to construct more such bridges in the country; 
ii. Current status of the ongoing ROB and RUBs projects in the country and their deadlines 
and targets; 
iii. Achievements of the Ministry, if any, in the construction of ROBs and RUBs in the 
country; 
iv. Details of the ROBs and RUBs constructed by the Ministry which have proved beneficial 
for other modes of transport, not only for those who are using the road  but beneficial 
even for rail connectivity, air connectivity and sea or inland waterways;  
v. Details of the Rail -cum Road Over -Bridges, ROBs and RUBs constructed by the 
Ministry which have contributed to road safety and minimizing road accidents and 
mishaps in the last five years and the assessment thereof;  

87 
 
vi. The salient features of the 'Setu Bharatam' Programme which aims at making all National 
highways,  Railway Level Crossings free by 2019 and the revised deadline; 
vii. The total number and length of Service Roa ds constructed in the country and whether 
such roads have proved beneficial and the steps taken to improve the quality of such 
service roads; 
viii. Number of  Service Road projects in the country where the deadlines were revised and 
the  challenges faced by the Ministry in this regard; 
ix. The steps taken to expedite the construction work of ROBs and RUBs, and resolve 
coordination issues between Ministries; 
x. Details of Budget allocated for construction of ROBS/RUBs and Service Roads in the 
country; 
xi. The process adopted by the Ministry to choose land for the development and construction 
of a road or a highway and the survey guidelines implemented for the same;  
xii. The coordination mechanisms adopted by the Ministry to coordinate with other Central 
and State Government depar tments and the challenges and difficulties faced in this 
regard; 
xiii. New initiatives taken by the Ministry to improve road connectivity across the country and 
the challenges and difficulties faced by the Ministry in constructing roads and various 
other road projects in various States; 
xiv.  Permissions/approvals  required from the State Governments for constructing roads and 
various other road projects in various States and  whether the process of obtaining such 
permissions/approvals is effective; and  
xv. Encroachments on service roads and the solutions thereof. 
 
4.  The Ministry presented a detailed PowerPoint Presentation on the following points: 
 Guidelines for construction of ROBs and RUBs; 
 Status of ROBs/RUBs/Level Crossings on National Highways; 
 Setu Bharatam Programme; 
 Clearances required in the implementation of ROBs/RUBs; 
 Difficulties being faced in the construction of ROBs/RUBs and action taken to expedite 
ROBs/RUBs construction; 
 Service Roads; 
 Status of service roads on National Highways; 

88 
 
 Length of Service Road (in km); 
 Surveys and Investigations carried out for DPR Preparation; and 
 Surveys & investigations conducted on existing roads under operation. 
5.  The Additional Secretary, MoRTH elaborated that the construction of ROBs/RUBs on 
National Highways is impo rtant for ensuring smooth traffic flow, improving logistics efficiency 
of freight movement, improving road safety and achieving better fuel efficiency. He informed 
that presently there are 765 existing ROBs/RUBs and 452 ROBs/RUBs are under construction. 
He also stated that selected level -crossings on already constructed NHs or proposed for 
construction are taken up under the Setu Bharatam.  To ensure better coordination with the 
Ministry of Railways, an MoU was signed on 10 th November 2014 regarding the cons truction of 
ROBs/RUBs on NH corridors in which construction of span over railway lines would be done on 
a single entity basis.  
6.  The Additional Secretary, MoRTH highlighted that the NH network is continuously 
expanding in the country during the last sev en to eight years, and has grown from less than 
90,000 kms to more than 1.4 lakh kms. The width of service roads can be from 7 meters to 5.5 
meters and the total existing length of service roads of a single lane is 1614 kms; the

2.         At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Members and informed them that the agenda 
of the meeting was to deliberate on the subject of “Construction of Road-Over-Bridges (ROBs) 
and Road-Under-Bridges (RUBs), Service Roads, and Review of Road Survey Guidelines etc.”. 
The Chairman also informed that the Committee has already heard the representatives from the 
Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, and Nat ional Highways Authority of India (NHAI), 
on the subject in its meeting dated 25.04.2023. 
(After the witnesses took their respective seats) 
3.           The Chairman welcomed the representatives of the Bridges Directorate and Bridges & 
Structure Directorate of Research Development & Standards Organization (RDSO), Ministry of 
Railways and the Indian Roads Congress.   Thereafter, the Chairman asked Member (Infra), 
Ministry of Railways to brief the Committee on the difficulties being faced in the construction o f 
ROBs/RUBs/Service roads and action taken to expedite their completion; the average waiting 
time at railway crossings due to the absence of ROBs/RUBs as also clearances required in the 
construction of ROBs/RUBs/Service Roads.  He asked the Ministry to elab orate on the inter -
governmental coordination mechanisms adopted and the surveys carried out on existing bridges 
along with abandoned bridges and the reasons for such abandonment. The Chairman also 
inquired about the effectiveness of the implementation of t he research and designs done by 
RDSO for the construction of ROBs and RUBs and the bottlenecks in this regard. He desired that 
the Committee may also be briefed regarding standards requirement for ROBs and RUBs and 
their compliance by G overnment agencies;  and technological advancements and process 
improvements done by Railways/RDSO. 
4.         The Chairman asked the Indian Roads Congress(IRC)  about various traffic surveys and 
investigations carried out for the construction of NHs/Bypass bridges and for deci ding the 
carriageway configuration width for 6 -lane, 4-lane and 2 -lane roads emphasizing the pros and 
cons of these three categories for NHs. The Chairman also sought information on the research 
and development criteria followed by IRC and the survey repor t on traffic count and its impact 
on road design, engagement of consultants and the expenditure incurred thereon. The Chairman 
also inquired about extant/proposed guidelines on the construction of ROBs and RUBs, hurdles 

95 
 
in their implementation and the extent to which it is being complied with by NHAI/Central/State 
Government/Departments. The Chairman also desired to know about initiatives undertaken by 
IRC for promoting environmental-friendly technologies and materials in road construction along 
with the ad option of global standards. He also sought suggestions from IRC to bring 
the construction of ROB/RUB/Service lanes on track along with the details of budgetary 
allocation and other challenges faced in their construction. 
5.         Thereafter, Member (Infr a), Railway Board made a presentation.   He informed the 
Committee that Indian Railways has been making efforts to improve safety as a  whole, 
particularly at level crossings. Indian Railways has been  able to eliminate 100% unmanned level 
crossings on broad gauge routes by January 2019. As of date, the railway network has 
17,720 manned level crossings on a broad gauge system and the Ministry is aiming to replace all 
the level crossing gates with ROBs and RUBs.  He explained the provision in the earlier system 
where the State Government proposed the construction of ROBs and the cost was shared by both 
the Railways and the State Government or the local government.   However, the allocation of 
limited funds by the State  Governments/Road owning Authorities, for road  crossing works led 
to delays in sanction and completion of these works. To address this issue, the Ministry of 
Railways has decided to eliminate those level crossing gates by constructing ROBs and RUBs at 
their cost to keep up with the pace. He, further, highlighted the issue of the cost of land as they 
were not getting land free from encumbrances and also touched upon the issue of utility shifting, 
which is now being managed and borne by the Ministry of Railway itself. He informed that the 
Ministry of Rai lways aims to accelerate road crossing works and a policy letter was issued in 
March 2023 to remove bottlenecks in sanctioning and progressing of these works at an 
accelerated pace. He apprised the Committee that under this new policy, they have already 
sanctioned 300 ROBs/RUBs with this proviso and 151 ROBs/RUBs in the last two months, i.e. 
April and May. He also informed about the MoU signed between the Ministry of Railways and 
NHAI to eliminate level crossing gates and provide technical assistance in the  clearance of their 
drawings under GAD arrangements. 
6.        On the query by the Chairman regarding the nodal agency responsible for ownership and 
management of land after the construction of ROBs/RUBs, Member (Infra), informed that the 
ownership of the land lies with the Railways if acquired by them, and ROBs are also managed by 
Indian Railways if they are on Railways property. Chairman, thereafter, enquired about the 
number of requests received from various State Governments for the construction of ROBs  and 

96 
 
RUBs and the number of such requests which have been accepted and rejected along with the 
reasons thereof. 
  
7.     Thereafter, Secretary - General, IRC made a presentation.   He informed that the Indian 
Roads Congress was established in 1934 as a Socie ty of Engineers and Professionals associated 
with the Highway Sector in the country. He informed the Committee about the Governing 
Council, its constitution and membership details. He emphasized that IRC does not get any 
grants from the Government. He appr ised the Committee that IRC also had MoUs with 
international partners like JICA, PIARC, AASTHO and International Road Federation. In 
addition, IRC also had research organizations like Central Road Research Institute and Highway 
Research Stations, Chennai. Moreover, it collaborates with Institutions like IITs, NITs, 
NATPAC and other engineering colleges and leading consultants, and contractors. It was 
submitted that the objective of IRC is to prepare national standards, guidelines and manuals for 
the entire road sector. 
8.         He also informed about the publication of proceedings, journals, periodicals and other 
literature with the assistance of technical committees, experts from MoRTH, State PWDs, NHAI, 
NHIDCL, BRO, Railways, IITs and International bodie s like World Bank, ADB and JICA.   
Elaborating about the Technical Committees, he informed that there are 26 committees divided 
into three streams viz. Highway Specifications & Standards Committee (H1 -H10), Bridge 
Specifications & Standards apex committee (B-1 to B-9) and General Specifications & Standards 
Committee (G-1 to G-7).  
9.         He apprised the Committee that for planning, design construction and maintenance of 
ROBs and RUBs, IRC has prepared a document IRC:SP:90 which provides guidelines for gr ade 
separators and elevated structures including planning aspects, general features, and geometric 
standards, environmental considerations, construction methods and constructability issues, safety 
requirement, inspection and maintenance. In addition, there are two separate documents for roads 
and bridges i.e. IRC:SP:19 and IRC:SP:54, respectively. These give details about the stages in 
project preparation, guiding principles for route selection, alignment improvement, survey of 
socio-economic profile, traff ic surveys and their analysis, recce surveys, topographic surveys, 
environmental impact assessment and rehabilitation and resettlement studies, feasibility report, 
staking final alignment on ground, soil and material survey, road inventory and condition su rvey, 

97 
 
drainage studies, preparation and presentation of DPRs, preconstruction activities and project 
analysis. Further, IRC:SP:09 which deals with traffic surveys has been recently revised in 2022 
based on the latest equipment available for traffic surveys . This document also covers 
information regarding current traffic, generated traffic and induced traffic. 
10.       Secretary-General, IRC also informed about the capacity of two -lane, four-lane, six-lane 
and expressways, which has been covered in differen t manuals.  Elaborating on the service level 
concept, he informed that level B service pertains to comfortable driving while level C means 
congestion; and that as the road reaches to congestion level, it is upgraded to a higher level lane. 
He also submitted that due to the fund crunch, IRC does not undertake any R&D initiative on its 
own. Instead, it compiles the latest research done in the country and publishes its document 
every year in its Annual session. With reference to guidelines on ROBs/RUBs, he inf ormed that 
IRC is totally guided by Railway authorities and as far as global standards are concerned.    IRC 
takes inputs from all the interested international agencies, particularly, World Bank, Asian 
Development Bank, JICA and TRL, UK. In addition, World Bank is also preparing the first draft 
for IRC on intersections and junctions. He also submitted that based on the exhaustive document 
prepared by IRC on environmental issues of the road sector, a report was prepared by the 
Environment Ministry, MoRTH and IRC only last month.   The combined report on  the 
requirement of environmental issues in the road sector will now be presented to the Supreme 
Court. 
11.       The Committee was also apprised that all the implementing agencies for the road sector, 
especially, under the Ministry of Roads, Transport & Highways like the NHAI, NHIDCL and 
PWDs, are following the IRC document.   However, modifications if any, are brought about 
through administrative orders of MoRTH as and where required. In respect of fund allocatio n, 
the Ministry is sanctioning all the priority areas and the research work for R&D requirements. 
For code preparation, the Ministry is acting through the Apex Body, i.e., the Chairman of the 
three Technical Committees. He informed that the Director Genera l, the Ministry of Road 
Transport is the Chairman of the three Apex Committees which are approving the IRC codes. 
12.       Vice-President, IRC threw light on the contribution of Central Road Research Institute 
(CRRI).  He stated that CRRI along with other eight academic institutes, carried out a study 
called Indo -Highway Capacity Manual to understand the width of the  National Highways 
depending on the traffic. He informed that CRRI is a 70 -year-old institute and has seven R&D 
divisions. The Bridge Engineering & Structures Division deals with ROBs and RUBs. 

98 
 
Geotechnical Engineering Division, Traffic Engineering and Saf ety Division, and Transport 
Planning & Environment Division deal with the traffic transportation aspects. Geotechnical 
Engineering Division provides support in developing RUBs which use Box Pushing Technology. 
Bridge Division assesses the condition of the Bridges by utilizing Mobile Bridge Inspection Unit. 
13.      He informed the Committee about the usage of different waste materials like steel slag 
waste in collaboration with different industries like MNS, JSW Steel, Rashtriya Ispat Limited 
and Tata Steel  to construct a bituminous road in Arunachal Pradesh. In Odisha, Alumina waste 
has been utilised for road construction. Also, CRRI works on the development of different new 
materials out of waste including waste plastic.   These R&D activities are largely s ponsored by 
the Council of Scientific & Industrial Research, MoRTH, NHAI, other line Ministries and the 
State Governments. CRRI also carries out a 15-Day Road Safety Audit Certificate Programme to 
provide trained auditors.   He also informed the Committee a bout IRC:SR:103, a document on 
pedestrian facilities. 
14.      Thereafter, Chairman enquired about the recommendations and standards set for 
ROBs/RUBs by the 26 Technical Committees under IRC and the details of such ROBs and 
RUBs which have not been constr ucted in accordance with these standards.  To a query by a 
Member, Member (Infra) stated that it is mandatory for all departments to follow IRC 
guidelines.  Clarifying the doubts regarding the elimination of Unmanned Level Crossings 
(ULCs) on broad gauge, he stated that they have eliminated ULCs on broad gauge and they are 
now replacing metre gauge and narrow gauge with broad gauge.   This is a continuing process 
and presently only 2000 km of stretch is left for conversion. However, heritage lines will not b e 
converted as these already have less traffic. 
15.       In response to another query by Chairman regarding Manned Level Crossings on Broad

detailed reply in writing

2.        At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Members and informed them that the agenda of 
the meeting was to deliberate on the subject of “Construction of Road -Over-Bridges (ROBs) and 
Road-Under-Bridges (RUBs), Service Roads, and Review of Road Survey Guidelines etc.”. The 
Chairman also informed that  the Co mmittee has already heard the representatives from the 
Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, and National Highways Authority of India (NHAI),  
and the representatives from the Bridge Directorate of the Ministry of Railways; Bridge & 
Structure Directorate  of Research Designs & Standards Organisation (RDSO) of Ministry of 
Railways, and Indian Roads Congress (IRC) on the above subject in its meeting held on 
25.04.2023 and 16.05.2023 respectively. 
(After the witnesses took their respective seats) 
3.          The Chairman welcomed the representatives of Central Road Research Institute, TRAX, 
and SaveLIFE Foundation to the meeting. Stating the importance of research on design, 
engineering, and technology in the construction of ROBs and RUBs in the country, he  asked 
CRRI to brief the Committee about the role of CRRI in the construction of ROBs/RUBs and the 
research conducted by it in this regard.; its contribution to the development of safety standards 
and guidelines for the construction and maintenance of ROBs an d RUBs in India;  innovative 
technologies and methodologies developed or adopted along with  the use of sustainable and eco-
friendly materials for ROB and RUB construction;  improvements done in existing design codes 
and junction improvements made. He also sought information regarding international agreements 
or collaborations undertaken/proposed to be undertaken by CRRI and the details of training, 
workshops, and seminars conducted by it. 
4.        The Chairman asked the NGOs, namely, TRAX and SaveLIFE Founda tion about their 
engagement with the Government agencies and policy-makers to advocate for the construction of 
ROBs and RUBs in areas prone to accidents. He also asked about their  engagement with local 
communities for raising awareness about the benefits a nd importance of ROBs and RUBs in 
enhancing transportation infrastructure; and how NGOs are addressing the potential 
environmental and social impacts associated with the construction of such structures. Further, he 
sought information about the major challenges being faced by them in promoting road safety and 
how they promote awareness regarding Good Samaritan Law. He also enquired about their 
engagements with local authorities, stakeholders, and the public to ensure transparency and 
community participation throughout the construction process and the measures taken to ensure 

104 
 
the safety of construction workers. The Chairman also sought suggestions to involve NGOs in 
the construction of ROB/RUB/service lanes and the challenges in this regard. The following 
issues were discussed: 
I.   CRRI 
(i) About CRRI: The Director, CRRI, gave a presentation on the establishment and vision of 
CRRI. He informed the Committee about its seven R&D divisions in the areas of traffic and 
transportation, namely, Transportation Planning and Environment; Traffic Engineering and Road 
Safety;  Pavement Evaluation Division; Flexible Pavements Division; Rigid Pavements Division; 
Geotechnical Engineering Division; and Bridges and   Structural Engineering Division. Further, 
CRRI is currently developing the Trip General Manual at the national level. He also apprised the 
Committee of the application of AI for road safety in Nagpur city, known as iRASTE -Nagpur, 
which is now being extended to iRASTE -Telangana. He stated that CRRI also conducts studie s 
with respect to noise mapping, identification of noise hot spots, and mitigation plans, especially 
in terms of the provision of noise barriers. With reference to the North -east engagement, he 
informed the Committee about the preparation of the ongoing In tegrated Transport Network 
Development Plan for Meghalaya. He also informed that CRRI also undertakes Skill 
Development on Road Safety Awareness for teachers/faculty of higher educational institutes. 
 (ii).       Pavement Engineering and materials used in projects: the Director  of CRRI informed 
that steel slag and prefabricated plastic panels were utilized in road construction in Arunachal 
Pradesh, Gujarat, Maharashtra, and Jharkhand.  In the case of bridges and structural engineering, 
CRRI carries out a con dition survey, and structural evaluation and suggests retrofitting and 
remedial measures.  Currently, CRRI has received a huge project for understanding the condition 
assessment of 308 bridges in the State of Odisha. The projects include design constructio n, 
supervision, and pavement performance evaluation of roads constructed by using red mud under 
geotechnical engineering.   He apprised the Committee about another project relating to 
sustainable road pavements at high altitude regions using geosynthetics a nd Hill Road Widening 
using Light Weight Geofoam Block, which is an alternative to earth cutting and filling.   He 
informed the Committee about the ' Indian Highway Capacity Manual', in which about seven 
academic institutes participated, and the document was  released in 2018.  This manual guides 
all capacities related to the highway sector in the country. He also informed about CRRI's 
clientele and associate institutes like the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, NHAI, 
NHIDCL, NRIDA, State PWDs, Delhi traffic police, Reliance, PCRA, RITES, etc. 

105 
 
(iii).    CRRI's contribution to ROBs/RUBs : CRRI has undertaken a study of 751 bridges 
including one project on Delhi Vadodara Expressway, near Bandiqui, Alwar, Rajasthan, and 
another project in Bareilly, to underst and the requirements of the major repairs and retrofitting 
measures in these projects. He also informed the Committee about the study of quality control 
undertaken on elevated highways and ROB from the Delhi -Ghaziabad border to the Meerut 
crossing at Ghaziabad as also a structural audit of 2.6 kilometres of the elevated road at Agartala 
Tripura. Also, CRRI has provided technical service in various ROB/RUB projects in   Kota, 
Rajasthan; Mahipalpur, New Delhi;   Jhalawar, Rajasthan; and Delhi He informed about the 
Mobile Bridge Inspection Unit, which is one of the new technologies used for condition 
monitoring of bridges. He added that it was patented in 2020 and received an innovation Award 
from NRDC.  He also informed that CRRI has undertaken forensic investig ations of failed ROB 
approaches and makes recommendations for remedial action in respect of these ROBs. 
(iv).        Studies conducted on traffic : CRRI uses RSA  documents for a detailed study at a 
railway crossing in Ahmedabad. The detailed design prepare d by CRRI has been implemented 
by Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation. Further, given that service roads alongside the four -lane 
and six -lane national highways are often found to be not appropriately designed, CRRI   
undertook a specific road safety audit and m ade recommendations on the design for the 
intersection of the service road and secondary road which is merging with the major arterial 
network. 
(v).        CRRI's mandate to work on waste to wealth : Different industrial waste materials are 
being utilized f or road construction. He gave some examples, like the usage of copper slag for 
road construction in Tuticorin, Tamil Nadu;   Phosphogypsum in the internal road network of 
Paradip Port Trust; red mud for National Highways in Koraput district in Odisha; Jarof ix for 
road construction in Chittorgarh, Udaipur; and burnt brickbats in the North -East. He apprised 
that the first steel slag -based road construction project was undertaken by CRRI and that they 
have developed a technology where steel slag can be utilized  for both bituminous and cement 
concrete road construction.   Further, CRRI has also developed some types of equipment, 
namely,  a simulation lab for driver diagnostics, a pothole repair machine, and a mobile cold 
mixer-cum-paver. Regarding training program mes conducted by it,   he informed that CRRI has 
an annual training calendar that encompasses all the seven R&D expertise. CRRI also organizes 
a 15 -day Certificate Course on 'Road Safety Audit and other Road Safety related aspects’ in 
collaboration with the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. 

106 
 
 
II. SaveLIFE Foundation 
(i) About SaveLIFE Foundation  : CEO, SaveLIFE Foundation (SLF), briefed the Committee 
about his NGO stating that it is a part of the technical drafting team for the Motor Vehicles 
Amendment Act, 2019 and that SaveLIFE is best known for its contribution to establishing the 
Good Samaritan law in the country. He stated that SLF is also advising the Supreme Court 
Committee on Road Safety on various facets of Section 136A which pertain to the enf orcement 
of traffic laws. He further stated that SLF also works at grass -root levels through Zero Fatality 
Corridors and Zero Fatality Districts programmes. He informed that currently, SLF is in the 
process of scaling the Zero Fatality Corridor and Zero Fa tality District work to a hundred 
Highways and hundred districts across the country in close partnership with the Government of 
India. He, further, informed that through the 'Crash Vulnerability Audits' programme, his team 
goes to various Highways across t he country to study exactly what is happening as far as safety 
elements are concerned, especially, service roads because service roads connecting to main 
carriageways are often major points where incidents or road crashes take place. 
(ii). Issues pertainin g to service roads:  CEO apprised the Committee about some issues 
pertaining to service roads such as discontinuous service roads, encroachments on service roads, 
inadequate treatment of gaps present in service roads, pedestrian challenges on service roads, and 
absence of pedestrian guardrails. He informed the Committee that the majority of deaths were 
happening not on the main highway but on the service roads alongside the highway. Thereby 
emphasizing that a significant amount of safety work needed to be ca rried out on service roads. 
SLF has also submitted a detailed report along with recommendations on ROBs, RUBs, and 
Service Roads. He also apprised in detail about the advocacy methodology adopted by them.   
With reference to engagement with communities, he informed that SLF carries out both informal 
and formal consultative processes with the local community to understand their views and, most 
importantly, also get them to buy into the changes that are being recommended. 
(iii).      Experience in ROBs/RUBs: President, SaveLIFE Foundation (SLF) submitted that SLF 
has a very limited experience in railway over -bridges and under -bridges. He raised the issue of 
lane drop, which is a significant safety hazard.   He also informed about the lack of illumination, 
the in sufficient height of crash barriers, the lack of pedestrian and cyclist facilities, and 
inadequate treatment of merging and diverging points as significant issues. He further informed 

107 
 
the Committee that SLF conducted a survey in September 2022 in Tamil Nad u, where there was 
a challenge of merging and demerging points which were leading to crashes, and fatalities on 
these routes. In this regard, SLF sent detailed recommendations to the Ministry of Road 
Transport and Highways, which were taken well into action. 
(iii).      Need for peripheral roads near villages on both sides for crossing the road: A Member 
drew attention to the road from Kota to Shivpuri, passing through Bara, which has Villages on 
both sides, and raised the issue of how villagers and animals are supposed to cross the roads. The 
Member emphasized the need to give peripheral roads near villages on both sides for crossing 
the road. In response, Chief Scientist & Head, CRRI informed that Indian Roads Congress has 
come out with the specific stipul ation that for any concession -driven project or EPC -driven 
project, it is necessary to have a service road either in the form of a vehicle underpass or a 
pedestrian underpass if a lesser number of people is going to cross it. If a lot of agriculture -
related movement is there, even a cattle underpass has to be provided. He stated that such issues 
are ignored by the concessionaire or EPC people. The Member also raised the issue of providing 
health and medical facilities on these roads and the use of helicopte rs for picking up people from 
crash sites. He also emphasized the need for education programmes for lorry drivers. 
(iv). Submission by TRAX:  President, TRAX informed that currently the road is acquired from 
the States and converted from two -lanes to four -lanes and making it a highway. However, the 
edge of the road is not defined.  So, there is trespassing from every place.  He, further, suggested 
that until there is provision for the cattle, etc., that road must not be announced as a National 
Highway.  A Member suggested that this was only possible by opening Greenfield expressways. 
He added that nothing has been done in this direction yet. He, f urther, enquired whether there is 
any country that has de -tagged the national highway to a street road or city road.   President, 
TRAX assured that they will submit the report on that. Another Member raised an issue about 
the large number of trucks at Moren a section of the toll and asked about the future planning of 
CRRI vis-à-vis tags and making the place more user-friendly.   
Submission by CRRI:  Director, CRRI replied that at present, there is no area licensing system. 
He cited the example of London having  a green tax that had to be paid if one was entering the 
city center.   In India, cities have pretty free entry and one does not have many restrictions.   
Specific to trucks, good highway -side amenities like developing truck terminals on the side of 
national highways can address these concerns.   Trucks can be easily parked there and the rest 
area can have fuel stations, toilets, etc.  

108 
 
(iv). Sending alerts to the driver on being sleepy:   A member also raised a query on sending 
alerts to the driver on being sle epy. Director, CRRI informed that rumble strips are there.   That 
provision is there in some places.   So, if the driver is sleepy, then an advanced driver assistance 
system is now going to be useful.  He informed about the iRASTE Telangana project where the y 
are trying to fit such devices which observe the blinking of the eyes of the bus drivers, especially 
the roads on which the buses are plying. CEO, SLF informed that as part of their current 
standards, there is a practice called Raised Profile Edge which is supposed to be on the edge of 
the road and is supposed to create a rumbling sound when a driver is departing that lane.   He 
added that this is a fairly recent inclusion in the road standards in the Maharashtra region. He 
also informed SLF has made a rec ommendation last year that fatigue detection devices and 
warning systems should be installed as a mandatory feature, just like a seat belt in every vehicle.  
(v). IRC Guidelines:     CEO, SLF concluded by saying that the majority of standards already 
exist within IRC.  The only need is to follow the IRC guidelines. He further, stated that Section 
198A of the Motor Vehicle (Amendment) Act, 2019 has been designed to hold road contractors 
and engineers accountable for faulty construction, faulty design, and fa ulty maintenance.   In 
order for that to be implemented, comprehensive rules under Section 210D of the Motor Vehicle 
(Amendment) Act have to be created by States. Rule 166 which the Union has to work on, 
pertains to roads owned by the unions, like National Highways and other MoRTH roads. He 
recommended starting enforcing Section 198A against shoddy construction maintenance and 
building of roads overall. He also informed that Section 135 of the Motor Vehicle Amendment 
Act calls for forensic investigation of c rashes which goes beyond the traditional notion of driver 
error being the sole responsible for a crash. It looks at the overall environment in which the crash 
happened. To realize such action, States need to create rules under Section 135. 
III. TRAX       
(i) Brief description of the organization:  Secretary, TRAX Society gave a brief description of 
their organization and their work. She also informed that TRAX is attached with members of 
different District and State Road Safety Committees. A Member interven ed and stated that the 
definition of the District Road Safety Committee must be defined and put in black and white. 
Secretary, TRAX, thereafter, proceeded to inform that it has worked at black spots regions like 
Hero Honda Chowk and Rajiv Chowk in Gurugram ; Ajmer Gate intersection; Surajkund, Pali, 
Trijunction. She also informed that TRAX has been a flag bearer for standard helmet advocacy 
as there are fake or non-standardized helmets available in the market. President, TRAX informed 

109 
 
that Hero Honda Chowk h as been converted into a zero -death intersection.  Only one death took 
place during the last one -and-a-half year.  With reference to junction design, he suggested that 
there should be a pedestrian facility, and there should be halt and go space because thi s is a basic 
need of any crossing. He stated that NHAI provides 4 -5-6 lane space under the flyovers which 
provokes the people for rash driving. At Hero Honda Chowk, TRAX reduced the number of 
lanes by one and converted that into a pedestrian path.   Now it has been converted into three 
lanes from four. Further, the islands have been covered almost everywhere in India by fencing or 
by doing vegetation on them. The main function of these islands is the servicing of pedestrians. 
(ii).      Construction of the service road: Secretary, TRAX recommended that there must be a 
single or intermediate lane for entry as there were faulty exits everywhere.   Hae added that 
although the code from the IRC was there, it is hardly followed on our highways in giving proper 
entries or exits. In the case of slip lanes also, he recommended that the IRC code must be made 
mandatory for all existing and new roads. He also suggested that there should be some penal 
provisions if authorities are not working as per the IRC codes.   With reference to lane marking, 
he stated that in almost 80 per cent of cases, lane marking is faulty, especially at exit and entry 
points. A Member, citing Right of Way, stated that it does not allow for constructing an extra 
lane.  If there are four lanes for exiting the highway, you need a fifth lane also now, which 
becomes a problem as space is not available there. The Member also enquired from the NGOs 
whether their recommendations are being implemented on the new highway s, the Greenfield 
Expressways. He emp hasized on the accountability of Concessionaires and Ministry of Road 
Transport and Highways officers to check quarterly.   He also stated that if we are constructing a 
national highway, four lanes or six lanes,  the same has to be raised. 
(iii)(a) Merging Traffic/Plantation issue: President, TRAX, informed that the entry and exit from 
Sohna is the worst example of merging of traffic in the case of the Delhi -Mumbai Expressway. 
He submitted that in six -lane roads, they have started eight -lane expressways, whi ch means 
including shoulder area, there are now five lanes.   From one lane, five lanes are opening, and 
from five lanes, only one lane is coming on the existing road.   This is the cause of accidents 
because high-speeding traffic is moving and merging with the local traffic from five lanes to one 
lane only. He further stated that lane markings are also missing. A Member added that some 200 
or 300 meters before the exit, an extra lane must be there. President, TRAX, compared the road 
structure in India and ab road, citing a focus on lane marking and space management. He also 
emphasized on dust pollution, and higher chances of accidents due to vegetation on dividers, at 

110 
 
the side of the roads as it reduces visibility. At the median, they are reducing it by 50 per  cent 
first, and then if service lanes are there or if an exit or entry is there, again, they are reducing it 
by 50 per cent.  So, visibility is happening to just 20 per cent or 30 per cent on our roads. 
(b).       A Member countered whether the organizati on has done any survey or research on his 
remark.  President, TRAX   replied that it is in the IRC codes itself. Chief Scientist & Head, 
CRRI clarified that in the median, the height of the plantation should not be more than 1.5 
metres, however, he said tha t there is no such guideline for the sides of the road. He also 
submitted that whenever a median opening is there, in a minimum of hundred metres, there 
should not be any vegetation. He stated that the clear zone should be two or three metres; a 
minimum of  three metres to five metres after the shoulder, which becomes a total of seven 
metres. The Member, further, enquired whether full -grown trees should be planted on the roads 
in the context of accidents taking place. Director, CRRI informed that a study was  done by the 
Ministry of Environment, Forests, and Climate Change, and it recommended having a plantation 
while developing   National Highways when trees are cut, and also due to vehicular emissions.   
So, to balance carbon emissions, tree planting has been  recommended, at least, for NHAI. The 
Member further enquired whether any such study has been undertaken by CRR. Director 
informed that they have done Road Safety Audit but it is difficult to say whether they have a 
record of accidents because of trees on the part of the cross -section.  Chief Scientist & Head, 
CRRI also raised the issue of overloaded vehicles being toppled by the wind. A Member asked 
whether any scientific study has been done in this regard. Director, CRRI informed they do not 
have a docume nted study.   CRRI would do it scientifically and look at the accident data they 
have. 
(c).      Chairman pointed out the contradiction on the plantation issue between the Department of 
Highways and CRRI.  He stated that one reason given by the Department o f Highways is that it 
is better to have plantations in the median so that the reflection of lights at night could be 
prevented. Whereas, Chief Scientist, CRRI has stated that the height of 1.5 metres is good for an 
anti-glare effect. Nowadays if the median  width is around five metres or six metres, even if a 
vehicle is moving on the left side of the carriageway, because of a mistake, he may run off to the 
other side.   If the plantation is very high, there could be a vehicle coming from the other 
direction w hich could get hit.   That is why the median plantation height of 1.5 metres would 
facilitate things. 

111 
 
(iv).      Effect of glare of lighting on vehicular traffic: A Member also raised the query on  the 
effect glare of lighting has on vehicular traffic. Direc tor, CRRI stated that glare is a very 
important problem.  There are certain solutions like Plantation. Then, there are anti -glare devices 
on National Highway-3, between Agra and Gwalior.   There are other devices like pre -fabricated 
panels, aluminum panels, etc, which can also be adopted. Further, Glare cutting is possible to be 
installed in front of the driver. President, TRAX informed that Entry and exit are problems 
everywhere.  Otherwise, there is no jam.  He also explained how this could impact the movement 
as at the same time, there is a median opening also.   From the extreme top service lane, one can 
come out from the extreme down service lane also
